title: Workspaces
text:
What Workspaces Are For

A workspace is where you do your research: data collections, cohorts, datasets, notebooks, apps, and files for one project
Have more than one (e.g., one per project or per tier)
Shareable with collaborators
Billed individually through the workspace’s pod, so set up billing first

title: Workspaces
text:
Sharing a Workspace
Only Owners can share. In the workspace, click Share (top right), then:

Enter your collaborator’s email: the one linked to their Workbench account
Choose their role: Owner, Writer, or Reader


They must already have a Workbench account. You can’t invite someone who hasn’t registered yet.
They get access to the resources you created in the workspace (buckets, datasets), at their role’s level
References to outside data are not shared automatically. The data’s owner has to grant access.
With a group policy, only group members can open it. You won’t be warned if you share with someone outside the group.







TipInstructor tip





For All of Us workspaces, collaborators also need their own All of Us data access (Registered or Controlled Tier) to see the data collection. Verily recommends sharing with Workbench groups rather than individuals for larger teams; that’s beyond what students need here.

title: Storage & Costs
section: Snippets Are Gone: Use Your Bucket Folder
text:
Snippets Are Gone: Use Your Bucket Folder
Classic Workbench: copy files to and from the workspace bucket with code snippets (e.g., copy_file_from_workspace_bucket.R) that ran gsutil
Workbench 2.0: no Snippets menu. Your buckets are automatically mounted as folders in every app:
/home/jupyter/workspace/<bucket name>/     standard apps (JupyterLab, R, SAS)
/home/dataproc/workspace/<bucket name>/    Spark (Dataproc) apps
So you save and read files with regular R or Python functions, as if the bucket were a local folder. (No bucket yet? See New Cloud Storage Bucket.)

Your own buckets: read and write
References, including data collection buckets (e.g., v9-genomics-folder): read-only. Don’t save outputs there.







TipInstructor tip





If you put a resource inside a folder on the Resources tab, the folder becomes part of the path (use quotes if the folder name has spaces). Mounts don’t update on their own: a bucket you add (or rename) after the app starts won’t show up until you restart the app or run wb resource mount (or wb resource mount –id= for one). A folder ending in _NO_ACCESS, _NOT_FOUND, or _MOUNT_FAILED means that mount failed. Duplicated workspaces keep their mounts. Source: Verily, “Access workspace files and folders”.

title: Storage & Costs
text:
Saving and Reading Files
R
bucket <- file.path(Sys.getenv("HOME"), "workspace", "workspace-bucket")

readr::write_csv(clean_df, file.path(bucket, "clean_data.csv"))   # save
clean_df <- readr::read_csv(file.path(bucket, "clean_data.csv"))  # read
Python
import os, pandas as pd
bucket = os.path.expanduser("~/workspace/workspace-bucket")

clean_df.to_csv(f"{bucket}/clean_data.csv", index=False)   # save
clean_df = pd.read_csv(f"{bucket}/clean_data.csv")         # read






TipInstructor tip





Replace workspace-bucket with your bucket’s name as shown in the Resources tab. HOME / ~ points to /home/jupyter or /home/dataproc depending on the app, so this code works in both. The folder tree under ~/workspace matches the folders in the Resources tab. Apps use a standard disk, so files saved anywhere else on the app (e.g., the home directory) are lost if the app crashes or is deleted.

title: Storage & Costs
text:
Workspace Variables
Some settings are already defined in every app. Others you define yourself.








Variable
Set for you?
What it is




GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT (also GOOGLE_PROJECT)
✅
Your workspace’s Google Cloud project; BigQuery bills queries to it


PET_SA_EMAIL
✅
Your workspace service account (used by dsub)


WORKSPACE_BUCKET
❌
Classic Workbench only. Use your bucket’s folder instead.


WORKSPACE_CDR
❌
Classic Workbench only. Define the dataset path yourself.


EXPORT_BUCKET
❌
Used by Data Explorer’s exported notebooks. Set it yourself.



project <- Sys.getenv("GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT")                              # set for you
bucket  <- file.path(Sys.getenv("HOME"), "workspace", "workspace-bucket")  # your bucket
CURRENT_DATASET <- "wb-silky-artichoke-2408.C2025Q4R6"   # CDR v9 (not from a Data Explorer query: those use v8)






TipInstructor tip





Checked in a new Workbench 2.0 workspace with env | grep -E ‘WORKSPACE|GOOGLE|PET_SA’. The tutorial workspaces define WORKSPACE_BUCKET and WORKSPACE_CDR in their setup scripts, so code copied from classic Workbench notebooks will find them empty (““) elsewhere. The CDR dataset path is in the queries Data Explorer generates (the FROM clause), and in the data collection’s BigQuery resources on the Resources tab.

title: Storage & Costs
text:
Storage

Workspace bucket: shared, permanent, and the cheapest option for long-term storage. Recommended. (You create it; see New Cloud Storage Bucket.)
App disk: attached to an app. Charged until the app is deleted, even when stopped. Files on it survive Stop but are lost on Delete.







TipInstructor tip





See What is an app? and Reading the cost estimate on the Apps page.

title: Storage & Costs
text:
Saving Money

Save your data to workspace storage
Stop or delete apps you aren’t using; keep autostop on
Your notebooks and data in workspace storage stay intact
Start a new app any time to pick up where you left off
Delete workspaces you no longer need

⚠️ Deleting a workspace permanently deletes everything created in it, including your bucket and its files. It can’t be undone. Copy anything you need first.






TipInstructor tip





Only Owners can delete a workspace. References (e.g., the All of Us data collection) are only pointers, so the underlying data isn’t affected.

title: Overview and Resources Tabs
text:
Overview Tab














The first thing you see when you open a workspace
Shows the description: what the project is about, e.g., its scientific questions, approaches, and anticipated findings
Helps collaborators (and you, later) understand the workspace at a glance

To update it: click Edit description, make your changes, and save. Update it as your project changes.
⚠️ The description is publicly accessible, so keep it accurate and leave out sensitive details.








TipInstructor tip





Good practice: keep the description in sync with your Research Use Statement answers, which are also public.

title: Overview and Resources Tabs
text:
Resources Tab










Where your workspace’s data and storage live:

Data collections you’ve added (e.g., the All of Us Controlled Tier resources)
Buckets you create to save files
Other cloud resources

Add more with + New resource or + Data from catalog








TipInstructor tip





More detail on each resource type is below.

title: Overview and Resources Tabs
text:
Adding New Resources
Resources tab → + New resource opens a menu of resource types:














Create new (folder, bucket, BigQuery dataset, cohort)

Lives in your workspace, shared with collaborators
Deleted if the workspace is deleted



Reference existing (bucket, object, BigQuery dataset or table)

A pointer to data that lives elsewhere; nothing is copied
Access is managed by the data’s owner









TipInstructor tip





Verily calls these “controlled” and “referenced” resources. The data collection resources you added from the catalog are referenced resources too.

title: Overview and Resources Tabs
text:
Which Resource Do I Need?








Resource
What it is
Use it when you want to…




Folder
A label for grouping resources on the Resources tab
Keep a busy workspace organized (e.g., Data, Results)


Cloud Storage bucket
Your own storage for files
Save CSVs, notebooks, plots, and cleaned data so they outlast your app


BigQuery dataset
Your own database for tables
Save large query results as tables you can query again with SQL


Reference a bucket, object, dataset, or table
A pointer to data that lives elsewhere
Use data you already have access to without copying it



👉 Most students need just one bucket. The others are optional.






TipInstructor tip





New Cohort is covered on the Data Explorer page.

title: Overview and Resources Tabs
text:
Buckets, Objects, Datasets, and Tables


Cloud Storage: files
bucket      my-workspace-bucket
└── object  data/results.csv

A bucket is a container; an object is one file in it
Address: gs://my-workspace-bucket/data/results.csv
Folders aren’t real: data/ is just the start of the file’s name, so an empty folder disappears



BigQuery: tables
project         wb-silky-artichoke-2408
└── dataset     C2025Q4R6
    └── table   person

A dataset is a collection of tables; a table has rows and columns
Address: project.dataset.table, used in SQL after FROM
You pay for the data a query reads, so select only the columns you need



👉 All of Us data uses both: tables in BigQuery (EHR, surveys, measurements) and files in a bucket (genomic and multi-omics data).






TipInstructor tip





Example: the Controlled Tier v9 tables are the dataset C2025Q4R6, which the notebooks call CURRENT_DATASET; the genomic files are objects in the vwb-aou-datasets-controlled bucket, mounted in apps under ~/workspace/. The Workbench and the Google Cloud console show object names containing “/” as folders to make browsing easier. Don’t confuse these with the Workbench’s New Folder resource (next section): that is only a label for grouping resources on the Resources tab, and its dialog says “Folders don’t affect cloud paths”.

title: Overview and Resources Tabs
text:
New Folder










Why: organize resources on the Resources tab, your way

Folder name (required)
Folder path: where the folder goes; the workspace itself by default
Description (optional)

Click Create folder
To put an existing resource in a folder: select it → Move (in its details pane)
Folders don’t change a resource’s cloud path (gs://…), but they do appear in the app’s mounted path: ~/workspace/<folder>/<bucket>








TipInstructor tip





Avoid spaces in folder names: they have to be quoted in file paths in code.

title: Overview and Resources Tabs
text:
New Cloud Storage Bucket










Why: new workspaces have no bucket, and you need one to save your work

Resource ID: the name inside Workbench (letters, numbers, -, _). The tutorials use workspace-bucket.
Folder path and Description
Bucket name: the name in Google Cloud. It must be globally unique, so keep the generated one: your Resource ID + the workspace’s project ID (↻ makes a new one).

Click Create bucket. You can use it right away; collaborators may wait up to 15 min.








TipInstructor tip





Controlled resources like this bucket are shared with workspace collaborators and deleted when the workspace is deleted. Apps that were already running won’t see a new bucket until you restart the app or run wb resource mount. Mounted folders cache file info for about a minute, so two people writing at once may not see each other’s changes right away. Migrated 1.0 workspaces already have a bucket: rw-migration-aou-rw-…

title: Overview and Resources Tabs
text:
Bucket Names: Good Practice

Lowercase letters, numbers, -, _, 3–63 characters, no spaces, no “google”
Bucket names are public: anyone can check whether a name exists

⚠️ No names, emails, NetIDs, or project details

A bucket name can’t be changed (the resource’s name and description can). To rename, create a new bucket and copy the files over.
Deleting a bucket frees its name for anyone to reuse

👉 Easiest: accept the generated name. It’s built from your Resource ID + the workspace’s project ID, so keep the Resource ID free of personal details too.






TipInstructor tip





Source: Google Cloud, “About Cloud Storage buckets” and “Create a bucket”. Files (objects) also can’t be renamed in place; renaming copies and deletes them. Avoid putting sensitive information in file names too.

title: Overview and Resources Tabs
text:
New BigQuery Dataset










Why: save large query results as tables, then query them again with SQL instead of re-running long queries or loading big CSVs

Resource ID, Folder path, Description
Dataset ID: the name in Google Cloud. Unique within your project; letters, numbers, _ only. Keep the generated one or choose your own. Can’t be changed later.

Click Create dataset. Collaborators may wait up to 15 min.








TipInstructor tip





Optional for most class projects; a bucket with CSV files is usually enough. BigQuery storage and queries are billed to your pod.

title: Overview and Resources Tabs
text:
Referencing Existing Data
A reference points to data that already exists elsewhere. Nothing is copied.







Reference
You’ll need




Cloud Storage bucket
The bucket name


Cloud Storage object (one file)
Its URL, e.g., gs://bucket-name/path/file.csv


BigQuery dataset
Project ID + Dataset ID


BigQuery table
Project ID + Dataset ID + Table ID



Every reference also has a Resource ID, Folder path, and Description. Then click Add to resources.
⚠️ Access isn’t shared automatically. The data’s owner controls it. In a Controlled Tier workspace, the perimeter may also block data from outside it.






TipInstructor tip





Example uses: point to a collaborator’s bucket, or to a shared file without copying it. The All of Us data collection resources you added earlier are references too. Deleting a reference removes the pointer, not the data. You can edit a reference’s name and description, but not the bucket name, project ID, dataset ID, or table ID; to fix those, delete the reference and add it again. Some outside buckets are “Requester Pays”: reading or browsing them is billed to your pod, and mounting them when an app starts can cost money too. The Workbench shows a warning when you add one.

title: Overview and Resources Tabs
text:
Getting and Reusing Data
Someone else’s data. A gs:// address says where data is, not that you may read it. The owner has to give you access:

Share the workspace (the expected route for All of Us data): the owner clicks Share and adds you as Reader or Writer. You get the buckets and datasets they created there, and you need your own All of Us access at the same tier.
A bucket outside a shared workspace: the owner grants your account access, then you add a reference to it.
References inside a shared workspace aren’t passed on: the original data’s owner has to grant access separately.

Your own data from another workspace: add a reference to that workspace’s bucket or dataset. Limits:

⚠️ Controlled Tier data, or anything made from it, can’t go to a Registered Tier workspace or outside the perimeter
⚠️ Person IDs changed between v8 and v9: files saved from v8 (or the classic Workbench) can’t be joined to v9 data
⚠️ Each workspace is one project with its own Research Use Statement: check with All of Us support before reusing participant-level results in another project







TipInstructor tip





To confirm before teaching: the exact Verily steps for granting someone access to a single bucket (Verily resource settings or Google Cloud permissions), and All of Us’s rule on reusing participant-level results across projects. Between two of your Controlled Tier workspaces, references should work, but the perimeter is enforced per workspace, so test with a small file first. For classes, rerunning the queries in each workspace is simplest. Source for the v8 to v9 ID change: CDR v9 release, All of Us Office Hours, 2026-07-24.

section: Viewing Your Bucket in Google Cloud
text:
Viewing Your Bucket in Google Cloud






















In your workspace, find Workspace details (right side) and click the Google Project link
The Google Cloud console opens: menu → Cloud Storage → Buckets
Click the bucket your files are in

The details panel also shows the workspace ID, default region, pod, and UUID.

title: Overview and Resources Tabs
text:
What You Can See (and Can’t)








✅ You can see folder and file names, sizes, and types, e.g., notebooks/, data/, and the bq_exports/ folder from a data snapshot


❌ You can’t open or download the files. The perimeter blocks it. Open them from an app in the workspace instead.


👉 Handy for checking that an export arrived, or finding a file’s path
🔒 The perimeter also means: you can’t reach the data from your own computer, even with the command-line tools (wb, gcloud, bq): work in an app. And downloading a file from an app to your computer is logged (egress logs). Large transfers can trigger alerts, an app shutdown, or suspended access. Keep data in the Workbench.






TipInstructor tip





This bucket (rw-migration-aou-rw-…) is the migration bucket of a workspace moved from the classic Workbench. The .Trash-1000 and .Trash-1001 folders are most likely JupyterLab’s trash for files deleted from the mounted bucket; they still take up storage until emptied. Bucket resources on the Resources tab also have a Browse button (seen on the vwb-aou-datasets-controlled-v9 bucket). Verily notes that in perimeter workspaces browsing only works if the perimeter administrator has enabled it; this training uses the Google Cloud console route instead.

title: Apps
text: Apps are where you run your analysis: JupyterLab, R, SAS, and more. This page walks through creating an AoU Jupyter app.

title: Apps
text:
The Apps tab











What’s here:

Your apps: the analysis environments in this workspace, with their status (Running, Stopped…)
Git repositories: code linked to the workspace (see Optional Extras)



To start an app: click + New app instance, then:

Select app
Choose config
Compute options
Review details → Create app









TipInstructor tip





You need Writer or Owner access to create apps. Our example uses AoU Jupyter.

Default configuration (AoU Jupyter):

Machine n1-highmem-4: 4 CPUs, 26 GB memory
500 GB data disk

Cost estimate panel:

Cost while running: $0.27/hour, or $194.32/month if left on 24/7
Disk cost (continuous): $21.60/month, even when stopped
How do we calculate? and GCP’s pricing calculator links

Click Next

Saved configurations you or a collaborator created also appear here as options. Prices are estimates and vary by region.




Reading the cost estimate
Example: default AoU Jupyter, used 20 hours in a month

title: Apps
text:
Step 3: Compute options




















Location: keep Region (recommended). It picks a zone with free capacity for you. The region comes from the workspace.
General or GPUs: General is fine for most analysis. GPUs cost much more and can’t be added later.
Machine type: CPUs + memory. More is faster but costs more; the estimate updates as you change it.
Scroll down for data disk size (50 GB–64 TB; default 500 GB) and autostop (default 4 hours idle)

Click Next








TipInstructor tip





Leave “Use a specific reservation” unchecked; it’s for reserved cloud capacity. This training workspace was created in us-central1, so that’s the region shown. You can change the machine type and disk later, but only while the app is stopped.

title: Apps
text:
Step 4: Review details














Config: shows Custom if you changed anything in step 3
Workbench ID: the app’s name in Workbench and the CLI (letters, numbers, -, _)
Instance name: the cloud machine’s name (lowercase, numbers, -). Can’t be changed later.
Description (optional)

Click Create app. The status goes Creating → Provisioning → Starting → Running. Then click the app’s name to open it.

title: Apps
text:
Managing your app
On the Apps tab:







Action
What happens




Open
Click the app’s name (when it’s Running)


Stop
Stops it right away, with no confirmation. Computing charges stop; disk charges continue.


Start
Restarts a stopped app in about a minute


Edit
Name, description, and autostop: any time. Machine type and disk: only when stopped.


Delete
Removes the app and its disk. ⚠️ Anything not saved in a bucket is lost.









TipInstructor tip





You can’t change an app’s image (app type) or instance name; create a new app instead. Apps that are Starting or Stopping can’t be changed until they finish. If someone loses Writer access to the workspace, their apps are stopped (“abandoned”); an Owner can restore the access or delete the app.

title: What’s New in Workbench 2.0
text:
What Is Verily Workbench?
A secure research environment for governing and analyzing biomedical data, built on Verily’s experience supporting All of Us







What it does
Where you’ll see it today




Organizes data of many types: clinical, omics, imaging
Data collections and the Resources tab


Explores data without code: point-and-click cohorts with visualizations
Data Explorer


Analyzes at scale with cloud computing
Apps (JupyterLab, R, SAS, Spark) and Workflows


Governs and secures data
Policies, perimeters, and group policies


Supports secure collaboration
Sharing roles: Owner, Writer, Reader


Offers interfaces for every skill level
Web interface, Data Explorer, command line (wb), cloud console









TipInstructor tip





Source: Verily, “Verily Workbench overview” (support.workbench.verily.com/docs/getting_started/overview/). Data types it supports include omics (BAM, CRAM, VCF), clinical (CSV/TSV, PDF, OMOP, CDISC), and imaging (DICOM, JPG). Compliance: ISO 27001/SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA. An activity monitor tracks data access and lineage. Policies can limit access by group membership and geography, and perimeters prevent data from being moved out.

text: The Home Page

title: Getting Access
text:
Getting Around


Left sidebar

Home: recent workspaces and data collections, plus running apps
Exchange: the data catalog for browsing data collections
Workspaces: your workspaces
Data collections: collections you have access to
Pods: billing (see Billing)
Support hub: help and documentation



Home page

+ New workspace
Running apps: check here so you don’t pay for apps you forgot to stop!
Tutorial workspace: Getting Started with Controlled Tier Data (v9), a good place to start
Did you know? Policies can’t be removed once applied









TipInstructor tip





Admin → Organizations shows the organization your account belongs to: for All of Us users, “aou-prod” (the All of Us production organization), with its terms of service and activity logs. Nothing to change there.

title: Workflows for Beginners
text: New to workflows? This page explains what they are, why researchers use them, and the ideas you’ll meet in the class Running Workflows. You don’t need to read it all at once, and you don’t need to know any of it to use the All of Us data: most projects never need a workflow.

title: Workflows for Beginners
section: The big picture: one oven, or a kitchen for hire
text:
The big picture: one oven, or a kitchen for hire
Imagine you have to bake 22 cakes, each from its own bag of ingredients.









Baking at home (your app)
Hiring a kitchen (a workflow)




Ovens
one, so one cake after another
one per cake, all baking at once


Size
your oven, whatever the cake
a big oven for the big cakes, a small one for the small ones


You
stay home until the last cake is done
send the order, and come back when it’s ready


Paying
for your kitchen, all day
for each oven only while it bakes



In workflow words:








In the kitchen
In a workflow
In the class




the recipe
the script: the commands to run
gwas_one_chr.sh


the ingredients
the inputs: files copied onto each machine
the ClinVar files for one chromosome, and our sample


a kitchen kit with every tool already in it
the image (container): the software, already installed
PLINK 2


the ovens
the machines (virtual machines in the cloud)
22 n2-standard-2 machines


the order ticket that lists every cake
the tasks file, or the workflow file
gwas_tasks.tsv


the head chef who hands out the work
the workflow engine: dsub, Cromwell, or Nextflow
dsub


the counter where finished cakes go
your bucket
data/workflows/


the kitchen’s notes on each cake
the logs
data/workflows/logs/

title: Workflows for Beginners
text:
Why researchers use workflows








Reason
What it means
Example




⏱️ Speed
many machines work in parallel
22 chromosomes in the time of the slowest one, instead of the sum of all 22


📈 Scale
each task gets a machine as big as it needs, far bigger than a laptop or an app
32 CPUs and 400 GB of disk for one chromosome of the full genome data


🔁 Reproducibility
the workflow file records every step, the software versions, and the settings. Rerun it next year and get the same results
a reviewer asks you to rerun with a different filter: change one line, run again


🤝 Sharing
a colleague runs your workflow on their data, or you run a published one
the GATK pipelines for finding variants; the nf-core pipelines for RNA-seq


🛟 Recovery
if one task fails, rerun only that task. Cromwell and Nextflow can resume a pipeline where it stopped
a machine is stopped after 3 hours: only its task starts again


💤 Hands-off
jobs run without you, even with your app stopped
launch before you go home; results in the morning


💰 Cost control
you pay for each machine only while it works, and can use cheap spot machines
(see Is it cheaper? below)




Why in All of Us in particular

The data is big. All of Us has hundreds of thousands of whole genomes. One chromosome of the main genome callset (ACAF) is tens to hundreds of GB; in the All of Us tutorial, just copying one onto a machine took an hour. An app can’t hold the whole genome at once.
The data can’t leave. At most universities, big jobs go to the university’s computing cluster. All of Us data must stay in the Workbench, so you can’t take it to a cluster (at Yale: the Center for Research Computing’s clusters). Workflows are how you get a cluster’s power inside the Workbench.
Apps are one machine. A bigger app costs more every hour it’s on, including while you read, write, or wait. Workflows use big machines only for the minutes they’re needed.
Publishing. Journals and reviewers increasingly ask for reproducible code. A workflow file in GitHub, with pinned versions, is exactly that, and it contains no data.



When not to use a workflow

Exploring the data, trying ideas, making plots: use the app.
Small data, or steps that take minutes: starting machines and copying files would take longer than the work.
BigQuery work (most of the core, survey, and wearables classes): BigQuery already runs in parallel on Google’s machines. You don’t need a workflow for SQL.
Steps you haven’t tested yet: get them working in the app first.

👉 Rule of thumb: if you’d run the same step on many files (or one very big one), and it already works in your app, consider a workflow.

title: Workflows for Beginners
text:
Is it cheaper?
Often faster; cheaper only sometimes. The total computing is about the same: 22 machines for 15 minutes cost about as much as 1 machine for 5½ hours.







A workflow saves money when…
A workflow costs more when…




the alternative is a big app running for hours (including while you wait, or forget to stop it)
the job is small: each machine takes a few minutes to start and copy its files, and that time is billed too


steps need different sizes: each task gets the machine it needs
every task copies the same big files


you use spot machines: much cheaper, and the engine restarts a task if Google stops its machine
a mistake runs in every task: 22 tasks, 22 times the cost. Test in the app first


you stop the app while the jobs run




In the class, the 22 tasks added up to about 2 hours of machine time (on SSD disks) but ran at the same time; the job cost well under $1.
Job machines and storage are billed to your workspace’s pod, like apps. They don’t appear in the app’s cost estimate, so estimate them yourself: machine price per hour × hours × number of tasks.

title: Workflows for Beginners
text:
Common workflow patterns

Scatter–gather: split, run in parallel, combine
The most common pattern, and the one in the class: scatter one job into many tasks, then gather the results.
                ┌─► chr1  ─┐
one analysis ───┼─► chr2  ─┼───► one table of results
  (scatter)     ├─► ...   ─┤        (gather)
                └─► chr22 ─┘
You can split by chromosome or region (genomics), by sample or person (sequencing data, images), by batch of files, or by setting (the same model with different parameters).


A pipeline: steps in order
Each step uses the outputs of the one before. Each step can scatter too.
raw files ──► quality control ──► analysis ──► summary and plots
dsub runs one step per job, so you’d run (and check) each step yourself. Cromwell and Nextflow run the whole chain, in the right order, and start each step as soon as its inputs are ready.


What researchers run as workflows







Field
Typical workflow




Genomics
GWAS by chromosome (as in the class); finding variants in each person’s sequence (CRAM → VCF); annotating or filtering variant files; polygenic scores


RNA-seq
from raw reads to counts, one task per sample (e.g. the nf-core rnaseq pipeline)


Imaging
processing each scan the same way


Text
running a language model over many documents


Wearables
summarizing minute-level data, one batch of people per task


Statistics
simulations, bootstraps, permutation tests: thousands of independent runs


Machine learning
trying many model settings at once

title: Workflows for Beginners
text:
The ideas behind them

Containers and images: the kitchen kit
An image is a packaged computer system with the software already installed: PLINK, R and its packages, Python, and so on. A container is a copy of the image, running. Every task runs inside one, so:

the software is the same on every machine, today and next year
you don’t install anything on the machines
others can rerun your work with the exact same software

Images live in registries (e.g. Docker Hub, Google’s Artifact Registry) and have tags, which name a version: plink2:alpha2.3_jan2020. Two rules:

Pin the version. A tag like latest changes when a new version comes out, and your results (or your job) can change with it. That’s what broke every dsub job in All of Us in November 2026 (see the class).
In All of Us, job machines can’t reach Docker Hub. Use images from Google’s registries, or Docker Hub images through the All of Us mirror.

You don’t need to build images to start: ready-made ones exist for most tools (e.g. the BioContainers project has images for most bioinformatics software).


Inputs and outputs: what the machine can see
Each machine starts empty. It sees only the files you list as inputs: the engine copies them in (localizing) before your script runs, and copies the outputs back to your bucket (delocalizing) afterwards. So:

every file the script uses must be an input (in the class: the .bim and .fam files too, though the script never names them)
copying takes time, and big files take a long time. Some engines can stream files instead of copying them (Nextflow in the Workbench can), which helps when a tool reads only part of a file
the disk matters. Cloud disks come in types: standard (cheap, slow, and slowest when small) and SSD (faster, a bit more per GB). In the class, chromosome 1 (a 27.7 GB file) took 101 minutes on dsub’s default standard disk, and 8 minutes on an SSD (--disk-type pd-ssd). Most of the difference was copying the file: about 8 MB a second onto the standard disk, about 130 onto the SSD



Parallelism and limits
Tasks that don’t depend on each other can run at the same time. But your project has limits (quotas) on how many machines and CPUs run at once. Above the limit, tasks wait in a queue: the job still finishes, just later. A task can also wait when Google has no free machine of the type you asked for: in the class, 21 of 22 tasks finished in under 8 minutes, and one waited 30 minutes for its machine. The job finishes when its slowest task does.


Logs: your first stop
Every task saves a log: the engine’s messages (copying files, starting the script) and everything your script printed. When a task fails, read its log before changing anything. When a task is slow, read its time stamps: they show whether the time went on copying files or on the analysis.


Retries, spot machines, and resuming

Retries: start a failed task again, automatically (--retries in dsub).
Spot machines (preemptible): much cheaper, but Google can stop them at any time. With retries, a stopped task starts again.
Resuming: Cromwell (call caching) and Nextflow (-resume) remember which steps finished, and skip them when you rerun the pipeline.



Reproducibility: write it down
Keep the workflow (script, tasks file, or workflow file) in GitHub, with the image versions pinned. Record the date and the data version (e.g. CDR v9). That’s your methods section, and it contains no data.

title: Workflows for Beginners
text:
The tools in the Workbench




dsub
Cromwell
Nextflow




You write
a shell script and one command
a WDL file, plus a JSON file of inputs
a Nextflow (.nf) file


Think of it as
“run this script on many files”
a pipeline described in a simple language
a pipeline described in a programming language


Best for
one step on many files
multi-step pipelines; many published genomics workflows
multi-step pipelines; the nf-core community pipelines


Run from
an app (terminal or notebook)
the Workflows tab, or an app
the Workflows tab, or an app


Also used at
Google Cloud
Terra (the Broad Institute’s platform), other clouds, clusters
clusters, laptops, every major cloud


Start with
the class Running Workflows
Dockstore for ready-made workflows
nf-core and Nextflow training



👉 Which should I learn? Start with dsub: it’s one command, and it teaches every idea on this page. Move to Nextflow or Cromwell when you need multi-step pipelines, or want to run a published one. Pick the one your field (or your collaborators) uses: much of genomics at the Broad Institute and on Terra uses WDL; nf-core uses Nextflow. What each does best in All of Us, from our tests: Which one should I use?

Outside the Workbench
The same ideas work everywhere, with your own data (not All of Us data):

University clusters (e.g. Yale’s Center for Research Computing) run jobs with a scheduler called Slurm. A Slurm job array (sbatch --array=1-22) is the same idea as dsub’s tasks file.
Nextflow and Snakemake (a Python-based workflow tool, popular in academia) run on laptops, clusters, and clouds with the same workflow file.
Terra runs WDL workflows on Google Cloud, for many large research programs.

So the skills from the class carry over to most research computing.

title: Workflows for Beginners
section: Workflows and the All of Us rules
text:
Workflows and the All of Us rules
Workflows don’t change the rules:







Rule
In a workflow




Data stays in the Workbench
Jobs run in your workspace’s cloud project and private network, and write to your bucket, so the data stays inside


Outputs are All of Us data
Job results and logs are as sensitive as anything else you make from the data. Keep them in your bucket


No individual-level data in logs
Don’t make scripts print rows of data, participant IDs, or dates: logs are saved, and are easy to copy


No counts of 1 to 20 when you share
The same for workflow results: summarize first, then check


Code goes to GitHub, data doesn’t
Scripts and workflow files: yes. Tasks files with participant IDs in them: no


Share notebooks through GitHub, with outputs cleared
Never download a notebook to share it, even one that looks free of data: its outputs leave the Workbench that way, and downloads are monitored

title: Workflows for Beginners
text:
Questions beginners ask
Do I need to know Docker? No. Use ready-made images (the class uses PLINK’s). Learn to build your own later, if you need software that isn’t in any image.
Can a job run R? Yes: use an image with R in it (e.g. one of the rocker images, through the All of Us mirror), and run Rscript my_script.R as the command. Any R packages the script needs must be in the image, or installed by the script.
Can I close my browser, or stop the app, while jobs run? Yes. The jobs run on their own machines, and their results go to your bucket. Check on them later with dstat, or on the Workflows tab for Cromwell and Nextflow. (dsub jobs don’t appear on that tab.)
How do I know what a job cost? There’s no per-job bill. Estimate it: machine price per hour × hours × tasks, plus disks. The class shows how to get each task’s run time.
What if one task out of 22 fails? Read its log, fix the cause, and rerun only that task (in dsub, with the task’s row number after the tasks file).
Can I run a published workflow? Yes. Find it on Dockstore or nf-core and add it on the Workflows tab. Check its images first: in All of Us, they must come from Google’s registries or the mirror.

title: Workflows for Beginners
text:
Words you’ll meet







Word
Means




Workflow (pipeline)
a set of steps, run for you, often on many files at once


Workflow engine
the program that runs it: dsub, Cromwell, Nextflow


Job, task
one launch of a workflow; the separate pieces of work inside it (e.g. one per chromosome)


Machine (virtual machine, VM)
a computer in Google’s cloud, rented by the minute


Image, container
packaged software; a running copy of it


Registry, tag
where images are kept; the name of one version


Mirror
a copy of Docker Hub inside Google Cloud, for All of Us workspaces


Localize, delocalize
copy inputs onto the machine; copy outputs back to the bucket


Scatter, gather
split work into parallel tasks; combine their results


Spot (preemptible)
cheaper machines that Google can stop at any time


Standard disk, SSD
a machine’s disk: cheap and slow, or faster and a bit dearer (--disk-type pd-ssd in dsub)


Quota
the limit on how many machines or CPUs your project can use at once


Google Batch
the Google Cloud service the engines use to run machines


WDL
Workflow Description Language, the language Cromwell runs


Call caching, resume
reusing finished steps when a pipeline is rerun

title: Workflows for Beginners
text:
A learning path

Read this page, then do the class Running Workflows: one script, one job, then 22.
Change the class’s script: a different filter, or a different PLINK command (e.g. allele frequencies of common variants). Test it in the app, then as a job.
Learn a workflow language on your own computer, with public example data: the free Nextflow training, or the WDL documentation.
Run a published workflow from Dockstore or nf-core on the Workflows tab, starting with its small test data.

title: Workflows for Beginners
text:
Further reading

dsub on GitHub: the documentation and examples
Verily Workbench documentation: workflows in the Workbench (Cromwell, Nextflow, dsub)
OpenWDL, Nextflow, and Snakemake documentation
Dockstore and nf-core: published workflows
The All of Us tutorial workspace: How to Use Workflow Tools (dsub, Cromwell, and Nextflow notebooks)
This site: the Workflows tab and the class Running Workflows

title: GitHub Guide
text:
A step-by-step guide for pushing notebooks and scripts from an All of Us workspace on Verily Workbench to GitHub. It covers two cases:
Using an AI assistant to write the code? The class Coding with AI and GitHub shows how to do it safely, with GitHub carrying the code between your computer and the Workbench.
It also covers how to keep All of Us data out of GitHub automatically (safety nets that stop a commit or a merge with outputs or data files), how to protect your account, what to do if something slips through, and a troubleshooting section based on problems we actually ran into.

title: GitHub Guide
text:
⚠️ Read this first: data protection
Everything you push to a public GitHub repo can be seen by anyone, and you can’t fully take it back once it’s pushed.
The All of Us Data and Statistics Dissemination Policy prohibits sharing:

Participant-level data of any kind
Aggregate counts or statistics based on 1–20 participants (this includes notebook outputs, tables, and plots)

Share code, not results. Before every push:

Clear notebook outputs (the command is in the steps below).
Leave out data files (.csv, .tsv, .parquet, .vcf, etc.).
Check for credentials (tokens, keys, passwords).
Run git status and look at every file before committing.

Check the current policy on the All of Us Research Hub if you’re unsure about anything.
A private repo doesn’t make it OK. All of Us data must stay in the Workbench. Pushing it to GitHub moves it out, whether the repo is public or private, and private repos can be made public, forked, or shared later.

What counts as data: the less obvious leaks
Clearing outputs catches most problems. These are the ones people miss:








Where data hides
Example
Instead




Notebook outputs
tables, printed rows, head() and glimpse()
clear outputs before every commit


Plots
images are saved inside the notebook file, as text you can’t see
clearing outputs removes them too


Printed SQL
a query printed with a list of participant IDs (WHERE person_id IN (…))
build ID lists in a variable; never print it


Error messages
a traceback that shows a row of data
clear outputs; don’t paste errors with data into issues


Code comments and markdown
“the outlier was person 1234567, aged 103”
describe results only as allowed aggregates


Data files
.csv, .tsv, .parquet, .rds, genotype files
keep them in your workspace bucket; list them in .gitignore


Screenshots
a screenshot of a notebook table or the Data Explorer
check every image before adding it


Your workspace details
your workspace’s Google project ID, your bucket name, your email in commits
keep them in one settings line you don’t commit; use GitHub’s noreply email (Step 2c)



Results you may share (aggregate statistics with no counts of 1 to 20, and nothing that lets one be worked out) still count as publishing All of Us results: report them through the All of Us Publication and Presentation Reporting Form at least two weeks before they go public.

title: GitHub Guide
text:
Safety nets: make mistakes hard
Checklists rely on remembering. These four habits catch mistakes automatically, before they reach GitHub.

1. A .gitignore for data files
A .gitignore file lists files Git should never add. Add one to every repo (Path B, step B3, shows how), and include your data folders:
cat >> .gitignore << 'EOF'
*.csv
*.tsv
*.parquet
*.rds
*.RData
*.vcf*
*.bam
data/
.ipynb_checkpoints/
Untitled*.ipynb
EOF


2. A pre-commit check
A pre-commit hook is a small script Git runs every time you commit. If it finds a problem, the commit stops. We use the course’s checker, tools/check_notebooks.py: it blocks notebooks with saved outputs, data files, files over 25 MB, and anything that looks like a key or token. It needs only Python, which every Workbench app has.
Set it up once in each repo (and again in each new app, since hooks aren’t pushed to GitHub):
cd ~/REPO-NAME
mkdir -p tools
curl -fsSL -o tools/check_notebooks.py \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/All-of-Us-Training-Resources/main/tools/check_notebooks.py

cat > .git/hooks/pre-commit << 'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
git diff --cached --name-only -z --diff-filter=ACM | xargs -0 python3 tools/check_notebooks.py
EOF
chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit
Now a commit with outputs fails like this:
✗ notebooks/analysis.ipynb: notebook with saved outputs in 12 cell(s): clear them first

1 problem(s) found. Nothing was committed or merged. Fix them, then try again.
Clear the outputs, git add the notebook again, and commit. Commit tools/check_notebooks.py itself, so collaborators have it too.






TipAn alternative: strip outputs automatically



The nbstripout package removes outputs every time you commit, without stopping you: pip install --user nbstripout, then nbstripout --install inside the repo. It doesn’t check for data files or credentials, so keep the .gitignore.




3. A check on GitHub, for shared repos
A hook only runs where it’s set up. For a repo that several people push to, add the same check on GitHub, so every push and pull request is checked, whoever made it. Create .github/workflows/check-notebooks.yml:
name: Check for outputs and data
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: git ls-files -z | xargs -0 python3 tools/check_notebooks.py
A failing check shows a red ✗ on the pull request, before anyone merges it. This course’s repo runs this check. Note that a check on GitHub runs after the push: it stops a merge, but the files are already on GitHub. That’s why the pre-commit hook comes first.


4. Look before you push
git status                    # which files changed?
git diff --cached --stat      # what's about to be committed, and how big?
git log origin/main..HEAD --stat   # what's about to be pushed?
On a pull request, read the Files changed tab before merging. A notebook change of thousands of lines usually means outputs slipped in.

title: GitHub Guide
section: Keep your personal settings out of Git
text:
Keep your personal settings out of Git
Notebooks often need one or two lines that differ for each person, such as your bucket name. If you edit them in a shared file, every git pull can conflict with your edit, and every commit risks pushing it.

Best: keep personal settings in a file Git ignores, and have the shared code read it. Our notebooks do this: 0.0 setup saves your bucket name in notebooks/my_settings.R, .gitignore lists that file, and aou_setup.R reads it. So git pull never clashes with it, and it can’t be committed by mistake.
If you did edit a shared file: git stash, then git pull, then git stash pop puts your edit back on top of the new version. Before committing, check git diff for your setting, and leave that file out: git restore --staged <file>.

title: GitHub Guide
text:
Protect your GitHub account

Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA): GitHub Settings → Password and authentication. GitHub now requires it for people who contribute code.
Each Workbench app has its own SSH key (Step 2b). In GitHub Settings → SSH and GPG keys, delete keys from apps you’ve deleted.
Never put a password, token, or key in a notebook, even in a cell you plan to delete: Git keeps the history. In the Workbench you don’t need one: the app is already logged in to Google Cloud, and SSH handles GitHub.
Public or private? Public repos are best for teaching code that others can reuse. Use private for work in progress. Either way, no data.

title: GitHub Guide
text:
Before you start
You need:

An All of Us workspace on Verily Workbench
A GitHub account
For Path A: write access to the existing repo (ask the repo or organization owner to add you)

You do not need to install anything on your own computer. Everything happens in a terminal inside a Workbench app, where the Workbench CLI (wb) and Git are already installed and you’re already logged in.
Work inside the app on purpose: Controlled Tier workspaces are in a security perimeter, so the data can’t be reached from your own computer, even with wb, gcloud, or bq. Git and GitHub work normally from inside the app. Only code should travel that way.

title: GitHub Guide
section: Step 1: Start an app and open a terminal
text:
Step 1: Start an app and open a terminal

In your workspace, go to the Apps tab and create an app.

AoU Jupyter is the simplest choice for Git work.
Avoid JupyterLab Spark cluster for AoU unless you need Spark. It costs more and starts slower.
R Analysis Environment for AoU also works. Use RStudio’s Terminal tab.

Once the app is running, open it.
Open a terminal: File → New → Terminal, or the Terminal tile in the Launcher (+ tab).
Confirm you’re logged in:

wb auth status

Tip: If you add a Git repo to the workspace (Apps tab → Git repositories → + Add repository) before creating the app, the app clones it automatically. Apps created earlier won’t get it. Clone it manually as shown below.

title: GitHub Guide
section: Step 2: Connect Workbench to GitHub (one-time setup)
text:
Step 2: Connect Workbench to GitHub (one-time setup)

2a. Test the connection
cd ~
ssh -T git@github.com
The first time, you may be asked Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no)?. Type yes.

✅ Success looks like: Hi YOUR-USERNAME! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access. (The “no shell access” part is normal.) Skip to 2c.
❌ Permission denied (publickey) means GitHub doesn’t know your key yet. Continue to 2b.



2b. Add your Workbench SSH key to GitHub
Get your public key:
wb security ssh-key get
If that errors because no key exists, run wb security ssh-key generate first.
Then, on GitHub:

Click your profile picture → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key
Title: Verily Workbench. Key type: Authentication Key
Paste the whole key line (starting with ssh-rsa or similar) → Add SSH key
If a Configure SSO button appears next to the key, click it and authorize your organization.

Run ssh -T git@github.com again to confirm.


2c. Set your Git identity
⚠️ Replace the example values with your own. Don’t paste them as-is.
git config --global user.name "your-github-username"
git config --global user.email "your-email@example.com"
git config --global --list    # confirm what's set
For a public repo, consider using your GitHub noreply email so your real address isn’t published. Find it at GitHub Settings → Emails. It looks like 12345678+username@users.noreply.github.com.

title: GitHub Guide
text:
Step 3: Find your notebooks
Your workspace notebooks are usually in a mounted bucket folder like:
/home/jupyter/workspace/<your-workspace-folder>/notebooks
List them:
ls -la /home/jupyter/workspace/<your-workspace-folder>/notebooks
Save any open notebooks in JupyterLab first (Ctrl/Cmd+S) so you copy the latest version.

Important: Do not run git init or git clone inside ~/workspace/.... It’s a mounted cloud bucket, and Git doesn’t work well there. Always clone into your home directory (~) and copy files over.

title: GitHub Guide
section: Path A: Add your work to an existing repo
text:
Path A: Add your work to an existing repo

A1. Clone the repo and create a branch
Use the repo’s SSH URL (green Code button on GitHub → SSH):
cd ~
git clone git@github.com:OWNER/REPO-NAME.git
cd REPO-NAME
git checkout -b add-my-notebooks
The cloned folder is named after the repo (REPO-NAME).


A2. Copy in your notebooks
Put them in a subfolder so they don’t clash with existing files:
mkdir -p notebooks
cp /home/jupyter/workspace/<your-workspace-folder>/notebooks/*.ipynb notebooks/
ls notebooks/

To use an existing folder or a name with spaces, use quotes: mkdir -p "Session 3" and cp ... "Session 3/"
To copy a single file whose name has spaces, quote the full path: cp "/home/jupyter/workspace/<folder>/notebooks/01. my notebook.ipynb" notebooks/



A3. Clean before committing
# Remove all outputs (keeps code and markdown)
jupyter nbconvert --clear-output --inplace notebooks/*.ipynb

# Check for credentials
grep -iE "token|key|secret|password" notebooks/*.ipynb
If the grep prints anything that looks like a credential, edit or remove that file before continuing. Pay special attention to notebooks that load environment variables or configuration.


A4. Commit and push
git status                     # review every file listed
git add notebooks
git commit -m "Add analysis notebooks from All of Us workspace"
git push -u origin add-my-notebooks


A5. Open and merge a pull request
The push doesn’t change main by itself. You need to merge your branch through a pull request:

Go to the repo on GitHub.
Click the yellow Compare & pull request banner. (If it’s not there: Pull requests tab → New pull request, with base: main and compare: add-my-notebooks.)
Check the Files changed tab. It should contain only the files you meant to add.
Click Create pull request, then Merge pull request → Confirm merge.
Optionally click Delete branch.



A6. Update your local copy
git checkout main
git pull

title: GitHub Guide
section: Path B: Create a new repo for your work
text:
Path B: Create a new repo for your work

B1. Create an empty repo on GitHub

On GitHub, click + (top right) → New repository.
Choose a name and set it to Public or Private.
Don’t add a README, .gitignore, or license. Leave it empty to avoid conflicts on the first push.
Click Create repository and copy the SSH URL.



B2. Set up the repo in your home directory
mkdir -p ~/my-new-repo/notebooks
cd ~/my-new-repo
git init
git branch -M main
git remote add origin git@github.com:YOUR-USERNAME/my-new-repo.git


B3. Copy, clean, and add a .gitignore
cp /home/jupyter/workspace/<your-workspace-folder>/notebooks/*.ipynb notebooks/
jupyter nbconvert --clear-output --inplace notebooks/*.ipynb
grep -iE "token|key|secret|password" notebooks/*.ipynb

# Keep data files and clutter out of Git
cat > .gitignore << 'EOF'
*.csv
*.tsv
*.parquet
*.vcf
*.vcf.gz
*.bam
*.rds
*.RData
.ipynb_checkpoints/
.DS_Store
EOF
Optionally create a README.md describing the project, the order to run the notebooks in, and what data access is required.


B4. First commit and push
git status
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit: analysis notebooks"
git push -u origin main
No pull request is needed here. The files go straight to main.

title: GitHub Guide
section: Finding your repo in the JupyterLab file browser
text:
Finding your repo in the JupyterLab file browser
The file browser often opens inside your workspace’s notebooks folder, so the repo you cloned to ~ won’t be visible at first. Click the folder icon at the start of the path bar to jump to the top level, and your repo folder will be there.
/home/jupyter/                      ← top level
├── REPO-NAME/                      ← your Git repo (synced with GitHub)
│   └── notebooks/
└── workspace/
    └── <your-workspace-folder>/
        └── notebooks/              ← your original copies (NOT in Git)

title: GitHub Guide
text:
Ongoing workflow: keeping in sync
After setup, work from the repo folder (~/REPO-NAME/notebooks/), not the original workspace folder.
Each session:
cd ~/REPO-NAME
git checkout main
git pull                       # get the latest from GitHub
# ...edit and run notebooks...
jupyter nbconvert --clear-output --inplace notebooks/*.ipynb
git status
git add notebooks
git commit -m "Describe your change"
git push
You can push straight to main if it’s your own repo, or use a branch and pull request (as in Path A) if others should review first.
Things to know:

There are two copies of your notebooks. git pull updates only the repo copy, not the originals in ~/workspace/.... Pick the repo copy as your working copy, or the two will drift apart.
Pulled notebooks have no outputs because you cleared them. Rerun the cells to regenerate results.
The clone lives on the app’s disk. If you delete the app, the clone goes with it. Always push before deleting an app, then clone again in the new one.
New apps need setup. In a new app, you may need to repeat git config (Step 2c) and clone the repo again.

title: GitHub Guide
text:
Sharing with colleagues
To use your code in their own All of Us workspace, colleagues run:
cd ~
git clone https://github.com/OWNER/REPO-NAME.git
No SSH key is needed to clone a public repo over HTTPS. They need the same data access tier your notebooks use (e.g., Controlled Tier).
To contribute back, colleagues need:

Write access to the repo (granted by the repo or organization owner)
Their own Workbench SSH key added to their GitHub account (Step 2b)
To clone with the git@github.com:... URL

Make notebooks portable: avoid hardcoded workspace paths. Build paths from your home folder, and keep the bucket name and dataset path in one place at the top of the notebook, so collaborators only change those lines:
# R
bucket <- file.path(Sys.getenv("HOME"), "workspace", "workspace-bucket")  # your bucket's name
CURRENT_DATASET <- "wb-silky-artichoke-2408.C2025Q4R6"   # CDR v9
# Python
import os
bucket = os.path.expanduser("~/workspace/workspace-bucket")  # your bucket's name
CURRENT_DATASET = "wb-silky-artichoke-2408.C2025Q4R6"   # CDR v9
WORKSPACE_BUCKET and WORKSPACE_CDR from the classic Workbench are not set in new Workbench 2.0 workspaces (see Workspace Variables).
To share results, share the workspace itself through Workbench’s sharing settings so data and outputs stay inside All of Us.

title: GitHub Guide
text:
Troubleshooting








Problem / message
What it means
Fix




“I don’t see a terminal app” when creating an app
There isn’t a separate terminal app
Terminals are inside each app. In JupyterLab: File → New → Terminal. In RStudio: Terminal tab.


fatal: not a git repository ... Stopping at filesystem boundary
You’re in a folder that isn’t a Git repo, often the mounted ~/workspace bucket
Normal before cloning. cd ~ and clone there. Don’t git init inside ~/workspace.


Permission denied (publickey)
GitHub doesn’t recognize a key from this app
Add your key from wb security ssh-key get to GitHub (Step 2b). If it still fails, run ls -la ~/.ssh. If the key is missing, restart the app, or create one with ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 -N "" and add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub to GitHub.


You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access
This is success
Nothing to fix. Carry on.


ERROR: Repository not found or Permission ... denied on push
Your account doesn’t have write access, or the URL is wrong
Check the URL with git remote -v. Ask the owner for write access, or fork the repo and push to your fork.


An error mentioning SAML SSO
Your organization requires SSO authorization for keys
GitHub Settings → SSH and GPG keys → Configure SSO on the Workbench key → authorize the org.


Commits show the wrong name or email (e.g., “Your Name”)
Placeholder values were used in git config
Rerun git config --global user.name/user.email with your real values. Check with git config --global --list.


destination path 'REPO-NAME' already exists
You already cloned it (or the app auto-cloned it)
Skip git clone and cd into the folder. Find it with find ~ -maxdepth 3 -type d -name "REPO-NAME".


Config option 'extra_template_paths' not recognized during nbconvert
Harmless warning
Ignore it. Outputs are still cleared.


Pushed, but files don’t show on GitHub’s main page
They’re on your branch, not on main
Create and merge a pull request (Step A5), or switch to your branch in GitHub’s branch dropdown to see them.


“Where’s my pull request?”
Pull requests aren’t created automatically
Click Compare & pull request on the repo page after pushing.


Can’t find the cloned repo in the JupyterLab file browser
The browser is showing a subfolder of ~/workspace
Click the folder icon at the start of the path bar to go to the top level.


No such file or directory with a filename containing spaces
The shell split the name at the spaces
Wrap the path in quotes: "01. my notebook.ipynb".


git pull refuses because of local changes
You have uncommitted edits to files that also changed on GitHub
git status, then commit your changes or discard them with git restore <file>, then pull again.


Merge conflict in a .ipynb file
Two people edited the same notebook
Notebooks are JSON and hard to merge. Keep one person per notebook where possible. To keep one side entirely: git checkout --ours <file> or git checkout --theirs <file>, then git add and commit.


Repo added to the workspace but not in my app
The app was created before the repo was added
In the app terminal: wb git clone --resource=<resource-name>, or git clone <url>.


Accidentally pushed outputs or data
Sensitive content is now on GitHub
See If something slips through, below.


✗ … notebook with saved outputs when committing
The pre-commit check found outputs
jupyter nbconvert --clear-output --inplace <notebook>, then git add it again and commit.


A red ✗ on a pull request
The GitHub check found outputs, data, or a credential
Click Details to see which file; fix it on the branch and push again. Don’t merge until it’s green.

title: GitHub Guide
text:
If something slips through
If outputs, data, or a credential reach GitHub:

Act now. Make the repo private (repo Settings → General → Danger Zone), so no one else can see it while you fix it.
Deleting the file in a new commit isn’t enough: it stays in the repo’s history. It has to be removed from the history (tools like git filter-repo), then force-pushed. Ask for help if you haven’t done this before.
Report it. Contact All of Us User Support (support@researchallofus.org): exposing participant data is a policy issue they need to know about, and they’ll tell you what else to do.
A credential? Revoke it right away (e.g. delete the token or key on GitHub or Google Cloud), even after removing it. Assume someone copied it.
Then add the safety nets above, so it can’t happen the same way again.

title: GitHub Guide
text:
Quick reference
# One-time setup (per app)
ssh -T git@github.com
wb security ssh-key get
git config --global user.name "your-username"
git config --global user.email "your-email"

# Clone, and add the pre-commit check (see Safety nets)
cd ~ && git clone git@github.com:OWNER/REPO.git && cd REPO

# Daily cycle
git pull                                  # your settings in my_settings.R are untouched
jupyter nbconvert --clear-output --inplace notebooks/*.ipynb
git status
git add notebooks
git diff --cached --stat                  # what's about to be committed
git commit -m "message"
git push
References: - Verily Workbench: Git integrations with cloud apps - Verily Workbench: Install and run the Workbench CLI - GitHub: Adding a new SSH key to your account

title: Coding with AI and GitHub
text:
A class for anyone who writes code for All of Us · about 90 minutes · no All of Us data leaves the Workbench
AI assistants (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, GitHub Copilot) are very good at writing, explaining, and fixing code. They can make All of Us research much faster, especially for people new to R, Python, or SQL. But All of Us data can’t leave the Workbench, and that includes sending it to an AI service.
This class shows a workflow that gets the benefits without the risk: the AI works on code on your own computer, GitHub carries the code, and the Workbench runs it. It’s the workflow we used to build every notebook in this course.
Hands-on: five exercises and copy-ready prompts are on Coding with AI: Exercises and Prompt Cards.

title: Coding with AI and GitHub
text:
Before class
The setup takes about 30 to 45 minutes, mostly installing. Do it before class, so class time goes on the exercises. Each item has a quick way to check it worked.

Ask it “What is a left join in R?”

On the course repository, click Fork. Then clone your fork (step 4) and add the pre-commit check (One-time setup, step 3). In your fork’s Actions tab, click the button to enable workflows, so the GitHub safety check runs there too
git remote -v shows your GitHub username

GitHub Guide, Steps 1 and 2, with your fork’s address

Why a fork? It’s your own copy of the course, with everything already in place: the notebooks, .gitignore, AGENTS.md, the safety check, and aou_setup.R. You can push to it, break it, and fix it without affecting anyone else. A fork of a public repository is public: the safety nets keep data and outputs out, as in any repository.
No Claude subscription? Every exercise works with a chat tool such as Clarity: you paste the code in, and copy the answer out.
