title: Coding with AI and GitHub
section: The one rule: the AI sees code, never data
text:
The one rule: the AI sees code, never data
All of Us allows AI tools, as long as you follow its policies. Its User Support Hub FAQ is clear about where they can run:

AI and machine learning tools used on participant data must run only within the Researcher Workbench, with no outgoing API.
“Transit of individual-level data to any external system is considered a DUCC violation, even if the data is not stored or used.” (DUCC: the Data User Code of Conduct.)
Summary statistics that follow the Data and Statistics Dissemination Policy (no counts of 1 to 20, and none that can be worked out) may be shared.

So:



✅ The AI may see
❌ The AI must never see




your code, with outputs cleared
query results, data files, notebook outputs


table and column names (the CDR data dictionary, the OMOP model)
screenshots of data


concept IDs from Athena or the Data Browser
participant IDs, dates, or values


error messages, after checking they quote no data
counts of 1 to 20


made-up test data with the same columns
error messages that print rows of data


summary results that follow the dissemination policy
anything you’d hesitate to publish



The Optional Extras page has more examples: What you can share with an AI.

What about the AI tools inside the Workbench?
Since April 2026, Workbench apps come with Claude Code and Gemini CLI pre-installed (Verily). They’re coding agents: they open files and run commands on their own, and send what they read to Anthropic’s or Google’s servers. In a workspace with All of Us data, one head data.csv or one notebook with outputs would send participant data out of the Workbench: exactly the “outgoing API” the FAQ rules out.
👉 Don’t use them in a workspace with All of Us data. They’re fine in a separate practice workspace with only synthetic data (see Practice with synthetic data).

title: Coding with AI and GitHub
section: The workflow: your computer ⇄ GitHub ⇄ the Workbench
text:
The workflow: your computer ⇄ GitHub ⇄ the Workbench
 YOUR COMPUTER                      GITHUB                     WORKBENCH APP
 (no All of Us data, ever)          (code only)                (the data stays here)

 AI assistant writes or      push   ┌──────────┐   pull        run the code
 fixes the code         ─────────►  │   repo   │ ─────────►    read the results
 test it on made-up data            └──────────┘               keep the results
                         ◄─────────               ◄─────────
                           pull                     push       (outputs cleared)
Why GitHub, and not copy and paste?

One true copy of the code, with every change recorded: you can see exactly what the AI changed, and undo it.
Safety nets check every commit and every pull request for outputs, data files, and credentials (see the GitHub Guide).
No files to move by hand: git pull in the Workbench brings in the new code in seconds.
Colleagues and students get the same code the same way.

title: Coding with AI and GitHub
section: Set up your project: folders, .gitignore, and a reference folder
text:
Set up your project: folders, .gitignore, and a reference folder
An AI assistant works much better on a tidy, predictable project: it finds the right file, follows your conventions, and guesses less. A clear structure also makes it obvious what belongs in Git and what never does.

A folder structure
my-aou-project/
├── README.md              what the project is, and the order to run things in
├── .gitignore             what Git must never add (next section): commit it FIRST
├── AGENTS.md              instructions for AI assistants (or CLAUDE.md, or .github/copilot-instructions.md)
├── notebooks/             your notebooks, outputs always cleared
│   ├── setup.R            settings (bucket, dataset) and shared helper functions
│   └── 01_cohort.ipynb …
├── sql/                   queries kept as .sql files, so they can be read and reused
├── tools/
│   └── check_notebooks.py the pre-commit check (below)
├── reference/             PUBLIC All of Us and OMOP documents, for the AI to read   ← ignored by Git
└── data/                  never used on your computer: in the Workbench, data lives in your bucket   ← ignored by Git
This is the same layout as this course’s repository: settings and helpers in one setup file, notebooks by topic, shared SQL in its own folder. Its files are working examples to copy: .gitignore, AGENTS.md, and reference/README.md.


The .gitignore: your first safety net
A .gitignore lists what Git must never add. Create it before your first commit, so nothing slips in on day one:
cat > .gitignore << 'END'
# Data: never in Git (and never on your computer)
/data/
*.csv
*.tsv
*.parquet
*.rds
*.RData
*.vcf*
*.bam
*.xlsx

# Reference documents: for the AI to read, not to publish
/reference/

# Private notes
/Notes/

# Clutter that Jupyter and your computer create
.ipynb_checkpoints/
Untitled*.ipynb
.DS_Store
END
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Add .gitignore"
Three things worth knowing:

Check a rule works: git check-ignore -v reference/data_dictionary.csv prints the rule that ignores the file. Nothing printed means it isn’t ignored.
Anchor folder names with / (/Notes/, not Notes/). Without it, the rule matches a folder with that name anywhere. On a Mac, where names ignore upper and lower case, Notes/ also matched a notes/ folder deep inside this course’s slide files.
A .gitignore doesn’t remove files Git already tracks. If a file was committed before the rule existed, remove it from Git (keeping it on disk) with git rm --cached <file>, and commit. If it contained data, see If something slips through.



A reference folder: public context for the AI
The AI’s most common mistakes in All of Us code are made-up names: a concept ID from memory, a column that doesn’t exist, the wrong table. The fix is to give it the real documentation. Keep public documents in reference/ on your computer, and tell the AI (in AGENTS.md) to check them:



Document
What it gives the AI
How to get it




CDR data dictionary
every table and column in the CDR, with descriptions
the Data Dictionaries article links a Google Sheet for each CDR version (e.g. CDR v9): File → Download → CSV for each tab you need


How the genomic and multi-omics data are organized
every genomic, RNA, and protein file: folders, formats, and columns
the PDF from the User Support Hub article; see also Where the omics data lives


OMOP Common Data Model
how the tables fit together (person, condition_occurrence, concept_ancestor, …)
the CDM documentation and the CDM wiki: save the pages for your CDM version


Concepts
real concept IDs and names
look them up in Athena or the Data Browser, and paste the ones you use into a small reference/concepts.md. Don’t download Athena’s vocabulary files into a project: they’re very large, and some vocabularies (e.g. CPT4) have licence terms


Example code
working All of Us code to learn from
this course’s notebooks (public, outputs cleared); All of Us tutorial notebooks: see below



Then add to AGENTS.md: “Public reference documents are in reference/. Check table names, column names, and concept IDs there before using them, and say if something isn’t there.”






WarningAll of Us tutorial notebooks: never download them from the Workbench



The tutorial and featured workspace notebooks are excellent examples, but:

Downloading any file from a Workbench app to your computer is logged as egress, whatever the file is. It can be flagged, and large or repeated downloads can lead to suspended access.
Many tutorial notebooks are saved with outputs, which can contain All of Us results.

Instead:

Look for a public copy first. Some All of Us example notebooks are published outside the Workbench. A public copy never touches the perimeter.
Otherwise, use the GitHub route: in the Workbench, copy the notebook into your repo folder, clear its outputs there, then commit and push it. The pre-commit check confirms no outputs leave the Workbench, and the notebook reaches your computer with git pull, like your own code.

title: Coding with AI and GitHub
text:
One-time setup
In the Workbench (once per app), follow the GitHub Guide, Steps 1 and 2: connect the app to GitHub, then clone your repo.
On your computer (once):

Install Git (git-scm.com), and sign in to GitHub. Turn on two-factor authentication (GitHub requires it for contributors).
Clone the same repo: git clone https://github.com/OWNER/REPO.git. Cloning code is safe: the repo has no data. For this class, clone your fork of the course repository (see Before class).
Add the pre-commit check, so nothing with outputs, data files, large files, or credentials can be committed, from your computer or from the Workbench. Run this once in each copy of the repo (on your computer, and in each Workbench app):

cd REPO
1mkdir -p tools
[ -f tools/check_notebooks.py ] || curl -fsSL -o tools/check_notebooks.py \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/All-of-Us-Training-Resources/main/tools/check_notebooks.py

2printf '#!/bin/sh\ngit diff --cached --name-only -z --diff-filter=ACM | xargs -0 python3 tools/check_notebooks.py\n' > .git/hooks/pre-commit
3chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit

1

Get the course’s checker script, if the repo doesn’t have it yet. Commit it, so collaborators have it too.

2

Write a two-line script into Git’s hooks folder. Git runs pre-commit before every commit: it lists the files you’re committing and passes them to the checker.

3

Make it executable. Without this, Git ignores it.


Now every commit is checked. A commit with outputs stops with ✗ notebook with saved outputs: clear them first. More in the GitHub Guide. 4. Choose an AI tool:








Kind
Examples
Sees




Chat
Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini in the browser
only what you paste


In your editor
GitHub Copilot or Claude in VS Code; RStudio’s Copilot
the files open in your editor


Coding agent
Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex, run on your computer
the files in the folder you start it in



All three are safe on your computer, because your computer has no All of Us data. Keep it that way: never download data or outputs from the Workbench, and an agent can’t send what isn’t there.

Give the AI the context once. Most tools read a project instructions file (e.g. CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, .github/copilot-instructions.md for Copilot, AGENTS.md for several others). Put the rules and the setting in it, so you don’t repeat them in every prompt:

# Instructions for AI assistants

This repo holds code for the All of Us Researcher Workbench 2.0 (Verily).
- Data: Controlled Tier CDR v9 in BigQuery (`wb-silky-artichoke-2408.C2025Q4R6`), OMOP CDM.
  SQL is BigQuery Standard SQL. R uses the tidyverse and bigrquery; settings and helpers are in notebooks/aou_setup.R.
- WORKSPACE_CDR and WORKSPACE_BUCKET are NOT set in Workbench 2.0.
- You will never see the data. Don't ask for data or outputs. Write code I'll run in the Workbench.
- Never write code that prints participant IDs or individual rows; show only summaries.
- Before sharing any table, small counts (1 to 20) must be hidden: use hide_small_counts().
- BigQuery charges by data read: select only the columns needed, and warn me about any query on a large table.
- Look up concept IDs; never invent them. Public reference documents are in reference/: check table names, column names, and concept IDs there first. Say when you're unsure.
- Test new code on a small made-up data frame with the same columns.

title: Coding with AI and GitHub
text:
Two popular setups
The workflow is the same whatever tool you use. Here’s how it looks in two setups that many researchers use.

Claude Code in Positron
Positron is a free code editor from Posit (the makers of RStudio), built for R and Python, with notebooks, a console, a data viewer, and a terminal in one window. Claude Code is Anthropic’s coding agent: it reads your project’s files, edits them, and runs commands: asking first, or on its own for steps it judges low-risk, depending on its permission mode. Together they’re a good setup for the computer side of the round trip.
Set up, step by step (once per computer, about 30 minutes):






Note1. Install R





Positron runs R code, but doesn’t include R itself.

Go to CRAN and choose your system:

macOS: download the .pkg for your Mac’s chip: arm64 for Apple silicon (M1, M2, …; check Apple menu → About This Mac), x86_64 for Intel. Open it and follow the installer.
Windows: Download R for Windows → base → Download R-4.x.x for Windows. Run the installer, accepting the defaults.

Check it worked: open a terminal (macOS Terminal; Windows Command Prompt) and type R --version. It prints the version number.

Optional: also install Python if you’ll work on the Python notebooks.









Note2. Install Git, and sign in to GitHub






Install Git from git-scm.com/downloads. On macOS, typing git --version in Terminal offers to install it for you.
Tell Git who you are (use the same email as your GitHub account, or GitHub’s noreply address):

git config --global user.name  "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.edu"

Make sure your GitHub account has two-factor authentication turned on (Settings → Password and authentication).










Note3. Install Positron






Download Positron from positron.posit.co: choose your system (macOS, Windows, or Linux).
macOS: open the .dmg and drag Positron into Applications. Windows: run the installer.
Open Positron. At the top right, the interpreter picker should show your R version (e.g. R 4.4.3). If it doesn’t, click it and choose R. Positron finds R and Python on its own.











Install the R packages the course uses, in Positron’s Console:

install.packages(c("tidyverse", "lubridate", "broom", "survival"))
These are for testing code on made-up data on your computer. (bigrquery isn’t needed locally: queries only run in the Workbench.)









Note4. Get your repo into Positron






In Positron: View → Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS, Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows), type Git: Clone, and paste your repo’s URL (e.g. https://github.com/OWNER/REPO.git). Choose a folder on your computer outside cloud-synced folders if you can (OneDrive and similar can slow Git down).







Or click the Source Control icon in the left bar, then Clone Repository:










Positron offers to open the cloned folder: say yes. Or later: File → Open Folder.
The first time you push, Positron asks you to sign in to GitHub in your browser. Allow it.
Add the pre-commit check (see Set up your project and the GitHub Guide): in Positron’s terminal (Terminal → New Terminal), run the commands from One-time setup, step 3, above.










Note5. Install the Claude Code extension






In Positron, open the Extensions view: the squares icon in the left bar, or View → Extensions (Cmd+Shift+X on macOS, Ctrl+Shift+X on Windows).
Search for claude. Choose Claude Code for VS Code, published by Anthropic (with a blue verified tick). It’s the official extension; the others in the list are from other companies. Positron gets extensions from the Open VSX marketplace, so it’s the same extension VS Code users install (identifier anthropic.claude-code).
Click Install. If Positron shows Restart Extensions (or Restart Required), click it.
A Claude icon (an orange spark) appears at the top right of the editor. Click it, and sign in with your Anthropic account: Claude Code needs a Claude subscription or API access (check whether your institution provides one).
Prefer the terminal? The extension page also describes the terminal version: run claude in Positron’s terminal. It works the same way, with the same CLAUDE.md and settings.










In this screenshot the extension is already installed, so it shows Uninstall and Restart Extensions; before installing, you’ll see an Install button instead.









Note6. Give Claude Code the rules, and keep it away from data files






Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md automatically at the start of every session. Point it to your instructions: a one-line CLAUDE.md containing @AGENTS.md loads them (as in this course’s repo).
Block it from reading data files, as a second safety net. Create .claude/settings.json in the repo:

{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": [
      "Read(./data/**)",
      "Read(**/*.csv)",
      "Read(**/*.tsv)",
      "Read(**/*.parquet)",
      "Read(**/*.rds)"
    ]
  }
}
Your computer shouldn’t hold any All of Us data anyway; this makes sure an agent couldn’t read a stray data file even if one appeared.

Test it: ask Claude Code “What’s in CLAUDE.md, and which files are you not allowed to read?” It should describe your rules.











Choose how much Claude Code may do on its own. The button at the bottom right of the prompt box shows the permission mode. In Auto mode (the default), Claude Code decides for itself which actions are low-risk and runs them without asking. While you’re learning, click it and choose a mode that asks before editing files and running commands, so you see and approve each step. Either way, the deny rules above still apply.




Working:

Ask in the terminal: “In notebooks/surveys/5.2, add alcohol frequency to the model, as in Part 5. Test it on made-up data first.”
Depending on its permission mode (step 6), Claude Code either asks before each edit or command, or runs the ones it judges low-risk. Either way, read every change before you commit: Positron’s Source Control panel shows every change in the repo, line by line.
Run the test on made-up data in Positron’s console or notebook. Then restart, clear, and save, and commit and push (Claude Code can do this too, when you ask, and the pre-commit check still runs).
In the Workbench: pull, run, and read the results there.

⚠️ Only run Claude Code on your computer. Inside a Workbench app with All of Us data, it would send what it reads outside the Workbench (see What about the AI tools inside the Workbench?).


Yale’s Clarity platform
Clarity is Yale’s AI chat platform (clarity-ai.yale.edu), free for current Yale faculty, staff, and students. It offers several models (agents) to choose from, such as GPT, Claude, and Gemini models, and Yale says conversations are never used to train AI models.
Can I use it with All of Us? For code and public documents, yes. For All of Us data, no, even though Clarity is approved for many kinds of Yale data:

Clarity runs outside the Researcher Workbench. The All of Us Data User Code of Conduct doesn’t allow participant data to leave the Workbench, whatever the destination.
Yale’s own Clarity page says users with external obligations, such as data use agreements, should confirm their use is appropriate. The All of Us Code of Conduct is one.

So Clarity sees exactly what any outside AI may see: code, error messages without data, public documents, and made-up test data.
Working with a chat tool is the round trip with copy and paste in the middle:

Start each conversation with the context. Paste the text of your AGENTS.md as your first message, or attach it. A chat tool doesn’t read your project folder.
Attach public reference documents when they help: the CDR data dictionary (CSV), the genomic data PDF, OMOP pages. Clarity accepts uploads of documents and spreadsheets. Never attach a file made in the Workbench.
Choose a model for the job. Clarity describes each one when you pick it: for example, one is described as best for writing and code, another for large document sets. Try a second model when the first one struggles.
Paste the code you want help with (outputs cleared), and ask for an explanation, a fix, or a test on made-up data.
Copy the answer into your editor (Positron, VS Code, or JupyterLab on your computer), review it, test it, then commit and push. In the Workbench: pull and run.
Organise conversations by project. Clarity lets you group chats, so you can find the conversation behind a change later. Note the change in your commit message too (e.g. “5.2: alcohol model; drafted with Clarity, tested on fake data”).

Custom agents: Clarity lets approved users create a Custom Agent with its own instructions and knowledge sources. An agent with your AGENTS.md as its instructions and the public reference documents as its knowledge would save pasting them each time. Check Yale’s requirements for creating one.









Claude Code in Positron
Clarity (chat)




Sees
the files in your project folder
only what you paste or attach


Reads AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md
automatically
paste it, or use a Custom Agent


Edits files
yes: asking first, or on its own (depends on the permission mode)
no: you copy the answer into your editor


Best for
multi-file changes, running tests, commits
questions, explanations, single functions, reviewing documents


Cost
an Anthropic subscription or API access
free for Yale users


All of Us data
never: run it only on your computer
never: code and public documents only

title: Coding with AI and GitHub
section: The round trip, step by step
text:
The round trip, step by step

1. On your computer: ask, review, test
cd REPO
git pull                          # start from the newest code
git checkout -b fix-smoking-code  # a branch for this change

Ask the AI for the change. Give it the code and the goal: “In 5.2, add alcohol frequency to the model, coded as in Part 5. Explain each step.”
Read every change it makes: git diff shows them line by line. Don’t accept code you don’t understand: ask the AI to explain it.
Test on made-up data. Ask the AI for a small fake data frame with the same columns, and run the code on it. This catches most bugs before you spend any Workbench time (see the worked example below).







WarningBefore every commit: restart, run, clear, save



Wherever you ran the notebook (on your computer or in the Workbench):

Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells. Does it run from top to bottom, with nothing left over from earlier runs? If not, fix it first: a notebook that only works in the order you happened to run it isn’t reproducible.
Kernel → Restart Kernel and Clear Outputs of All Cells, or from the terminal: jupyter nbconvert --clear-output --inplace notebooks/*.ipynb
Save the notebook (File → Save, or Ctrl/Cmd+S). Clearing doesn’t change the file until you save.
Commit. The pre-commit check confirms no outputs slipped through.

In the Workbench, step 1 runs queries again and costs money: skip it for slow or costly notebooks, and run them in full only when needed.


jupyter nbconvert --clear-output --inplace notebooks/*.ipynb   # clear outputs (if not done in the menu)
git add notebooks
git commit -m "5.2: add alcohol frequency to the model"         # the pre-commit check runs here
git push -u origin fix-smoking-code


2. In the Workbench: pull, run, read
In your app’s terminal:
cd ~/REPO
git fetch
git checkout fix-smoking-code     # your bucket name is in my_settings.R, which Git ignores
git pull
Open the notebook and run it. The results stay here. Read them in the Workbench.


3. If something fails: bring back only what’s safe

An error message: read it first. If it quotes a value, an ID, a date, or a row, remove those before pasting it to the AI.
A wrong-looking result: describe it in words, or share an allowed summary: “the model returns NA for every coefficient”, “the odds ratio is 0.26, I expected above 1”. Never paste the output table.
Back on your computer, fix, commit, push, and pull again in the Workbench.



4. When it works: merge
Open a pull request on GitHub. Read the Files changed tab one last time, wait for the green ✓ from the safety check, and merge. Everyone (including your other apps) gets it with git pull.
Near the bottom of the pull request’s Conversation tab, GitHub shows the checks. The safety check runs twice (once for the push, once for the pull request): wait until every check is green before you click Merge pull request. A red ✗ means it found outputs, data files, or a credential: click Details to see which file.








Editing in the Workbench too?
You can also edit notebooks in the Workbench. Before pushing from there: clear outputs (jupyter nbconvert --clear-output --inplace …), commit, and push. Then git pull on your computer before asking the AI for more changes, so it works on the newest version.
⚠️ Two people (or you and an AI, in two places) editing the same notebook at once leads to merge conflicts that are hard to fix in notebooks. Pull before you start, and push when you stop.

title: Coding with AI and GitHub
text:
A worked example
The full round trip, for a small task. The prompt (on your computer, with the instructions file in place):

Write an R function count_by_group(data, var) that counts the levels of var in each cohort, shows the percent within each cohort, and hides counts of 1 to 20 (show them as NA). Then make a small fake data frame to test it.

What the AI wrote first:
library(tidyverse)

count_by_group <- function(data, var) {
  data %>%
1    filter(!is.na(.data[[var]])) %>%
    count(cohort, level = .data[[var]]) %>%
2    mutate(n = if_else(n <= 20, NA_integer_, n)) %>%
    group_by(cohort) %>%
3    mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n, na.rm = TRUE), 1)) %>%
    ungroup()
}

4set.seed(1)
fake <- tibble(
  person_id      = as.character(1:120),
  cohort         = sample(c("case", "control"), 120, replace = TRUE),
  smoking_status = sample(c("Never", "Former", "Current", NA), 120, replace = TRUE,
                          prob = c(0.55, 0.25, 0.17, 0.03))
)

5count_by_group(fake, "smoking_status")

1

Leave out missing answers, so they aren’t counted as a level.

2

Hide counts of 1 to 20 (shown as NA), as All of Us policy requires.

3

The percent of each cohort in each level.

4

Made-up data with the same column names as the real file: no All of Us data is involved. set.seed() makes the fake data the same every time. Only 120 people, on purpose, so some counts are small enough to be hidden.

5

Test it.


The test finds a bug. Current and Former are hidden, as they should be, but Never shows 100% in both groups: the percents were calculated only from the cells left showing. Looks fine, runs fine, wrong. With the real data (larger counts) you might never have noticed.
The fix, after telling the AI what the test showed: calculate the percents from all the counts, then hide both the small counts and their percents:
count_by_group <- function(data, var) {
  data %>%
    filter(!is.na(.data[[var]])) %>%
    count(cohort, level = .data[[var]]) %>%
    group_by(cohort) %>%
1    mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
2    mutate(percent = if_else(n <= 20, NA_real_, percent),
           n       = if_else(n <= 20, NA_integer_, n))
}

count_by_group(fake, "smoking_status")

1

Percents from all counts, so Never gets its true share.

2

Then hide small counts and their percents: a percent next to a known total would reveal the count.


Run the test again: Never now shows its real share, and the hidden rows show NA for both.
More review questions to ask before accepting it: What happens if var is a factor? If a cohort has no rows? Could anyone work out a hidden count from the others? The last is the derived-counts rule from 3.1: with only one hidden row in a group, its count can be worked out from the percents of the others. If that happens, combine small levels first (e.g. Current and Former into Ever smoked).
Then: save it in notebooks/helpers.R, restart and clear, commit (the check runs), push, and in the Workbench:
1source("~/repos/REPO/notebooks/helpers.R")
2survey_basics <- load_data("survey_basics.csv", col_types = cols(person_id = "c"))
3count_by_group(survey_basics, "smoking_status")

1

The function, pulled from GitHub into the Workbench.

2

The real data, read from your bucket: it never leaves the Workbench.

3

Run it, and read the result in the Workbench. If you want to share it, it’s an aggregate table that passes the small-count rule, but remember that sharing results publicly needs the reporting form.

title: Coding with AI and GitHub
text:
Check everything the AI writes
AI assistants are fluent and confident, and sometimes wrong. While building this course, an AI made each of these mistakes; each was caught by a check, not by trusting the answer:








The AI…
How it was caught
The check to use




wrote concept IDs from memory
a cell printed each ID’s name from the dictionary before using it
always look IDs up: the dictionary, Athena, or a query on concept; keep the ones you use in reference/


“found” trailing spaces in a survey name, and wrote a lesson about them
nchar() gave the same length with and without trimws()
test the claim, don’t just read the explanation


searched survey answers for “self”, which matched every answer (“Including yourself…”)
a table of each answer and its group
after any recoding, count the categories


ran a query on a 6 TB table because a dry run priced it at $0 (dry runs can’t price tables clustered by person)
checking what the query actually billed, and how the table is stored
price queries first, then check the bill: run_if_cheap() and last_query_cost() (6.1)


predicted that non-drinkers would have higher odds (the “sick quitter” idea)
the real result was the opposite
let the data answer; revise the explanation



The pattern: the AI suggests, the data decides. Use the checks from the course: print what IDs mean, count before and after every recode, check the number of rows after every join (2.3), price queries before running them (6.1), and compare results with what’s known.

title: Coding with AI and GitHub
text:
Use AI responsibly

You’re responsible for the code and the results, whoever wrote them.
Say so when AI helped: many journals ask authors to describe how AI was used.
Reproducibility: the code in GitHub is the record. Commit messages and pull requests show what changed and why.
Your institution’s rules may add to these: check its AI guidance for research.
Learning: if you’re learning to code, ask the AI to explain, then write the next piece yourself.

title: Coding with AI and GitHub
text:
Try It Out






Tip✋ Try It Out · 55 minutes · five exercises



The exercises are on their own page: Coding with AI: Exercises and Prompt Cards.

Safe to share? (5 min): sort ten items into “may paste” and “never paste”.
Explain this code (5 min): an AI explains the cohort query’s first step; you check it against the comments.
Fix this error (10 min): a real join error from the course, on made-up data.
Spot the mistakes (10 min): an AI’s answer that looks right and breaks at least seven rules.
The full round trip (25 min): improve count_by_group() on your computer, push it, and run it on real data in the Workbench.

✅ Check: the function works on both the fake and the real data; the real result never left the Workbench.

title: Coding with AI and GitHub
text:
Instructor notes






TipInstructor tip






Start with the rule and the diagram. Students’ first question is “can I use ChatGPT?”: the answer is “yes, for code, outside the Workbench”.
Show a real AI mistake from the table, and how a one-line check caught it. It’s the most persuasive part of the class.
The pre-installed Claude Code and Gemini CLI come up every time. The All of Us FAQ’s “no outgoing API” rule is the answer for workspaces with All of Us data.
Live demo: steps 1 to 4 of the round trip take about 10 minutes with a prepared branch.
Check the setup before class. Send the Before class checklist a week ahead. In class, the most common problems are a missing fork in the Workbench and a Workbench app not yet connected to GitHub: pair those students with a neighbour for exercises 2 to 4, and fix their setup during the break.
Exercises 2 to 4 work with any AI tool, and give different answers each time. Compare answers across the room: the differences are a lesson in themselves.
Source for the policy: All of Us User Support Hub, “Frequently Asked Questions” (support.researchallofus.org/hc/en-us/articles/52861503885460).

title: Coding with AI and GitHub
text:
Key takeaways

The AI sees code, never data: work with it on your own computer, which has no All of Us data
Give every project a predictable folder structure and a .gitignore from day one
Keep public reference documents (data dictionary, OMOP docs, concepts) in reference/, so the AI checks names instead of guessing
Never download tutorial notebooks from the Workbench: use a public copy, or clear them and push through GitHub
Claude Code in Positron and Yale’s Clarity both fit the round trip: Claude Code edits your project on your computer; Clarity answers questions about code you paste. Neither ever sees All of Us data
GitHub carries the code both ways; the Workbench runs it and keeps the results
Don’t use AI coding agents (including the pre-installed ones) in a workspace with All of Us data
Review every change, test on made-up data, and check results: the AI suggests, the data decides
The safety nets (pre-commit check, GitHub check, pull request review) catch outputs and data before they leave

Related: Exercises and Prompt Cards · GitHub Guide · Optional Extras: AI tools

Migrated from 1.0:

Files and notebooks in your workspace bucket
They’re in a new bucket named like rw-migration-aou-rw-…

Not migrated:

title: Tutorial Workspaces
text:
Setting Up Your Environment (R)
The tutorial’s setup script defines your workspace variables:
source("/home/jupyter/workspace/aou-tutorial-notebooks/Setting_Env_Variables_p2.R")

library(bigrquery)
library(tidyverse)

CURRENT_DATASET <- Sys.getenv("WORKSPACE_CDR")   # the CDR in this workspace

download_data <- function(query) {
  tb <- bq_project_query(Sys.getenv("GOOGLE_PROJECT"), query)
  bq_table_download(tb)
}

The script sets WORKSPACE_BUCKET and WORKSPACE_CDR. Without it, they don’t exist (see Workspace Variables).
The All of Us app image in 2.0 is smaller, so you may need to install packages
In a migrated workspace, set WORKSPACE_BUCKET to your migration bucket (gs://rw-migration-…)

title: Tutorial Workspaces
text:
Updating SQL Queries
Replace hard-coded 1.0 dataset paths with CURRENT_DATASET:
1.0: won’t run ❌
query <- str_glue("SELECT * FROM `fc-aou-cdr-prod-ct.C2024Q3R8.condition_occurrence` LIMIT 5")
2.0: runs ✅
query <- str_glue("SELECT * FROM `{CURRENT_DATASET}.condition_occurrence` LIMIT 5")
df <- download_data(query)
The standard OMOP tables (condition_occurrence, person, measurement…) keep their names. Only the path changes.

title: Data Explorer

A point-and-click tool for building datasets from All of Us data collections

Building a Cohort

Three R classes on the All of Us wearable data, with the same cohort as every other series: people with type 2 diabetes compared with people without diabetes.

title: 6.2 Steps and Type 2 Diabetes
text:
Overview
Do people who take more steps a day develop type 2 diabetes less often? In this class we follow every All of Us participant with Fitbit data forward in time: their daily steps are measured first, and then we watch who is diagnosed with type 2 diabetes later, and when. It’s the design of a published All of Us study, and it fixes the biggest problem we met in the survey series: answers given after a diagnosis.

Why this class matters
In 5.2, most people with diabetes answered the Lifestyle survey after their diagnosis, so their answers could reflect the diagnosis (people quit smoking, or cut down on alcohol, because of it). A prospective design, where the exposure is measured before the outcome, is the standard way around that, and wearables make it possible: Fitbit records steps day by day, with exact dates.


By the end you’ll be able to

Explain a prospective cohort design, and why it avoids reverse causation
Build baseline steps, eligibility, and follow-up from dates, mostly inside BigQuery
Calculate incidence rates per 1,000 person-years
Draw Kaplan–Meier curves and fit a Cox model for a new outcome (from 3.4)
Choose what to adjust for: confounders vs a possible mediator
Test the result with a sensitivity analysis (a lag)



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
Among adults without diabetes, do those who take more steps a day develop type 2 diabetes less often?


🧪 The analysis
Baseline steps over each person’s first 6 months of Fitbit data; follow-up for a new diagnosis; incidence rates; Kaplan–Meier curves; Cox models (age and sex, then + BMI); a 1-year lag


🎯 Why
Steps measured before any diagnosis can’t be the result of it. Survival methods use everyone’s follow-up, however long


✅ What we conclude
How the rate of new type 2 diabetes differs by daily steps


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Cause. People who walk more differ in many ways (income, health, diet). And Fitbit users aren’t typical


🔗 Connections
Valid days and costs from 6.1; the cohort query from 1.1; survival methods from 3.4; reverse causation from 5.2; confounders and mediators from 5.3





Time and cost







⏱️ Class time
95 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 5 minutes


💰 Cost
about $1 per student: the cohort query, and one query for everyone’s baseline steps and BMI ($0.18 in our test run)


📋 Before class
6.1 is helpful (valid days, costs), and 3.4 (survival analysis)

title: 6.2 Steps and Type 2 Diabetes
text:
Key concepts

Measure first, then follow
first valid           end of baseline                          end of follow-up
Fitbit day            (6 months later)                         (last EHR visit, death, or 2025)
    |──── baseline ────|──────────────── follow-up ─────────────────────|
      median daily          does type 2 diabetes appear? when?
      steps
excluded: anyone with type 2 diabetes (or another kind of diabetes) before the end of baseline
This design avoids reverse causation by construction: steps are measured before any diagnosis, so the diagnosis can’t have changed them. It follows the published All of Us study of step counts and chronic disease (Master et al., Nature Medicine, 2022).
Why not use our sample of 5,000 cases and 5,000 controls? The cases were chosen because they already had diabetes, and for most of them Fitbit data starts after the diagnosis. Only a few hundred have Fitbit data at all (6.1). Following all Fitbit users forward is both larger and more honest.


Words for this design







Term
Means




Baseline
when the exposure is measured: each person’s first 6 months of valid Fitbit days


Exposure
what might affect the outcome: median daily steps at baseline


Incident case
a new diagnosis during follow-up. A prevalent case already had diabetes at baseline: excluded


Censoring
follow-up ends without the outcome: the last EHR visit, death, or the end of the data


Person-years
total time followed: 100 people for 2 years = 200 person-years


Incidence rate
new cases ÷ person-years, often per 1,000 person-years


Hazard ratio
the rate in one group ÷ another, at any moment: HR 0.5 = half the rate





What to adjust for








Variable
Role
Adjust?




Age, sex
affect both steps and diabetes risk: confounders
yes


BMI
a confounder (heavier people may walk less) and a possible mediator (walking → lower weight → less diabetes)
show both models



The model without BMI is the main result. The model with BMI shows the part of the link not explained by weight.

title: 6.2 Steps and Type 2 Diabetes
text:
Code walk-through

Baseline steps for everyone, in one query
1WITH wear AS (…),
valid AS (…),
first_day AS (
2  SELECT person_id, MIN(date) AS first_valid FROM valid GROUP BY person_id
),
baseline AS (
  SELECT v.person_id,
         MAX(v.date) AS baseline_end,
         COUNT(*)    AS baseline_days,
3         APPROX_QUANTILES(v.steps, 100)[OFFSET(50)] AS baseline_steps
  FROM valid AS v JOIN first_day AS f ON v.person_id = f.person_id
4  WHERE v.date < DATE_ADD(f.first_valid, INTERVAL 6 MONTH)
  GROUP BY v.person_id
),
5bmi AS (…)
6SELECT … FROM baseline … WHERE baseline_days >= 10

1

Wear minutes and valid days, as in 6.1.

2

Each person’s first valid Fitbit day.

3

BigQuery’s fast median: the 50th of 100 percentiles.

4

Only the first 6 months: the baseline.

5

The latest BMI in the 2 years before the end of baseline.

6

One row per person with at least 10 valid baseline days. BigQuery does the work; only tens of thousands of rows come back, instead of tens of millions.




Follow-up, from dates
followup <- joined %>%
  filter(cohort != "excluded",
1         !(cohort == "case" & t2d_date <= baseline_end),
         age_at_baseline >= 18,
2         followup_end > baseline_end) %>%
3  mutate(event     = as.integer(cohort == "case" & t2d_date <= followup_end),
         exit_date = if_else(event == 1, t2d_date, followup_end),
4         years     = as.numeric(exit_date - baseline_end) / 365.25)

1

Leave out prevalent cases: diagnosed before baseline ended.

2

Keep people with some EHR follow-up after baseline.

3

The event: a type 2 diabetes diagnosis during follow-up.

4

Years from the end of baseline to diagnosis, or to censoring.




Cox models, on the same people
1m_age_sex <- coxph(Surv(years, event) ~ steps_group + age10 + sex_at_birth, data = cox_data)
2m_bmi     <- coxph(Surv(years, event) ~ steps_group + age10 + sex_at_birth + bmi5, data = cox_data)
3m_per1000 <- coxph(Surv(years, event) ~ steps_1000 + age10 + sex_at_birth, data = cox_data)

1

The main model: adjusted for the confounders, age and sex.

2

Plus BMI: what’s left after accounting for weight.

3

Steps as a number: the hazard ratio for each extra 1,000 steps a day.

Main result: people taking 10,000 or more steps a day had about a quarter of the rate of new type 2 diabetes of those taking under 5,000, adjusted for age and sex. Each extra 1,000 steps a day went with a 14% lower rate.
BMI explained part of the link (hazard ratios moved toward 1), but most remained.
The 1-year lag barely changed the results: early, undiagnosed illness doesn’t explain them.
The benefit levels off above about 7,500 steps. “10,000 steps a day” isn’t a threshold.

💬 Discuss: this is still an association, in a selected group. What else differs between people who walk more and less? Could people who walk more see doctors less, and be diagnosed later? What evidence would convince you that walking itself lowers the risk?

title: 6.2 Steps and Type 2 Diabetes
text:
Instructor notes






TipInstructor tip






Draw the timeline before anything else. Most of the class follows from it.
“Avoids reverse causation by construction” is the key phrase: compare with 5.2, where most survey answers came after diagnosis.
BMI: confounder or mediator? Ask students to argue both sides before showing model 2.
The flow table is worth slowing down for: each rule is a decision a reader needs to know about.
Kaplan–Meier curves end early on purpose: where few people remain, curves describe very few people and jump around.
Proportional hazards: the check gave p = 0.004 for steps. Discuss what it means for activity measured once, over 6 months, but followed for years.
Likely question: “Is 10,000 steps magic?” No: the number came from a 1960s Japanese pedometer advertisement. Look at the gradient, which levels off above about 7,500 here.

Three R classes on the All of Us survey data, with the same cohort as every other series: people with type 2 diabetes compared with people without diabetes.
Surveys tell us what health records rarely do: smoking, family history, income, food security, access to care. title: 5.2 Family History and Lifestyle
text:
Overview
Type 2 diabetes runs in families, and is linked to habits like smoking and drinking. Health records rarely capture these, but the All of Us surveys do. In this class we turn family history of diabetes, smoking, and alcohol into variables, and ask how they relate to type 2 diabetes. Along the way we meet the biggest trap in survey analysis: answers given after a diagnosis.

Why this class matters
A survey answer describes a person when they answered, and most people with diabetes answered years after their diagnosis. Their answers can reflect the diagnosis (people quit smoking after it), and other differences between groups, like income, can create links that aren’t causal. This class shows how to check these explanations, not just name them.


By the end you’ll be able to

Code a select all that apply family history question into one variable per relative
Choose the right denominator: who could have answered a question at all
Compare self-reported diabetes with the health records
Check when a survey was answered relative to a diagnosis, and explain reverse causation
Fit age- and sex-adjusted logistic regression models, and run sensitivity analyses



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
Are family history of diabetes, smoking, and alcohol use linked to type 2 diabetes?


🧪 The analysis
Percents by group; logistic regression adjusted for age and sex; the same model with only cases who answered before diagnosis; two ways to code a skipped answer


🎯 Why
Logistic regression compares the odds of diabetes, adjusted for age and sex, which differ between groups


✅ What we conclude
How strongly each factor is linked to type 2 diabetes, and how much answer timing and coding choices matter


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Cause. Most answers came after diagnosis; income and health can confound; family history is reported, not verified


🔗 Connections
Uses files from 5.1; models from 3.2; family history connects to the genetics of 4.2; confounding by income leads to 5.3





Time and cost







⏱️ Class time
90 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 3 minutes


💰 Cost
about $1.50 per student: two queries on ds_survey, plus the app


📋 Before class
run 5.1: this class uses its question dictionary and survey_basics.csv

Code walk-through

One column per relative
family <- family %>%
  mutate(member   = if_else(str_starts(answer, "PMI:"), answer,
1                            str_trim(str_extract(answer, "[^?:-]+$"))),
         relative = case_when(
           str_starts(answer, "PMI:")                                     ~ "non-answer",
           str_detect(member, regex("^self$", ignore_case = TRUE))        ~ "self",
2           str_detect(member, regex("grand", ignore_case = TRUE))         ~ "grandparent",
           str_detect(member, regex("mother|father", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "parent",
           …))

family_wide <- family %>%
  filter(relative != "non-answer") %>%
3  distinct(person_id, relative) %>%
  mutate(value = TRUE) %>%
4  pivot_wider(names_from = relative, values_from = value, values_fill = FALSE)

1

Keep only the family member, the text after the last ?, -, or :. The question says “Including yourself”, so searching the whole answer for self matches every row.

2

Order matters: Grandmother contains mother, so grandparents are checked first.

3

One row per person per group: Mother and Father make one parent.

4

One TRUE/FALSE column per group (2.2).




Only cases who answered before diagnosis

1  filter(cohort == "control" | lifestyle_date < first_t2d_date)

m_before <- glm(t2d ~ age10 + sex_at_birth + smoking_status + alcohol_use,
2                family = binomial, data = before_data)

1

title: 5.2 Family History and Lifestyle
text:
What we found
Results from our test run in October 2026 (CDR v9), 5,000 cases and 5,000 controls.

Timing and family history

77% of cases answered the Lifestyle survey after their diabetes was first recorded, a median of 2.6 years after.
Family history (a parent or sibling): 45% of cases and 26% of controls who took the survey.
Self-report vs records: only 59% of cases reported Self, and about 2% of controls did. Neither source is perfect.
PMI: Skip was one of the most common answers to the select-all family question: about 1 in 5 people who took the survey had only a skip, more often controls.



Odds ratios








Adjusted for age and sex
All cases
Cases who answered before diagnosis




Family history (parent or sibling)
2.47 (2.16 to 2.83)



Former smoker (vs never)
1.24 (1.12 to 1.38)
1.25 (1.06 to 1.48)


Current smoker (vs never)
1.32 (1.16 to 1.50)
1.71 (1.41 to 2.06)


Alcohol: none in past year (vs never drank)
0.87 (0.73 to 1.03)
0.76 (0.58 to 0.98)


Alcohol: monthly or less
0.74 (0.64 to 0.87)
0.70 (0.55 to 0.88)


Alcohol: 2–4 times a month
0.48 (0.41 to 0.57)
0.59 (0.46 to 0.77)


Alcohol: 2+ times a week
0.26 (0.22 to 0.30)
0.31 (0.24 to 0.41)





Family history had the strongest link: about two and a half times the odds. Counting a skipped answer as “no family history” instead of unknown raised it to 2.95 (2.59 to 3.36), because controls skipped more often. The link is strong either way, but its size depends on the coding choice: report both.
Current smoking rose from 1.32 to 1.71 with cases who answered before diagnosis, as reverse causation predicts: some smokers quit after diagnosis, which hides part of the link in later answers.
Alcohol: the more often people drank, the lower their odds, and this barely changed with answers given before diagnosis. So it isn’t mainly people cutting down after diagnosis. It still doesn’t show that alcohol prevents diabetes: confounding by income, education, and health is a likely explanation, which 5.3 examines.

💬 Discuss: cases who answered before their diagnosis were diagnosed after joining All of Us. How might they differ from cases diagnosed long ago?

title: 5.2 Family History and Lifestyle
text:
Instructor notes






TipInstructor tip






The alcohol result always prompts “so drinking prevents diabetes?” Ask students for explanations before Part 7: reverse causation, sick quitters, confounding by income and health. Part 7 rules out the first as the main one; 5.3 looks at income.
The “self” bug is worth showing: searching the whole answer for self matches every row, because the question says “Including yourself”. Always check how answers were grouped.
Family history and genes: link back to 4.2. Family history captures many genes and a shared household.
Why not count everyone without an answer as “no family history”? Half the sample never took the survey: they’re unknown, not “no”.

title: 5.2 Family History and Lifestyle
text:
Key takeaways

A select-all question becomes one column per relative, after checking how each answer was grouped
Choose the denominator carefully: no answer can mean “no”, “never asked”, or “skipped”
Self-reported diabetes and the records mostly agree: a useful check of any case definition
Most answers came after diagnosis: test for reverse causation, and think about confounding
Sensitivity analyses show which conclusions hold up

title: Precision Medicine: Why All of Us Exists, and Where Our Classes Fit
text: All of Us was created for precision medicine. This page explains what that means, and how each series in this course connects to it. It’s a good starting point for any class, and a good closing discussion for every series.
crumbs: Precision Medicine: Why All of Us Exists, and Where Our Classes Fit

title: Precision Medicine: Why All of Us Exists, and Where Our Classes Fit
text:
What is precision medicine?
Most medical advice is based on the average person in a study: the same screening age, the same first drug, the same advice for everyone. Precision medicine tailors prevention, diagnosis, and treatment to the individual, by taking into account how people differ in their genes, environment, and way of life.
The program’s founding paper describes its purpose like this:

“The All of Us data repository should permit researchers to take into account individual differences in lifestyle, socioeconomic factors, environment, and biologic characteristics in order to advance precision diagnosis, prevention, and treatment.” — The All of Us Research Program Investigators, New England Journal of Medicine, 2019 (doi:10.1056/NEJMsr1809937)

The program began in 2015 as the Precision Medicine Initiative cohort program. You’ll still see the old name, PMI, in the survey data (class 5.1).
crumbs: Precision Medicine: Why All of Us Exists, and Where Our Classes Fit

title: Precision Medicine: Why All of Us Exists, and Where Our Classes Fit
section: Why precision medicine needed a program like All of Us
text:
Why precision medicine needed a program like All of Us
The founding paper names three problems with earlier studies: they were too small, they lacked diversity, and they didn’t collect enough kinds of data about each person. All of Us was designed to fix all three:








Earlier studies
All of Us
Why it matters for precision medicine




Thousands to hundreds of thousands of people
A goal of 1 million or more
Differences between people are often small; finding them needs very large numbers


Mostly people of European ancestry
A focus on groups underrepresented in biomedical research: by 2019, 80% of participants with biospecimens were from these groups
A treatment or risk score built on one group may not work as well for others


One or two kinds of data
Health records, surveys, physical measurements, genomes, RNA and proteins, and wearables, for the same people
“Genes, environment, and lifestyle” can only be studied together if they’re measured on the same people


Data downloaded project by project
One cloud workbench, open to any approved researcher
More researchers, and more questions, from the same data
crumbs: Precision Medicine: Why All of Us Exists, and Where Our Classes Fit

title: Precision Medicine: Why All of Us Exists, and Where Our Classes Fit
section: How our series connect to the program’s goals
text:
How our series connect to the program’s goals
The founding paper lists the program’s scientific goals. Our series, all on the same type 2 diabetes question, touch most of them:



Program goal (from the founding paper)
Where you practise it
What it looks like in our classes




Discover genetic and environmental correlates with disease
Omics 4.1–4.4; Surveys 5.2–5.3
A genetic risk variant (rs7903146 in TCF7L2); family history, smoking, income, education, and food security


Discover disease biomarkers
Omics 4.5–4.7
Genes and blood proteins that differ in type 2 diabetes, and which of them are genetically controlled


Connect mobile health, digital health, and sensor data with clinical outcomes
Wearables 6.1–6.3
Daily steps, sleep, and heart rate measured before a diagnosis, then followed forward to new type 2 diabetes


Improve understanding of health disparities
Surveys 5.3; Core 3.1–3.2; Omics 4.1–4.2
Diabetes by income, education, and insurance; differences between groups in Table One; genetic ancestry


Enable machine-learning applications
Machine learning 7.1–7.4
Predicting who will develop type 2 diabetes, from data collected before diagnosis


Develop new disease classifications; improve predictions of therapeutic safety and efficacy; support clinical trials
Not covered yet
Ideas for future classes, e.g. medication response (pharmacogenomics)



The Core series underpins all of them: finding the right people (cohorts), cleaning and joining their data, and the models every later class uses.
crumbs: Precision Medicine: Why All of Us Exists, and Where Our Classes Fit

title: Precision Medicine: Why All of Us Exists, and Where Our Classes Fit
section: What our results can, and can’t, say about one person
text:
What our results can, and can’t, say about one person
Precision medicine is about individuals. Almost every result in our classes is about groups. Keeping the two apart is the most important lesson of this page.



Our classes find…
Which means…
It does not mean…




An odds ratio of about 1.25 per copy of rs7903146’s T allele (class 4.2)
On average, each copy goes with about 25% higher odds of type 2 diabetes
That a person with the allele will get diabetes, or one without it won’t. One common variant changes an individual’s risk only a little


People with type 2 diabetes more often had low household incomes (class 5.3)
A pattern across groups
That income causes diabetes, or that it tells you about a single person


People who walked more had lower rates of new diabetes (class 6.2)
An association, in a design that reduces reverse causation
That walking more will prevent diabetes for you: that needs a trial



The founding paper is candid about these limits too:

“Association does not necessarily translate into causation.” It points to methods such as Mendelian randomization and polygenic risk scores as ways to learn more, and to clinical trials to test it.
The sample isn’t random. The program “was not designed with a formal statistical sampling method”, so some results don’t describe the US population (class 5.1: no survey weights).
Health records are messy. EHR data “can be fragmented, incomplete, and inaccurate” (class 2.1, and the case definition in the shared cohort query).


From group results to individual care
Getting from our kind of result to precision medicine takes several steps, and each one is an active research area:

Combine many factors. One variant, or one survey answer, predicts little. Polygenic risk scores add up thousands of variants; prediction models combine genes, records, surveys, and wearables (our machine learning series).
Check it works for everyone. Today’s polygenic risk scores are several times more accurate in people of European ancestry than in other groups, because most genetic studies so far were in people of European ancestry. Using them in clinics could widen health disparities (Martin et al., Nature Genetics, 2019, doi:10.1038/s41588-019-0379-x). This is exactly the gap All of Us’s diversity is meant to close.
Show cause, not just association, with designs such as Mendelian randomization and, finally, clinical trials.
Show it helps patients: that tailoring care on the new information leads to better health than usual care.
crumbs: Precision Medicine: Why All of Us Exists, and Where Our Classes Fit

title: Precision Medicine: Why All of Us Exists, and Where Our Classes Fit
text:
💬 Discussion questions
Use these at the end of any series.

Which kind of data in this series (genes, records, surveys, wearables) would you most want for your risk of type 2 diabetes? Why?
Who is missing? Which groups are still underrepresented in our cohort (for example, people with no health records, or no smartphone for a wearable)? How could that affect a prediction made for them?
Group vs individual: pick one result from the series. What would you need to know before telling a patient it applies to them?
Harm: how could a precision medicine tool built on these data make care less fair? (The Research Use Statement asks about this too: see Research Use Statement.)

title: Where the Omics Data Lives
text: A reference page for the omics series. The All of Us genomic and multi-omic data is a large set of files, in many formats, for different groups of participants. This page puts it all on one map: where each data type is, what format it’s in, who has it, and which file to start from for a question.

title: Where the Omics Data Lives
text:
Finding the files
In a Workbench 2.0 app, the data is mounted as a folder in ~/workspace/, named something like vwb-aou-datasets-controlled-v8r9, with one subfolder per data release. The course helper aou_data_dir() (in aou_setup.R) finds it for you:
source("../aou_setup.R")
AOU_DIR <- aou_data_dir("v9")    # e.g. ~/workspace/vwb-aou-datasets-controlled-v8r9/v9
list.files(AOU_DIR)              # wgs, microarray, multiomics
Listing folders and checking file sizes is free. Reading files costs only your app’s time, except the raw sequencing reads (below).

title: Where the Omics Data Lives
text:
The map
v9/
├── wgs/
│   ├── short_read/
│   │   ├── snpindel/                 SNPs and small insertions/deletions
│   │   │   ├── acaf_threshold/       common variants        ← 4.1–4.4
│   │   │   ├── exome/                variants in genes (exons)
│   │   │   ├── clinvar/              variants listed in ClinVar
│   │   │   ├── vds/                  every variant, whole genome (very large)
│   │   │   └── aux/                  ancestry, relatedness, QC, annotations…  ← 4.1–4.4
│   │   └── structural_variants/      large deletions, duplications, inversions
│   ├── long_read/                    long-read genomes, by sequencing centre
│   └── cram/                         raw sequencing reads (costly to read)
├── microarray/                       genotyping array data
└── multiomics/
    ├── rnaseq/                       RNA sequencing, whole blood   ← 4.5, 4.7
    └── proteomics/                   Olink proteins, blood plasma  ← 4.6, 4.7

title: Where the Omics Data Lives
text:
Choosing a short-read callset
The full set of variants, the VDS, covers the whole genome for everyone, and is very large: most analyses would first have to filter and convert it (“densify”), which takes time and money. All of Us has done that already for three common uses:








Callset
Contains
Start here when…




ACAF threshold
variants with allele frequency above 1%, or allele count above 100, in any ancestry group
GWAS, PheWAS, ancestry: most questions (this series)


Exome
variants in the exons of protein-coding genes (plus 15 bases either side)
rare variants in genes, gene-based tests


ClinVar
variants listed in the ClinVar database, whatever their effect
known disease-causing variants


VDS
everything
only if none of the above has your variants



Each smaller callset comes in PLINK 2 (pgen), PLINK 1 (plink_bed), BGEN, VCF, and Hail (splitMT: one alternate allele per row; multiMT: several), with one file per chromosome. Use the format your tool reads: PLINK 2 in 4.2, Hail splitMT in 4.3.






TipHave an rsID, not a position?



The callsets identify variants by position (chr10:112998590). To find an rsID’s position, use the Variant Annotation Table (aux/vat/), which also has each variant’s gene, predicted effect, and allele frequencies. For one well-known variant, dbSNP works too (use the GRCh38 position).

title: Where the Omics Data Lives
text:
Technical variables worth checking
Samples were collected, extracted, and sequenced in different ways and places. These technical differences can create patterns that look like biology (batch effects), so check them, and adjust for them if they differ between your groups:








Data
Technical variables
In this series




Genomes
sequencing centre (Broad, University of Washington, Baylor); sample source (blood or saliva); DNA extraction method (Autogen or Chemogen): in the genomic metrics and extraction-method files
not needed for common variants; matters for coverage, mitochondrial copy number, and rare variants


RNA-seq
RNA quality, sequencing depth, processing batch: in rnaseq_metadata.tsv and the RNA-SeQC 2 metrics
4.5 adjusts for RNA quality


Proteomics
plate, sample and assay QC flags; 127 technical replicate samples (removed in the reps_removed file)
4.6 checks plates and QC flags

title: Where the Omics Data Lives
text:
Precomputed results: QTLs
All of Us has already linked genetic variants to RNA and protein levels. These files are summary statistics (no individual data), so they’re quick to read:









Results
Folder
Has
In this series




cis-eQTL
rnaseq/eqtl/
each gene’s strongest nearby variant; every gene–variant pair tested; fine-mapped variants
4.5, 4.7


cis-sQTL
rnaseq/sqtl/
variants linked to splicing (which exons are kept)



cis-pQTL
proteomics/pqtl/
each protein’s strongest nearby variant; fine-mapped variants
4.6, 4.7



Fine-mapping goes one step further than “the strongest variant”: it groups variants that are inherited together into a credible set, and gives each a PIP (posterior inclusion probability), the probability that it’s the variant really driving the signal. A variant with a high PIP for both a protein and a disease is a strong lead.
Each QTL analysis was run in everyone together (COMB) and within each genetic ancestry group.

title: 4.7 RNA and Protein Together
text:
Omics series, class 7 of 7 · R · 120 minutes
Open the notebook on GitHub Omics series overview Omics for Beginners

title: 4.7 RNA and Protein Together
text:
Overview
Almost everyone in All of Us with RNA-seq also has proteomics. In this class we put the two side by side, for the same people: for each gene, does a person’s RNA level go with their protein level? And do RNA and protein tell the same story about type 2 diabetes? Then we pull together what the whole series showed.

Why this class matters
It’s tempting to assume more RNA means more protein. Often it doesn’t, especially when RNA comes from blood cells and proteins from plasma. Seeing where the layers agree and disagree, and why, is the basic skill of multi-omics integration, and a guard against over-reading any single layer.


By the end you’ll be able to

Explain why RNA and protein levels often don’t agree, especially in blood
Load both layers for the same people, and match each protein to its gene with stable IDs
Calculate and interpret RNA–protein correlations
Compare differential results across two layers
Summarise what each layer can and can’t tell us about a disease



Analysis at a glance







❓ Questions
Does a gene’s RNA go with its protein, across people? Do RNA and protein tell the same story about type 2 diabetes?


🧪 The analysis
A Spearman correlation for each gene–protein pair; the diabetes results from both layers (limma), compared pair by pair


🎯 Why
Spearman uses ranks, so extreme values don’t dominate; comparing t-statistics combines each effect’s size and certainty


✅ What we conclude
Which proteins track their blood RNA, and whether diabetes signals are shared


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Anything outside blood; which layer is closer to the cause


🔗 Connections
Combines 4.5 and 4.6, and summarises the series





Time and cost







⏱️ Class time
120 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 15 minutes. Slowest: loading the proteins (3–5 min) and the RNA counts (a few min)


💰 Cost
about $1 to $2 per student: one BigQuery query, reading two large files (pennies), plus the app


📋 Before class
easier after 4.5 and 4.6; run the setup cell to install the packages

title: 4.7 RNA and Protein Together
text:
Key concepts

Why RNA and protein disagree
Using the IKEA analogy: RNA is the copy of the assembly instructions, protein is the furniture.








Reason
In the analogy
In the body




Different places
furniture built in another store
many plasma proteins are made in the liver, kidney, or fat, not in the blood cells whose RNA we measured


Different timing
furniture lasts years after the instructions are recycled
proteins can last hours to weeks; RNA minutes to hours


Control after RNA
plenty of instructions, but not enough pieces
cells control how much protein each RNA makes


Different samples

RNA from whole blood; proteins from plasma





Spearman correlation
The usual correlation, but on ranks, so a few extreme values don’t dominate. From −1 to 1; 0 means no relationship.

title: 4.7 RNA and Protein Together
text:
Code walk-through

Matching proteins to genes
uniprot_to_gene <- read_tsv(file.path(PROT_DIR, "pqtl", "cis_pqtl", "AoU_v9_COMB.cis_pqtl.txt.gz"),
1                            col_select = "phenotype_id", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
2  transmute(UniProt = str_remove(phenotype_id, "_.*"),
3            gene_id = str_remove(str_remove(phenotype_id, "^[^_]*_"), "\\..*")) %>%
  distinct()

1

The pQTL file from 4.6 names each protein as P09769_ENSG00000000938.13: a ready-made lookup table from protein to gene. col_select reads only that column.

2

The UniProt ID: everything before the underscore.

3

The Ensembl gene ID: everything after the underscore, without the version number (.13), which can differ between files.




Correlation, pair by pair
pairs <- pairs %>%
1  mutate(rho = map2_dbl(rna_row, OlinkID,
2                        ~ cor(logcpm[.x, ], npx[.y, ], method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")))

1

map2_dbl() runs the next line once for each pair: .x is the gene’s row in the RNA matrix, .y the protein’s row in the protein matrix.

2

The Spearman correlation across our people, using everyone with both values.

title: 4.7 RNA and Protein Together
text:
What we found
Results from our test run in October 2026 (CDR v9), 300 cases and 300 controls with both layers.







People with both layers
8,801 of 8,980 with RNA-seq


Correlations
median about 0.01: most pairs barely correlate


Significant
510 positive and 79 negative (FDR < 0.05)


Best-agreeing pairs
immune-cell proteins: B cells (TCL1A, FCRL1, FCRL3), NK and T cells (GZMH, GNLY, FCRL6), neutrophils (OLFM4, VSTM1); also MDGA1, SPESP1, PVALB


Diabetes effects, RNA vs protein
correlation of t-statistics about 0 (−0.04): the layers don’t line up


Proteins overall
shifted a little higher in diabetes, whatever their RNA did



💬 Discuss:

Why might proteins that aren’t made by blood cells (MDGA1, PVALB) still correlate with their RNA? (A genetic variant that raises both: an eQTL and a pQTL at once.)
Why might many proteins be higher in diabetes regardless of RNA? (One idea: lower kidney clearance, since the kidneys remove many proteins from the blood. Test it by adjusting for kidney function, eGFR.)

title: 4.7 RNA and Protein Together
text:
The whole series









Class
Layer
Main finding (our test runs)
What it can’t tell us




4.1
DNA
the T allele is more common in cases (OR ≈ 1.17, unadjusted)
cause or tissue


4.2–4.3
DNA
adjusted OR ≈ 1.25; a peak across TCF7L2; PLINK and Hail agree
which variant is causal


4.4
DNA + EHR
rs7903146 goes with diabetes, its treatments and complications, and slightly less obesity
consequence vs direct effect; collider bias


4.5
RNA (blood)
a few dozen genes differ, many from neutrophils; rs7903146 barely affects TCF7L2 in blood
other tissues; cell mix


4.6
Protein (plasma)
hundreds differ, pointing to the kidney, fat, and gut; strong pQTLs
cause vs consequence vs treatment


4.7
Both
RNA and protein agree mainly for immune-cell proteins; diabetes effects don’t line up
anything outside blood



DNA tells us about lifelong risk and can help argue about cause. RNA and proteins show what’s happening now, including consequences and treatment. Each layer answers a different question; combining them carefully is how multi-omics studies get closer to how a disease works.

title: 4.7 RNA and Protein Together
text:
Key takeaways

RNA and protein often disagree, especially in blood: many plasma proteins are made elsewhere

title: 4.5 RNA-seq: Gene Activity in Type 2 Diabetes
text:
Overview
DNA is the same in every cell and fixed from birth. RNA shows which genes are active, and how much, when a sample was taken. All of Us has measured gene activity (RNA sequencing, RNA-seq) in whole blood for about 9,000 participants. We ask which genes are more or less active in people with type 2 diabetes, then connect back to DNA: does the T allele of rs7903146 change how much TCF7L2 is made in blood?

Why this class matters
RNA-seq is one of the most common omics measurements, and its analysis has a step that’s easy to get wrong without noticing: normalization. The statistics package (limma) doesn’t normalize for you; it will happily give p-values for badly normalized data. This class shows each step, checks it, and ends by linking DNA to RNA with an eQTL.


By the end you’ll be able to

Explain what RNA-seq measures, and counts vs TPM
Use the RNA quality measures, and add RNA quality to the model
Normalize counts (TMM, log-CPM), and check that it worked
Run differential expression with limma-voom, and read a volcano plot
Test whether a variant is linked to a gene’s activity (an eQTL), and look it up in All of Us’s results



Analysis at a glance







❓ Questions
Which genes are more or less active in the blood of people with type 2 diabetes? Does rs7903146 change TCF7L2 activity in blood?


🧪 The analysis
Counts normalized (TMM) and log-transformed; a linear model per gene with limma-voom, adjusted for age, sex, and RNA quality; then an eQTL test


🎯 Why
Raw counts can’t be compared until normalized; expression is a number, so linear models; ~29,000 genes, so an adjusted p-value (FDR)


✅ What we conclude
Which genes and processes differ, and whether the variant acts through blood


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Cause vs consequence vs treatment; other tissues; whether cells changed or the mix of cells changed


🔗 Connections
The variant from 4.1–4.4; proteins in 4.6; both in 4.7. GWAS + eQTL = colocalization





Time and cost







⏱️ Class time
120 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 10 minutes (plus 5–10 the first time, to install limma and edgeR). Slowest: loading the counts


💰 Cost
about $1 to $2 per student: one BigQuery query, reading files (pennies), plus the app


📋 Before class
run the setup cell once, to install the packages

Key concepts

Counts need normalizing








Problem
Example
Fixed by




Sequencing depth
person A sequenced twice as deeply: every gene has twice the reads
counts per million (CPM)


Composition
a few hugely active genes “use up” reads, making every other gene look lower
TMM (edgeR): assumes most genes don’t change, and scales each person so they line up


Skew
a few genes have huge counts
the log₂ scale (a step of 1 = twice as much)


Low counts are noisy
genes with few reads vary a lot by chance
voom: gives each value a weight



All of Us did the processing (aligning reads, counting them per gene), but not the normalization: that’s our job, and limma doesn’t do it.


Whole blood
The RNA comes from blood: a mix of cell types, mostly white blood cells. Much of type 2 diabetes happens in the pancreas, liver, muscle, and fat, which blood doesn’t show. And a difference between groups can come from a change in the mix of cells, not each cell’s activity.

title: 4.5 RNA-seq: Gene Activity in Type 2 Diabetes
text:
Code walk-through

Filter and normalize
1dge <- DGEList(counts = counts, genes = genes, samples = samples)

2keep_genes <- filterByExpr(dge, group = samples$group)
dge <- dge[keep_genes, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]
3dge <- calcNormFactors(dge)

4logcpm <- cpm(dge, log = TRUE)

1

One object holding the counts (genes × people), the gene names, and the sample table.

2

Keep genes with enough reads, in enough people, to analyse (about 29,000 of 78,000).

3

TMM normalization: one factor per person, correcting for composition. The notebook then checks these factors and shows boxplots before and after.

4

Normalized log₂ counts per million, for plots and PCA.




Differential expression
1design <- model.matrix(~ group + age + sex_at_birth + rqs, data = samples)

2v   <- voom(dge, design, plot = TRUE)
3fit <- eBayes(lmFit(v, design))

4results <- topTable(fit, coef = "groupcase", number = Inf)

1

The model for every gene: group (case vs control), adjusted for age, sex, and RNA quality (rqs), a technical covariate.

2

voom turns counts into log values with a weight each, and draws the mean-variance trend (a smooth downward curve is what you want).

3

Fit the model to every gene; eBayes() shares information across genes, which makes each test more reliable.

4

The results for the case-vs-control term, every gene, sorted by p-value.

title: 4.5 RNA-seq: Gene Activity in Type 2 Diabetes
text:
What we found
Results from our test run in October 2026 (CDR v9), 300 cases and 300 controls.







People with RNA-seq
1,312 cases, 5,538 controls


Cases vs controls
older (64 vs 52); RNA quality almost identical (7.7 vs 7.8)


Genes kept
28,902 of 77,814


PCA
PC1 split everyone into two clusters: sex, not diabetes


Significant genes
a few dozen (adjusted p < 0.05)


Higher in diabetes
many neutrophil genes: MMP8, LTF, CRISP3, HP, ANXA3


Lower in diabetes
ABCG1 (cholesterol transport), NRCAM (the top gene)


Normalization check
medians uneven before, level after TMM; voom trend smooth and downward


Pathways (GO)
up in diabetes: immune system process (p ≈ 7 × 10⁻⁶), defense response, TNF production, phagocytosis; few genes per term, so a supporting theme


Neutrophil challenge (369 people with a count)
neutrophil genes’ logFC shrank about 20–45% (e.g. MMP8 0.70 → 0.54) but didn’t disappear: the cell mix explains part of the signal


TCF7L2
not different between groups (adjusted p ≈ 0.95)


Our eQTL test
no effect of the T allele on TCF7L2 (estimate ≈ −0.01, p ≈ 0.6)


All of Us eQTLs (~9,000 people)
TCF7L2’s strongest eQTL is a different variant (chr10:112951996_C_T, slope −0.25); rs7903146’s effect is tiny (slope 0.02, p ≈ 0.004)



💬 Discuss:

Are the neutrophil genes higher because each neutrophil changed, or because people with diabetes have more neutrophils (inflammation)? How would you tell? (Adjust for neutrophil counts: the challenge exercise.)
rs7903146 is one of the strongest diabetes risk variants, yet it barely touches TCF7L2 in blood. What does that say about tissue? (Its known effects are in the pancreas, where insulin is made.)


The plots


The PCA plot, the before/after normalization boxplots (one box per person), and the genotype boxplot show people: they stay in the notebook.

title: 4.3 A GWAS with Hail (Python)
text:
Overview
Hail is the Python library All of Us uses for its own large genomic analyses, including the All by All results. In this class we run the same GWAS as 4.2 in Hail, on the same people, and check that the two tools agree. You don’t need to know Python already: the notebook has a guide for R users.

Why this class matters
Two reasons. Reproducibility: a result that changes with the software is a warning sign, and checking a key finding with a second tool is good practice. Scale: PLINK is fast on one computer, but genome-wide analyses of hundreds of thousands of genomes need a tool that can spread the work over a cluster, and Hail is built for that.


By the end you’ll be able to

Explain what Hail is, and how a MatrixTable holds genomic data
Read part of the All of Us genomes with Hail, and save a small working copy (a checkpoint)
Run QC and a logistic-regression GWAS with Hail
Turn Hail results into a pandas table, and plot them
Compare Hail’s results with PLINK’s, and explain the small differences



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
Does a second tool, Hail, give the same GWAS results as PLINK?


🧪 The analysis
The same QC and logistic regression per variant as 4.2, in Hail; then a variant-by-variant comparison with PLINK


🎯 Why
Reproducibility, and learning the tool All of Us uses at scale


✅ What we conclude
Whether the tools agree, and why small differences arise


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Nothing new about diabetes: this class is about tools and data structures


🔗 Connections
Compares with 4.2; the approach behind the All by All results in 4.4





Time and cost

120 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 5 minutes. Slowest: reading the genomes into the checkpoint (2–3 minutes)

about $1 per student: no BigQuery query; the app (about $0.27 an hour)

Key concepts

The MatrixTable



Part
In All of Us
Example fields




Rows
variants
locus, alleles


Columns

Entries
one person’s genotype at one variant
GT


Globals
facts about the whole dataset






Lazy evaluation
Hail plans first and works later: filtering and annotating only add to the plan, and finish instantly. Nothing is read until you ask for an answer (a count, a table, a file). So one cell, the checkpoint, does all the slow work: it reads our window for all 535,000 people, keeps our 5,000, and saves a small copy that every later step reads in seconds.


splitMT: one row per ALT allele
All of Us provides Hail genomes in two versions. multiMT keeps a variant with several ALT alleles in one row; splitMT, which we use, splits it into one row per ALT allele, because regression needs one allele per row. So Hail has more rows than PLINK for the same window.
