title: 4.3 A GWAS with Hail (Python)
text:
Code walk-through

Keep our window and our people
1mt = hl.filter_intervals(mt, [hl.parse_locus_interval(WINDOW)])
2mt = mt.semi_join_cols(samples_ht)
3mt = mt.annotate_cols(pheno = samples_ht[mt.s])

1

Keep only variants in our 200,000-letter window (like PLINK’s --chr --from-bp --to-bp).

2

Keep only the people in our sample table (like a semi-join in R, or PLINK’s --keep).

3

Add each person’s phenotype and covariates: samples_ht[mt.s] means “the row of the sample table matching this person’s ID”. All three lines are instant: they only add to the plan.




The checkpoint
if REBUILD or not os.path.exists(CHECKPOINT_PATH):
1    mt = mt.checkpoint(CHECKPOINT_PATH, overwrite=True)
else:
2    mt = hl.read_matrix_table(CHECKPOINT_PATH)

1

Run the plan and save the result to the app’s disk: the slow step (150 seconds in our test).

2

If the copy already exists (e.g. when rerunning), just open it.




The GWAS
1covariates = [1.0, mt.pheno.age, mt.pheno.sex_male] + [mt.pheno[pc] for pc in PCS]

gwas = hl.logistic_regression_rows(
2    test="wald",
3    y=mt.pheno.is_case,
4    x=mt.GT.n_alt_alleles(),
    covariates=covariates,
)

1

The covariates. 1.0 is the intercept: Hail needs it written out (R and PLINK add it for you). [... for pc in PCS] builds a list of the 10 PCs.

2

The standard Wald test.

3

The outcome: case or control.

4

The genotype as 0, 1, or 2 copies of the ALT allele.

title: 4.1 Introduction to Genomic Data
text:
Overview
All of Us has sequenced the genomes of more than 535,000 participants. This class answers the first questions anyone has about that data: what is it, where is it, who has it, and how do I connect it to people’s health records? It ends with a first look at rs7903146, the variant in the gene TCF7L2 that is the strongest known genetic risk factor for type 2 diabetes.

Why this class matters
Every later genetics class (4.2–4.4) depends on what happens here: the cohort linked to genomes, the related people removed, the genetic ancestry that every model adjusts for, and a small extract of the genome that’s cheap to work with. Doing these steps carefully once, and understanding them, prevents the most common mistakes in genetic studies.


By the end you’ll be able to

Explain DNA, variants, alleles, and genotypes in plain language
Describe the All of Us genomic data and its file formats
Find the genomic files, and the ready-made ancestry and relatedness files
Link genomes to the type 2 diabetes cohort and choose a fair sample
Use PLINK 2 to extract one region of the genome, and look at one famous variant



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
Where is the genomic data, who in our cohort has it, and is the T allele of rs7903146 more common in people with type 2 diabetes?


🧪 The analysis
Counts and allele frequencies in cases and controls; a first logistic regression of case status on the number of T alleles (unadjusted)


🎯 Why
Before any genome-wide analysis, check that the genomes link to the cohort and that a known signal shows up. Logistic regression, because the outcome is yes/no


✅ What we conclude
The direction and rough size of a well-known association, and a sample ready for 4.2


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
The effect after accounting for age, sex, and ancestry; anything about other variants; whether the variant causes diabetes


🔗 Connections
Saves the sample and files used by 4.2 and 4.3; its ancestry PCs are used in 4.2–4.4





Time and cost







⏱️ Class time
120 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 5 minutes to run every cell. Slowest: the cohort query (1–2 minutes)

about $1 to $2 per student: one BigQuery query (under $1) plus the app (about $0.27 an hour)

title: 4.1 Introduction to Genomic Data
text:
Key concepts
The essentials are below. Omics for Beginners has the full glossary.

Variants and genotypes
People’s DNA is 99.9% the same. The places where it differs are variants. At rs7903146, people have a C or a T (and, very rarely, a G). Each person has two copies (one from each parent), so their genotype is counted as 0, 1, or 2 copies of the T allele:



Genotype
Copies of T




C/C
0


C/T
1


T/T
2



Each extra copy of T raises the odds of type 2 diabetes by about 30 to 40% in large published studies. TCF7L2 affects how the pancreas releases insulin.


How the genomic files are organised
All of Us provides the genomes in several formats, one set of files per chromosome. We use the PLINK 2 format, a set of three files:
acaf_threshold.chr10.pgen   genotypes (compressed): 80 GB
acaf_threshold.chr10.pvar   the variants: one row each
acaf_threshold.chr10.psam   the people: one row each
ACAF is the subset of common variants (above about 1% frequency in at least one ancestry group).
One chromosome is 80 GB, so the class never reads a whole one: PLINK jumps to the region we need and reads only that.


Why remove related people, and adjust for ancestry?

Relatives share long stretches of DNA, which makes results look more certain than they are. All of Us provides a list of people to remove so that no two remaining people are closely related.
Genetic ancestry affects both allele frequencies and disease rates. Without accounting for it, a variant can look linked to a disease just because both are more common in one group (confounding). All of Us provides each person’s ancestry group and principal components (PCs): a few numbers that summarise their genetic ancestry, used as covariates from 4.2 on.

title: 4.1 Introduction to Genomic Data
text:
Code walk-through
The key steps, line by line. The notebook explains every cell; these are the ones beginners most often ask about.

Linking genomes to the cohort
1cohort <- run_query(str_glue(cohort_sql, AGE_DATE = "2025-01-01")) %>%
2  mutate(person_id = as.character(person_id))

psam <- read_tsv(file.path(pgen_dir, "acaf_threshold.chr10.psam"),
3                 col_types = cols(.default = "c"))
4genome_ids <- psam[["#IID"]]

5cohort <- cohort %>% mutate(has_genome = person_id %in% genome_ids)

1

Run the shared type 2 diabetes query (in notebooks/sql/t2d_cohort.sql), with age calculated on 2025-01-01, the v9 data cutoff.

2

Turn person_id into text. The genome files store IDs as text, and a number never matches text in R, even with the same digits.

3

Read the .psam file (one row per person with a genome), with every column as text.

4

The ID column is called #IID. The # is part of its name, so it’s written in quotes inside [[ ]].

5

%in% asks, for each person in the cohort: is your ID in the genome list? The answer (TRUE or FALSE) becomes a new column.




Choosing a fair sample
eligible <- cohort %>%
1  filter(cohort %in% c("case", "control"),
2         has_genome,
3         !person_id %in% related$sample_id,
4         between(age, 18, 100),
5         sex_at_birth %in% c("Female", "Male"))

6set.seed(2026)
gwas_samples <- eligible %>%
7  arrange(person_id) %>%
  group_by(cohort) %>%
8  slice_sample(n = 2500) %>%
  ungroup()

1

Keep cases and controls (drop the “excluded” group, e.g. people with type 1 diabetes).

2

Keep people with a genome.

3

Drop people on the relatedness list (! means “not”).

4

Ages 18 to 100: a few recorded ages above 100 are probably data errors.

5

Sex at birth is a covariate later, so it must be recorded as Female or Male.

6

Fix the random number generator, so everyone gets the same “random” sample.

7

Sort first: BigQuery doesn’t return rows in a fixed order, and the same seed only gives the same sample if the rows start in the same order.

8

Pick 2,500 at random within each group (because of group_by()).




Counting the T allele
1write_lines("chr10:112998590:C\tT", allele_file)

system(str_glue(
  "plink2 --pfile {shQuote(out_prefix)} ",
2  "--chr 10 --from-bp 112998590 --to-bp 112998590 ",
3  "--export A --export-allele {shQuote(allele_file)} ",
  "--out {shQuote(lead_prefix)}"
), intern = TRUE)

1

A one-line file: the variant’s ID and the allele to count. \t is a tab.

2

Just one position: rs7903146.

3

--export A writes each person’s genotype as 0, 1, or 2 copies of an allele. Because rs7903146 has two ALT alleles (T and G), PLINK would count the REF allele (C) by default; --export-allele tells it to count T.


The PLINK command that extracts the region is explained line by line on the Omics for Beginners page.

535,662 people had a short-read genome. Chromosome 10 was 80 GB in the PLINK 2 format and 846 GB in PLINK 1. PLINK extracted the TCF7L2 region for our 5,000 people in about 10 seconds: 14,430 variants.
💬 Discuss: most people in our cohort have a genome, but not all. Who might be missing, and could that matter?

The three smallest groups are combined: on their own, some were 20 or fewer, and with the column totals (2,500) a hidden count could be worked out. That’s the All of Us rule on derived counts (more in 3.1).
💬 Discuss: cases include more people of African and Admixed American ancestry than controls do. Why does that make adjusting for ancestry important in 4.2?


rs7903146

In All of Us as a whole, rs7903146 is multi-allelic: REF C, ALT T or G. About 28% of alleles are T; G is extremely rare.
Variant IDs in the files are chromosome:position:REF (chr10:112998590:C), not rsIDs.





Cases
Controls




T allele frequency
0.301
0.270



Odds ratio per T allele (unadjusted): 1.17 (95% confidence interval 1.07 to 1.27; p = 0.0006).
💬 Discuss: large published studies report about 1.3 to 1.4, mostly in people of European ancestry. Why might our first estimate be smaller? (Mixed ancestry, no adjustment, diagnosis codes as the case definition, younger controls who may develop diabetes later.) In 4.2, after adjustment, it rises to about 1.25.






NoteWhy the first odds ratio was 0.86 (a lesson from testing)





The first time we ran this notebook, the odds ratio came out below 1 (0.86). The variant hadn’t changed: PLINK was counting the C allele, because for a multi-allelic variant it counts REF by default. 1 ÷ 0.857 = 1.17, the same result counted the other way. Always check which allele a result is “per copy” of: the column name in PLINK’s output ends with it (_T).

Instructor notes






TipInstructor tip: timing and pitfalls






Run Part 3’s cohort query during Part 2’s discussion if the class is short on time: it takes 1–2 minutes.
The most common error is IDs stored as numbers. If --keep: 0 samples remaining, check that person_id was turned into text before keep.txt was written.
Stuck git pull: in our testing, a pull that looked stuck had actually finished. Press Enter before assuming it’s frozen.
Questions to expect: “Is genetic ancestry the same as race?” (No: one is estimated from DNA, the other is a social category people report.) “Why not use everyone?” (Cost and time: 5,000 people are enough to see the TCF7L2 signal.)










TipInstructor tip: a newer approach to ancestry





A newer method, genomic-relatedness-matched association (GRMA), compares people with their closest genetic relatives instead of adjusting for PCs (All of Us Office Hours, 2026-08-28). It’s a good discussion point on whether PCs remove all confounding.

title: Machine Learning Series
text:
R classes on prediction, with the same cohort as every other series: people with type 2 diabetes and people without diabetes. The question in every class: from data collected before a diagnosis, who will be diagnosed with type 2 diabetes in the next few years?
The earlier series asked why: is steps, income, or a genetic variant linked to diabetes? This series asks who: for one person, what’s the risk? That’s one of All of Us’s scientific goals, and a step towards precision medicine (“precision prevention”).
New to machine learning? Start with Machine learning for beginners: prediction vs explanation, training and test data, overfitting, AUC, calibration, and leakage.

text:
The design: time zero
A prediction model may only use data from before the outcome. So every class has a time zero: predictors are measured before it, and only new diagnoses after it count.
                time zero                                    2 years later
                    |──────────────── follow-up ─────────────────|
  predictors measured here                    a NEW type 2 diabetes diagnosis? yes / no
  excluded: anyone already diagnosed
We checked this design before building any class, in a planning notebook (ML data check):

about 5,800
about 380



About 77% of people with type 2 diabetes in All of Us were diagnosed before they enrolled. They’re left out of every model: their data describe life with diabetes.
The proteomics time zero. The proteomics files have no sample date. The genome files do: a biosample_collection_date for each genome sample. For people with proteomics, the median gap between enrollment and that blood draw was 0 days (80% within 30 days). So 7.3 starts the clock at the later of the two, assuming the proteins and the genome came from the same visit.

section: Keep All of Us data in the Workbench
text:
Keep All of Us data in the Workbench
Don’t download, screenshot, or share participant-level data, or counts of 1 to 20 (including counts that could be worked out from others). Two traps in this series:

ROC curves from roc_curve() have a point for every person’s predicted risk. Our classes draw them from 50 cut-offs, each summarising hundreds of people.
Calibration tables by risk group often have small counts in the lowest-risk groups: they’re hidden, with one more if only one would be.

The results on these pages come from the All of Us Research Program’s Controlled Tier Dataset v9, available to authorized users on the Researcher Workbench. We gratefully acknowledge All of Us participants for their contributions. See Acknowledgment and data availability.

title: 7.1 A First Prediction Model
text:
Overview
Can we tell, on the day someone joins All of Us, who is likely to be diagnosed with type 2 diabetes in the next 2 years? In this class we build that prediction from what’s known at enrollment: age, sex, BMI, blood pressure, and a few survey answers. We fit a logistic regression, test it on people it has never seen, and then try LASSO, a method that chooses predictors for us.

Why this class matters
Every earlier class explained: is income, steps, or a variant linked to diabetes? Prediction asks a different question, for one person, and has different traps. The biggest is leakage: using information you wouldn’t have had at the time. In All of Us, most people with diabetes were diagnosed before they joined, so a careless model learns the consequences of diabetes, not its warning signs.


By the end you’ll be able to

Turn a research question into a prediction question: who, from what, predicting what, by when
Build an outcome that only uses the future, and predictors that only use the past
Split the data into training and test sets, and say why
Fit a logistic regression with tidymodels, and measure it with the AUC
Check calibration: do predicted risks match what happened?
Tune a LASSO with cross-validation, and compare it with the simple model



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
From what’s known at enrollment, how well can we predict a new type 2 diabetes diagnosis within 2 years?


🧪 The analysis
Adults without diabetes at enrollment, with BMI and blood pressure measured then; a 75/25 train/test split; logistic regression (age and sex, + BMI, + everything), then LASSO tuned by 5-fold cross-validation


🎯 Why
Logistic regression is the standard first model for a yes/no outcome. Testing on held-out people shows how it would do on new people


✅ What we conclude
How well enrollment data separate people who will and won’t be diagnosed (AUC), whether the risks are right (calibration), and how much each kind of data adds


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Cause: a predictor can predict without causing anything. And whether the model works outside All of Us


🔗 Connections
The cohort query from 1.1; plausible values from 2.1; logistic regression from 3.2; survey answers from 5.1–5.3; “measure first, then follow” from 6.2





Time and cost



⏱️ Class time
95 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 10 minutes, plus up to 15 minutes the first time to install tidymodels


💰 Cost
about $1 to $2 per student: the cohort query, and one query for everyone’s enrollment data, priced first


📋 Before class
read Machine learning for beginners; 3.2 (logistic regression) is helpful

title: 7.1 A First Prediction Model
text:
Code walk-through

What’s known at enrollment, in one query
Enrollment is each person’s first survey. BMI and blood pressure are the values closest to it, within a year before and 30 days after; survey answers must be given by 30 days after. Later answers could be leakage.
answers AS (
  SELECT s.person_id, s.question_concept_id, s.answer, s.survey_datetime
  FROM `{CURRENT_DATASET}.ds_survey` AS s
  JOIN enroll AS e ON s.person_id = e.person_id
  WHERE s.question_concept_id IN (...)
1    AND DATE(s.survey_datetime) <= DATE_ADD(e.enroll_date, INTERVAL 30 DAY)
)

1

Only answers given by 30 days after enrollment: what a model used at enrollment could know.




A flow table, one rule at a time
1keep <- accumulate(rules, `&`)

tibble(rule = names(rules), people = map_int(keep, sum)) %>%
  mutate(removed = lag(people) - people,
2         across(c(people, removed), ~ if_else(removed %in% 1:20, NA_integer_, .x)))

1

accumulate() combines each rule with every rule before it: rule 1, then 1 and 2, then 1, 2 and 3, …

2

A step that removes 1 to 20 people would show a small count: it’s hidden.




Three models, one function
fit_logistic <- function(predictors) {
  workflow() %>%
1    add_formula(reformulate(predictors, response = "t2d_future")) %>%
    add_model(logistic_reg()) %>%
2    fit(data = train)
}

test_auc <- function(fit, model) {
3  augment(fit, new_data = test) %>%
4    roc_auc(truth = t2d_future, .pred_yes, event_level = "second") %>%
    transmute(model, test_auc = round(.estimate, 3))
}

1

reformulate() builds a formula from a list of names: t2d_future ~ age + sex_at_birth + bmi.

2

Fitted on the training set only.

3

augment() adds each test person’s predicted risk, .pred_yes.

4

The outcome’s levels are no, yes, so the event, yes, is the second level.




LASSO, tuned by cross-validation
lasso_recipe <- recipe(t2d_future ~ ., data = train) %>%
1  step_spline_natural(age, bmi, sbp, deg_free = 4) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
2  step_interact(terms = ~ starts_with("sex_at_birth"):matches("^(age|bmi|sbp)_")) %>%
3  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

lasso_tuning <- tune_grid(lasso_workflow,
4                          resamples = vfold_cv(train, v = 5, strata = t2d_future),
                          grid      = grid_regular(penalty(range = c(-5, -1)), levels = 20),
                          metrics   = metric_set(roc_auc))

5chosen <- select_by_one_std_err(lasso_tuning, desc(penalty), metric = "roc_auc")

1

Natural splines: each number becomes 4 columns, so its effect can bend.

2

Interactions with sex: the curves can differ for women and men.

3

All columns on the same scale, so the penalty treats them fairly.

4

5-fold cross-validation, on the training set only.

5

The largest penalty (the simplest model) within one standard error of the best.

What we found
From our test run in November 2026 (CDR v9). The query read 31.8 GB, about $0.20.

Who was studied

295,908

health records for 2 years, or diagnosed sooner
152,586

8,487 people (5.6%) were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes within 2 years of enrolling (2017 to 2024). The 2-year rule removed the most people: those who enrolled recently, and those whose health records stop. A survival model (3.4, 6.2) could keep them.
The 75/25 split gave 114,439 people for training and 38,147 for testing, each with about 5.5% new cases.


How well the models predict







Model
Test AUC




1. Age and sex
0.577


2. + BMI
0.709


3. All enrollment data (+ blood pressure, general health, income, education, smoking)
0.743


4. LASSO: splines and interactions
0.748





Age and sex barely beat a coin toss: everyone here was free of diabetes at enrollment, at every age.
BMI added the most.
The survey answers added a useful amount more, mostly through general health.
LASSO matched logistic regression: with a few strong predictors, bending the lines added little.



What the model uses
Odds ratios from model 3, with 95% confidence intervals:



Predictor
OR (95% CI)




BMI, per unit (kg/m²)
1.07 (1.07 to 1.07): about 1.40 per 5 units


Male (vs female)
1.43 (1.35 to 1.51)


Age, per year
1.02 (1.02 to 1.02)


General health Good (vs Excellent)
2.13 (1.86 to 2.43)


General health Fair
3.21 (2.80 to 3.68)


General health Poor
4.74 (4.06 to 5.54)


Income under 25k (vs 100k or more)
1.39 (1.26 to 1.54)


Less than high school (vs college degree)
1.56 (1.42 to 1.72)


Current smoker (vs never)
1.07 (0.99 to 1.16)



Self-rated health was the strongest survey predictor: people who rate their health as poor may already have diabetes, undiagnosed. That helps a prediction, and says nothing about cause.


Are the risks right?

Predicted risks ranged from about 0.9% in the lowest tenth to 18% in the highest, and the observed rates followed them closely, up to 16.4% in the top tenth: a little over-predicted. The two lowest-risk tenths had 1 to 20 new cases, so they’re hidden.
A screening rule: the 10% of people with the highest predicted risk included 30% of all future cases. 16.4% of them were diagnosed within 2 years, compared with 4.2% of everyone else.


Choosing the LASSO penalty

The AUC was flat for small penalties, then fell as the penalty removed useful predictors. At the largest penalties, every coefficient was zero, and the AUC was 0.5: the same risk for everyone.

text:
Instructor notes

Draw the timeline first: time zero, predictors before it, the 2-year window after it. Most of the class follows from it.
Open with the surprise: about 77% of people with type 2 diabetes in All of Us were diagnosed before they enrolled. Ask: what would a model learn from them?

AUC vs calibration: ask which matters for a patient told “your risk is 8%”.
LASSO ≈ logistic regression here is a result, not a failure: with a few strong predictors, more flexibility adds little. 7.2 tests that with trees.

title: 7.1 A First Prediction Model
text:
Key takeaways

A prediction question has four parts: who, from what (known when?), predicting what, and by when.
Leakage is avoided by dating every predictor, and starting the clock at time zero.
Judge a model on a test set it never saw: AUC for ranking, calibration for the numbers.
Cross-validation chooses settings on the training set, so the test set stays honest.
A simple model with the right predictors is hard to beat.

title: Core Series: Cohorts to Analysis
text:
Nine R classes that take one study from start to finish, with All of Us health records: people with type 2 diabetes compared with people without diabetes, including how quickly people with diabetes develop chronic kidney disease (CKD).

The bigger picture: how this series connects to All of Us’s goal of precision medicine: see Precision Medicine: where our classes fit.

title: 3.4 Survival Analysis
text:
Overview
Among people with type 2 diabetes, how long until chronic kidney disease (CKD), and who gets it sooner? With the dates gathered in 1.2 (time zero, the event, censoring), we draw Kaplan–Meier curves and fit a Cox model.

Why this class matters
“How long until” questions are everywhere in health research: time to a complication, to a hospital readmission, to death. Survival methods are built for them, because they use everyone’s follow-up, including people who leave the records without the event. This class also lists the traps specific to health record data, which a tidy-looking curve can hide.


By the end you’ll be able to

Build time-to-event data with censoring
Estimate and plot Kaplan–Meier curves with ggplot2, and compare them with a log-rank test
Fit a Cox model, and read hazard ratios
Check the proportional-hazards assumption
Explain the pitfalls of survival analysis in health records



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
After a type 2 diabetes diagnosis, how quickly do people develop CKD, and is it faster with higher HbA1c?


🧪 The analysis
Kaplan–Meier curves by HbA1c group, a log-rank test, then a Cox model adjusted for age at diagnosis, sex, and BMI


🎯 Why
People are followed for different lengths of time; censoring uses all of it


✅ What we conclude
The share CKD-free over time, and hazard ratios


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Cause. HbA1c and BMI are the latest values, often measured after time zero


🔗 Connections
Dates from 1.2, joined in 2.3; builds on 3.2 and 3.3

Term
Means

Censored

Hazard

Code walk-through
1km_fit <- survfit(Surv(time_years, status) ~ hba1c_group, data = surv_data)
2km_df  <- tidy(km_fit) %>%
  mutate(group = str_remove(strata, "hba1c_group="))

ggplot(km_df, aes(time, estimate, colour = group)) +
3  geom_step(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_step(aes(y = conf.low),  linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_step(aes(y = conf.high), linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.6)

4survdiff(Surv(time_years, status) ~ hba1c_group, data = surv_data)

cox_model <- coxph(Surv(time_years, status) ~ age10_at_t2d + sex_at_birth + BMI5 + hba1c_group,
5                   data = cox_data)

1

Surv(time, status) is the outcome: follow-up time, and 1 for CKD or 0 for censored. survfit() estimates one Kaplan–Meier curve per HbA1c group.

2

tidy() turns the curves into a table that ggplot2 can draw (the notebook also adds a starting point at 100%).

3

Kaplan–Meier curves are steps, not smooth lines; the dashed steps are the 95% confidence limits. This replaces the survminer package, which doesn’t install in the app.

4

The log-rank test: are the curves different?

5

The Cox model: hazard ratios for several predictors at once, each adjusted for the others.

💬 Discuss the pitfalls:

title: 3.2 Logistic Regression
text:
Overview
Table 1 showed that cases are older and heavier, with different blood pressure and cholesterol. But those differences overlap: older people are also heavier, on average. Logistic regression asks how each characteristic goes with the odds of type 2 diabetes while holding the others constant.

Why this class matters
Logistic regression is the most common model in health research for yes/no outcomes, and the same model powers the GWAS in 4.2. This class also shows two of its classic traps in real data: adjusting for a variable that defines the outcome (HbA1c), and reverse causation (LDL cholesterol after treatment).


By the end you’ll be able to

Explain odds and odds ratios
Fit univariable and multivariable models with glm(), and read them with broom::tidy()
Put predictors on readable scales
Compare models fitted on the same people
Explain why HbA1c is left out, and what reverse causation is



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
Which characteristics go with higher odds of type 2 diabetes, accounting for each other?


🧪 The analysis
Logistic regression: type 2 diabetes ~ age + sex + BMI + blood pressure + LDL, built up step by step


🎯 Why
A yes/no outcome; multivariable, because the predictors are related (confounding)


✅ What we conclude
Adjusted odds ratios, e.g. per 5 BMI units, at the same age and sex


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Cause. Measurements taken after diagnosis can reflect the disease or its treatment


🔗 Connections
The same model as the GWAS in 4.2; 3.3 is the version for a numeric outcome

title: 3.2 Logistic Regression
text:
Key concepts

Odds = chance it happens ÷ chance it doesn’t (20% → 0.25).
Odds ratio (OR): the odds in one group ÷ another. 1 = no difference; 2 = twice the odds.
For a number like BMI, the OR is per unit, so we choose a readable unit: per 5 BMI units, per 10 years.
Our sample is half cases by design (a case-control sample). That makes risk meaningless here, but odds ratios stay valid: that’s why case-control studies report them.





Univariable
Multivariable




Model
diabetes ~ one predictor
diabetes ~ several


OR is
crude
adjusted for the others

Try It Out






Tip✋ Try It Out · 10 minutes · Part 5, “Your turn”

✅ Check: many more people (especially controls), and a similar BMI OR: a sensitivity analysis.

title: 3.2 Logistic Regression
text:
Code walk-through
1model_data <- fa %>% drop_na(t2d_binary, age10, sex_at_birth, BMI5, SBP10, LDL10)

models <- list(
2  "1. Age + sex"             = glm(t2d_binary ~ age10 + sex_at_birth,  data = model_data, family = binomial),
  "2. + BMI"                 = glm(t2d_binary ~ age10 + sex_at_birth + BMI5, data = model_data, family = binomial),
  "3. + blood pressure, LDL" = glm(t2d_binary ~ age10 + sex_at_birth + BMI5 + SBP10 + LDL10,
                                   data = model_data, family = binomial)
)

3imap(models, ~ tidy(.x, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>% mutate(model = .y))

1

One data set with every model variable present, so all three models use the same people. Otherwise a change in an OR could just be a change in who’s in the model.

2

glm(…, family = binomial) is logistic regression. age10, BMI5, … are the predictors divided by 10 or 5, for readable ORs.

3

tidy(exponentiate = TRUE) turns coefficients into odds ratios, with 95% confidence intervals; imap() labels each model’s rows.

text:
What we found
Results from our test run in October 2026 (CDR v9).




Crude OR
Adjusted OR (model 3)




Age, per 10 years
1.43
1.41


Male (vs female)
1.25
1.14


BMI, per 5 units
1.46
1.59


Systolic BP, per 10 mm Hg
1.15
1.09


LDL, per 10 mg/dL
0.87
0.88




The multivariable models used 6,397 people out of 9,905: mostly controls without an LDL result.
BMI got stronger after adjusting for age: younger people are heavier on average but have less diabetes, which hid part of BMI’s link. Adjustment can move an OR either way.
LDL’s OR is below 1, which looks protective. It isn’t: most people with diabetes take statins, and our LDL is each person’s latest value, usually measured after treatment began. That’s reverse causation: diabetes affects LDL, not the other way round.
AIC fell from 8,400 to 7,761 to 7,512: each step improved the fit, BMI most of all.

💬 Discuss: which other predictors could be affected by having diabetes or its treatment? (Weight, with some diabetes medicines; blood pressure, often treated too.) What would fix it? (Measurements from before diagnosis.)

title: 2.3 Join and Bind
text:
Overview
Our data is in four tables: the cohort, the measurements, the survey answers, and the CKD dates. An analysis needs them together, one row per person. Binding stacks tables on top of each other; joining lines them up side by side by a shared key (person_id). We learn the join types on a tiny example first, then check every real join.

Why this class matters
Joins are where analyses most often go silently wrong. An inner join where a left join was meant quietly drops people; a key that isn’t unique quietly duplicates them. The numbers still look reasonable, which is what makes these mistakes dangerous. A few routine checks catch nearly all of them.


By the end you’ll be able to

Stack tables with bind_rows()
Explain left, inner, full, and anti joins, and choose the right one
Check a join: key types, unique keys, unmatched IDs, and row counts
Build the analysis table that 3.1–3.4 use



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
How do we combine four tables without losing or duplicating people?


🧪 The analysis
bind_rows() to stack; left_join() by person_id; anti_join() and counts to check


🎯 Why
A wrong join can silently drop or duplicate people, changing every result after it


✅ What we conclude
One analysis table: 10,000 rows, one per person


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Anything about diabetes yet


🔗 Connections
Uses files from 1.2, 2.1, 2.2; saves final_analysis.csv for 3.1–3.4





Time and cost

title: 2.3 Join and Bind
text:
Key concepts
     x            y
  ┌─────┐      ┌─────┐
  │  A  │      │  A  │      A, B: in both
  │  B  │      │  B  │      C: only in x
  │  C  │      │  D  │      D: only in y
  └─────┘      └─────┘









Join
Keeps
Result
Use it when




left_join(x, y)
every row of x; y’s columns where they match
A, B, C
adding information without losing anyone: our default


inner_join(x, y)
rows in both
A, B
you only want people with both, and know who you drop


full_join(x, y)
rows in either
A, B, C, D
combining two lists of people


anti_join(x, y)
rows of x with no match
C
checking: who doesn’t match?



If the key appears more than once in y, each x row is repeated once per match (one-to-many): usually a sign you forgot to reshape first.

title: 2.1 Clean
text:
Overview
Real health data is messy: the same answer written several ways, people who skipped a question, the same measurement in different units, impossible values typed by mistake, and duplicate rows. Cleaning turns that into data you can analyse, with every decision written down. We clean the cohort, the survey answers, and the measurements from 1.1.

Why this class matters
An impossible BMI of 999, or “PMI: Skip” counted as an answer, can change a mean, a model, or a conclusion, and nobody would notice. Cleaning is where most of the real work of a study happens, and where the most judgment calls are made. Doing it carefully, and logging it, is what makes the rest of the analysis trustworthy.


By the end you’ll be able to

Check that every column has the right type
Tell real answers from non-answers, and turn non-answers into NA
Pull the useful part out of messy text with str_extract()
Find and remove duplicates, and choose which of several answers to keep
Clean measurements with units and plausible ranges, after looking at the values unit by unit
Explain what missing data costs, and keep a cleaning log



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
Which values can we trust, and what do we do with the rest?


🧪 The analysis
Counting labels and values, then rules: recode non-answers, extract answers, remove duplicates, keep plausible measurements


🎯 Why
Every later result depends on it


✅ What we conclude
Clean versions of the three files, and a log of what was removed and why


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Whether a plausible value is correct: cleaning removes the impossible, not every error


🔗 Connections
Uses the files from 1.1; 2.2 reshapes them; 2.3 joins them





Time and cost

105 minutes

about 2 minutes

about $0.50: no queries, only app time

title: 2.1 Clean
text:
Key concepts








Problem
Example from our data
What we do




Wrong type
an ID read as a number
set types when reading the file


Non-answers
PMI: Skip, I prefer not to answer, None Indicated
turn into NA, and say so


Messy text
“Are you still seeing a doctor … (PTSD)? - Yes”
extract the part we need: Yes


Duplicates
the same measurement row twice; two answers to one question
remove exact copies; a rule for the rest (the latest)


Units
BMI with the unit “link for Gunter’s chain”; HbA1c in g/dL
look at the values for each unit; keep or drop


Impossible values
BMI of 0 or 999
keep a plausible range, chosen before the analysis


Missing data
no LDL test for a third of people
keep the NA; decide per analysis




NA is not “No”
Someone may have no answer because they skipped the question, preferred not to answer, or were never asked (follow-up questions appear only after certain answers: skip logic). None of these means “No”.

title: 2.1 Clean
text:
Code walk-through

Extracting the survey answer
survey_clean <- survey_raw %>%
1  mutate(question = case_when(question_concept_id == 43528846 ~ "ptsd_treatment",
                              question_concept_id == 43530361 ~ "ptsd_doctor"),
2         answer_clean = str_extract(answer, "(?<= - ).*$"))

3survey_clean %>% count(question, answer_clean)

1

A short name for each question, chosen by its concept ID, which never changes (the wording could).

2

A regular expression: (?<= - ) means “just after ’ - ’”, .*$ “everything to the end”. PMI: Skip has no ” - “, so it becomes NA: exactly right for a non-answer.

3

Always check a recoding by counting the new values: a typo in a pattern can silently turn everything into NA.




The measurement cleaning log
1step1 <- step0 %>% anti_join(WRONG_UNITS, by = c("measure", "unit"))
step2 <- step1 %>%
  filter(!is.na(value_as_number)) %>%
  left_join(RANGES, by = "measure") %>%
2  filter(between(value_as_number, low, high))
step3 <- step2 %>%
3  distinct(person_id, measure, measurement_date, value_as_number, .keep_all = TRUE)

cleaning_log <- tibble(step = c("Start", "1. …", "2. …", "3. …"),
                       rows = c(nrow(step0), nrow(step1), nrow(step2), nrow(step3))) %>%
4  mutate(removed = lag(rows) - rows)

1

Drop units that mean another measure: here, HbA1c in grams or milligrams per deciliter. anti_join() keeps rows that don’t match the list.

2

Drop missing values, then keep each measure’s plausible range (e.g. BMI 12 to 80), looked up from a small table.

3

Drop exact duplicates: the same person, measure, date, and value.

4

The log: rows left after each step, and how many each removed. Report a table like this with your results.

Duplicates were by far the biggest problem: 13% of all rows, likely the same result recorded by two systems.
Checking values unit by unit changed a decision. We’d planned to drop BMI recorded in “percent”, assuming they were children’s BMI percentiles. The values were ordinary adult BMIs (median 28.6), so we kept them. HbA1c in “milligram per deciliter” had a median of 132: probably an estimated average glucose, so we dropped it.
Non-answers were common in demographics: for race, None Indicated (about 1,400 people), PMI: Skip, and I prefer not to answer. Some odd-looking labels, such as Sex At Birth: Sex At Birth None Of These, are real answers (“none of these describe me”).

title: 1.1 Build the Cohort

Overview
A cohort is a group of people chosen by written rules. In this class we pull ours out of the All of Us database with SQL: adults with health records who either have type 2 diabetes (cases) or have no diabetes (controls). Then we take a sample, and download what the rest of the series needs: survey answers and measurements (BMI, blood pressure, cholesterol, HbA1c).

Why this class matters
Every later result depends on who is in the study. Writing the rules down once, in a query anyone can read and rerun, is what makes a study reproducible. And this class is where you first meet the real data: its tables, its codes, and its quirks.


By the end you’ll be able to

title: 1.1 Build the Cohort
text:
Key concepts

OMOP tables and concept IDs
The All of Us data is a set of tables in BigQuery, in a standard layout called the OMOP Common Data Model. Every table shares person_id, which links a person’s data across tables. Instead of text like “Type 2 diabetes”, the tables store a number, a concept ID (201826), that points to the concept dictionary. Look up any concept at athena.ohdsi.org.


The concept hierarchy
Type 2 diabetes mellitus has more specific concepts under it (e.g. with diabetic nephropathy), and a doctor may record any of them. The concept_ancestor table lists every “this is under that” pair, so one join finds them all:
SELECT co.person_id
FROM condition_occurrence AS co
JOIN concept_ancestor AS ca ON co.condition_concept_id = ca.descendant_concept_id
WHERE ca.ancestor_concept_id = 201826     -- type 2 diabetes, and everything under it


SQL in one table

combine matching rows
inner_join()

left_join()

keep rows that meet a condition
filter()


GROUP BY + MIN(), COUNT()
one row per group, with a summary
group_by() + summarise()

a named step, used later in the query

Code walk-through

Running the shared query
1cohort_sql <- read_file("../sql/t2d_cohort.sql")

2cohort <- run_query(str_glue(cohort_sql, AGE_DATE = "2025-01-01")) %>%
3  mutate(person_id = as.character(person_id))

4cohort %>% count(cohort)

1

Read the SQL from the shared file in notebooks/sql/. The notebook prints it next, so you can read every step.

2

str_glue() fills in the placeholders {CURRENT_DATASET} and {AGE_DATE}; run_query() (from aou_setup.R) sends the query to BigQuery and returns a data frame.

3

Store IDs as text: they’re labels, not numbers, and as text they match IDs in every other file.

4

One row per group: case, control, excluded.




A repeatable sample
1set.seed(2026)
cohort_sample <- cohort %>%
2  filter(cohort %in% c("case", "control"), between(age, 18, 100)) %>%
3  arrange(person_id) %>%
  group_by(cohort) %>%
4  slice_sample(n = 5000) %>%
  ungroup()

5save_data(cohort_sample, "cohort_sample.csv")

1

Fix the random number generator, so everyone gets the same “random” sample.

2

Cases and controls only, aged 18 to 100 (a few recorded ages above 100 are probably errors).

3

Sort first: BigQuery doesn’t return rows in a fixed order, and the seed only repeats if the rows start in the same order.

4

5,000 at random within each group.

5

Save to your bucket: later classes load this file instead of querying again.

title: 1.2 Data for the Survival Analysis
text:
Overview
In 3.4 we’ll ask: after a type 2 diabetes diagnosis, how long until people develop chronic kidney disease (CKD)? A “how long until” question needs more than who has the disease: it needs dates, and a careful idea of how long we could see each person in their health records. This class gathers those dates.

Why this class matters
Survival analysis is easy to run and easy to get wrong. Most mistakes happen before any model: a wrong start date, follow-up that runs past the end of someone’s records, or events that happened before the clock started. This class gets the ingredients right.


By the end you’ll be able to

Explain time zero, event, censoring, and follow-up
Explain why follow-up should end at the last health record
Find the first date of a diagnosis with SQL (MIN(), GROUP BY)
Check a concept ID before using it
Describe how many people had the event, and how long they were followed



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
Among people with type 2 diabetes, who developed CKD after their diagnosis, and how long was everyone followed?


🧪 The analysis
A SQL query for each person’s first CKD date; then, for cases, time from diabetes to CKD or to the end of their records


🎯 Why
A survival analysis needs a clear start, a clear event, and a fair end for people without the event


✅ What we conclude
How many cases had CKD after diabetes, how many before, and how long people were followed


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Risk or what predicts it: that’s 3.4


🔗 Connections
Uses the sample from 1.1; joined in 2.3; analysed in 3.4





Time and cost







⏱️ Class time
60 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 3 minutes


💰 Cost
about $1 per student: two small queries, plus the app


📋 Before class
run 1.1

text:
Key concepts








Term
Means
In our study




Time zero
when each person’s clock starts
the first type 2 diabetes date


Event
what we’re waiting for
the first CKD date, after time zero


Censoring
the clock stops without the event
the earlier of the last EHR visit and death


Follow-up
time zero to the event, or to censoring
in years



diabetes      last EHR visit
   │─────────────────│           censored: no CKD while we could see them
   │──────────X                  event: CKD here
CKD ──X  diabetes                excluded: CKD came first
Why the last EHR visit? A diagnosis can only appear while someone gets care at a site that shares data with All of Us. After their last visit, CKD elsewhere would be invisible. We don’t use All of Us’s observation_period table, because it also counts survey dates, which can stretch follow-up past the last health record.

title: 1.2 Data for the Survival Analysis
text:
Code walk-through

First CKD dates
ckd_sql <- str_glue("
SELECT co.person_id,
1       MIN(co.condition_start_date)            AS first_ckd_date,
2       COUNT(DISTINCT co.condition_start_date) AS ckd_code_days
FROM `{CURRENT_DATASET}.condition_occurrence` AS co
JOIN `{CURRENT_DATASET}.concept_ancestor` AS ca
  ON co.condition_concept_id = ca.descendant_concept_id
3WHERE ca.ancestor_concept_id = {CKD_CONCEPT}
4  AND co.person_id IN ({ids_sql})
5GROUP BY co.person_id
")

1

Each person’s earliest CKD diagnosis.

2

How many different days had a CKD code (useful for a stricter definition).

3

CKD (concept 46271022) and everything under it: stages, CKD due to diabetes, and so on.

4

Only our 10,000 people.

5

One row per person, like group_by() + summarise() in R.




Time zero, event, censoring
cases <- cohort_sample %>%
  filter(cohort == "case") %>%
1  left_join(ckd_dates, by = "person_id") %>%
  mutate(
2    end_of_records = pmin(last_ehr_date, death_date, na.rm = TRUE),
    timing = case_when(
      !is.na(first_ckd_date) & first_ckd_date <= first_t2d_date ~ "CKD before or on diabetes date",
      !is.na(first_ckd_date)                                     ~ "CKD after diabetes",
3      TRUE                                                       ~ "no CKD"),
    followup_end   = if_else(timing == "CKD after diabetes", first_ckd_date, end_of_records),
4    followup_years = as.numeric(followup_end - first_t2d_date) / 365.25
  )

1

Add each case’s first CKD date (NA if they never had one).

2

The end of what we can see: the earlier of the last EHR visit and death. na.rm = TRUE ignores a missing death date.

3

Sort each case into one of three groups. case_when() uses the first rule that matches.

4

Follow-up in years, from the first diabetes date to CKD (events) or the end of records (censored).

title: 2.2 Reshape
text:
Overview
Our clean measurements have many rows per person: every blood pressure reading, every BMI. Models and tables need one row per person, with one column per variable. This class chooses one value per person for each measure, and turns tables from long to wide (and back).

Why this class matters
Reshaping looks like a technical step, but one part of it is a research decision: which value to keep when someone has 46 blood pressure readings. The choice changes the results, and the class shows exactly how (it explains the surprising LDL result in 3.2).


By the end you’ll be able to

Tell long from wide data, and say when each is useful
Choose one value per person, and explain the choice
Use pivot_wider() and pivot_longer()
Fix the most common pivot_wider() problem: values that aren’t unique



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
How do we get from many measurements per person to one row per person?


🧪 The analysis
Per-person summaries (slice_max()), then pivot_wider(); pivot_longer() for plotting


🎯 Why
Models need one row per person; which value we keep is a research decision


✅ What we conclude
One row per person with BMI, SBP, HbA1c, and LDL, and one with the PTSD answers


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Whether the kept value was measured at a meaningful time (e.g. before diagnosis)


🔗 Connections
Uses 2.1’s clean files; 2.3 joins the wide tables





Time and cost

about 1 minute

Which value?








Choice
Good for
Watch out for

for cases, usually after diagnosis and treatment

Code walk-through
measurement_latest <- measurement_clean %>%
1  group_by(person_id, measure) %>%
2  slice_max(measurement_date, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

measurements_wide <- measurement_latest %>%
3  pivot_wider(id_cols = person_id, names_from = measure,
              values_from = value_as_number)

4nrow(measurements_wide) == n_distinct(measurements_wide$person_id)

One group per person per measure.

2

Keep the row with the latest date in each group; with_ties = FALSE keeps just one if two share a date.

3

4

title: 3.1 Table One
text:
Core series, class 6 of 9 · R · 75 minutes

title: 3.1 Table One
text:
Overview
Almost every health study starts with a Table 1: who is in each group, and how they differ. It describes the groups, shows differences that later models must account for (like age), and reveals missing data. We build one for our cases and controls, writing small functions to do it, and then make a version that’s safe to share.

Why this class matters
A Table 1 is the first thing readers check, and the first place a study’s problems show: groups that differ in age, data missing mostly in one group. It’s also where the All of Us rule on small counts bites most often, including counts that aren’t printed but can be worked out from the others.


By the end you’ll be able to

Explain what a Table 1 shows, and why every study has one
Summarise categorical variables (n, %) and continuous ones (mean and SD, or median and IQR)
Choose and read a chi-square test and a t-test
Write your own function, and run it on many variables with map()
Report missing data, and make a table safe to share



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
How do people with and without type 2 diabetes differ?


🧪 The analysis
n (%) with chi-square tests; mean (SD) with t-tests; percent missing by group


🎯 Why
To describe the groups, and spot confounders (age, most of all)


✅ What we conclude
Where the groups differ, and how much data each variable has


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Why they differ. And our sample is half cases, so percents describe the sample, not the population


🔗 Connections
Uses final_analysis.csv from 2.3; guides the models in 3.2–3.4





Time and cost



⏱️ Class time
75 minutes


⏱️ Run time
under 1 minute

about $0.35: no queries, only app time

Key concepts









Variable type
Example
Summary
Test




Categorical
sex at birth, age group, race
n (%) per group
chi-square


Continuous
age, BMI
mean (SD), or median (IQR) if skewed
t-test (or Wilcoxon if skewed)



With thousands of people, even tiny differences give small p-values: judge the size of a difference, not just the p-value.

Small and derived counts
All of Us policy: no counts of 1 to 20 in anything you share, including counts that can be calculated. If a group has 5,000 people, 3,092 female and 1,858 male, then 50 people have another answer or a missing one. If the missing answers were left out of the table, the small count could be worked out exactly. So small categories are combined with the missing answers.

title: 3.1 Table One
text:
Code walk-through
1summarise_categorical <- function(data, var) {
  counts <- data %>%
2    filter(!is.na(.data[[var]])) %>%
    count(level = as.character(.data[[var]]), t2d) %>%
3    pivot_wider(names_from = t2d, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

4  p <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(as.matrix(counts[, c("No", "Yes")]))$p.value)

  counts %>%
5    mutate(`No diabetes` = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", No,  100 * No  / sum(No)),
           `Diabetes`    = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", Yes, 100 * Yes / sum(Yes)), …)
}

6table_cat <- map(categorical_vars, ~ summarise_categorical(fa, .x)) %>% list_rbind()

1

A function: a named recipe with two inputs, the data and a column name.

2

.data[[var]] means “the column whose name is in var”, so one function works for any column.

3

One row per level, with a column of counts for each group.

4

A chi-square test: are the groups’ distributions different?

5

Text like 3,092 (62.4%): %d a whole number, %.1f one decimal, %% a percent sign.

6

Run the function once per variable and stack the results.

title: 3.3 Linear Regression
text:
Overview
Diabetes and high blood pressure often go together. Here the outcome is a number, systolic blood pressure (SBP), so we use linear regression: how much higher, on average, is SBP for each year of age, each BMI unit, and in people with type 2 diabetes, holding the others constant?

Why this class matters
Linear regression is the foundation of most statistical models, including the gene-by-gene models in 4.5 and 4.6. This class also shows that a model can explain little of the variation (a low R²) and still estimate a real difference well, and how to check a model with its residuals.


By the end you’ll be able to

Explain a coefficient: the average change in the outcome per unit of a predictor
Fit and read models with lm(), tidy(), and glance()
Compare models with R², adjusted R², and AIC
Check a model’s residuals



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
Is type 2 diabetes linked to higher SBP, after accounting for age, sex, BMI, and LDL?


🧪 The analysis
Linear regression, built up step by step, on the same people


🎯 Why
SBP is a number; adjusting separates diabetes from age and weight


✅ What we conclude
The adjusted difference in SBP (mm Hg), and how much each model explains


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Cause, or untreated blood pressure: many people take medicine for it


🔗 Connections
The logistic version is 3.2; the same kind of model is used per gene in 4.5

title: 3.3 Linear Regression
text:
Key concepts
\[\text{SBP} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{BMI} + \dots + \text{error}\]

Each coefficient is the average change in SBP (mm Hg) per unit of that predictor, holding the others constant. For type 2 diabetes (yes/no), it’s the average difference between the groups.
R²: the share of variation explained (0 to 1). AIC: fit vs complexity, lower is better, only on the same data.
Blood pressure varies a lot from reading to reading, so R² is low here. That doesn’t make the coefficients wrong.

Tip✋ Try It Out · 5 minutes · Part 3, “Your turn”



Fit SBP ~ t2d on its own. How much higher is SBP in cases, before any adjustment?
✅ Check: the t2dYes row: the crude difference in mm Hg. Compare it with the adjusted one in Part 4.

title: 3.3 Linear Regression
text:
Code walk-through
1model_data <- fa %>% drop_na(SBP, age10, sex_at_birth, BMI5, LDL10, t2d)

m1 <- lm(SBP ~ age10 + sex_at_birth,                      data = model_data)
m2 <- lm(SBP ~ age10 + sex_at_birth + BMI5 + LDL10,       data = model_data)
2m3 <- lm(SBP ~ age10 + sex_at_birth + BMI5 + LDL10 + t2d, data = model_data)

bind_rows("1. Age + sex" = glance(m1), "2. + BMI, LDL" = glance(m2),
3          "3. + type 2 diabetes" = glance(m3), .id = "model")
4tidy(m3, conf.int = TRUE)

1

Every model on the same people, as in 3.2.

2

lm() fits a linear regression. Model 3 adds type 2 diabetes last, so its coefficient is adjusted for everything before it.

3

glance() gives one row of fit statistics per model (R², AIC); bind_rows(.id = "model") labels them.

4

tidy() gives each coefficient with its 95% confidence interval.

title: Optional: Build the Cohort in the Data Explorer
text:
Overview
In 1.1 we build the cohort with SQL. Workbench 2.0 also has a point-and-click tool, the Data Explorer, that builds a cohort from a menu of criteria: no code needed. This page shows how to build our type 2 diabetes cases with it, how to save a data snapshot, and how to read a Data Explorer cohort into a notebook.






ImportantThe Data Explorer uses CDR v8; the course notebooks use CDR v9



As of October 2026, the Data Explorer offers only version v8r9, the All of Us Controlled Tier CDR v8 (BigQuery dataset C2024Q3R9). The course notebooks use CDR v9 (C2025Q4R6). Participant IDs changed between v8 and v9, so:

Use the Data Explorer to learn the tool, and to explore quickly.
Don’t combine a Data Explorer cohort with the course notebooks’ files: the IDs won’t match.
Don’t copy the dataset name from a Data Explorer query into aou_setup.R.




Why it’s worth knowing

It’s the fastest way to see how many people meet a set of rules, and to try changes, without writing a query.
Its Summary and Queries tabs show the SQL it writes: a good way to learn how a cohort turns into a query.
Collaborators who don’t code can build and share cohorts in the same workspace.



Same rules, different numbers
Built in the Data Explorer, our cases came to 65,710 people and our controls to 311,871. The SQL in 1.1 found 80,919 and 331,912. Same rules, different counts:

Click Add to your workspace. The cohort opens with an empty Cohort filter: everyone in the data collection.

Each group is a set of criteria; groups combine with AND. Within a group, choose Meet any criteria. Click Add some criteria to open the list:

The search box finds a criterion by its name (e.g. type 2 diabetes), by its vocabulary code (e.g. the SNOMED code 73211009 for Diabetes mellitus), or by its OMOP concept ID (e.g. 201820). Searching by code or ID finds exactly the concept you mean, which helps when several names look alike.

For group 2, ticking Type 2 diabetes mellitus also includes every more specific concept under it: the rows below it in the list are ticked automatically (the same idea as concept_ancestor in 1.1). View in hierarchy shows the tree.

title: Optional: Build the Cohort in the Data Explorer
text:
Save a data snapshot
A data snapshot saves the cohort’s data (as CSV files) and/or the queries that produce it (as a notebook) to a bucket. Click Save data snapshot at the top right of the cohort.

Select data: choose the tables, then the columns.

On the left, Demographics and Tables that contain cohort-defining criteria are ticked by default; + Browse more data adds other tables (e.g. measurements).
The Tables tab is where you choose which columns to include: every column has a checkbox. Untick the ones you don’t need. Fewer columns means smaller files and less data to look after.


The same table with the concept ID columns unticked, keeping the readable names (GENDER, RACE):







Note“Tables that contain cohort-defining criteria” holds only the criteria’s rows



This option adds, for example, the condition_occurrence table, but only the rows for the criteria’s own concepts: for the cases, their diabetes diagnoses, not all their diagnoses. For the controls, whose rule is no diabetes, that table is therefore empty: their query asks for diabetes codes among people with no diabetes. To get other diagnoses, add them with + Browse more data.


The Summary tab lists the criteria and the tables, in plain words: a good check before saving.

The Queries for each table tab shows the SQL for each table. Queries for the cohort shows the complete code, in Python (Jupyter) or R: choose with the drop-down, then Copy.

Select file format: CSV tables (zipped), and/or a notebook with the queries, in R or Python.

Select destination bucket: pick your workspace bucket, then Save.

The cohort appears on the Resources tab, in the folder you chose:

title: Optional: Build the Cohort in the Data Explorer
section: Use a Data Explorer cohort in a notebook
text:
Use a Data Explorer cohort in a notebook
Two ways. The first is simpler, and works with the course’s aou_setup.R.

A. Run its query from R (simplest)

In Save data snapshot → Queries for each table → person, click Copy.
In an R notebook in notebooks/core/, paste it between r"---( and )---":

source("../aou_setup.R")   # run_query() and BILLING_PROJECT

de_person_sql <- r"---(
  -- paste the query here: it starts with SELECT and ends with the WHERE clause
)---"

de_cases <- run_query(de_person_sql) %>%
  mutate(person_id = as.character(person_id))

nrow(de_cases)                    # should match the Data Explorer's count
de_cases %>% count(T_DISP_sex_at_birth)

r"---( … )---" is a raw string: R keeps everything inside as it is, quotes and backslashes included, so the SQL needs no editing.
The query reads the Data Explorer’s own tables (C2024Q3R9 and C2024Q3R9_index_…), so the people are CDR v8 participants.
Columns starting T_DISP_ are the display names of concept IDs (e.g. T_DISP_race for race_concept_id).
💰 A few cents: it reads the person table and the Data Explorer’s index tables.



B. Use the snapshot’s own notebook
If you chose Queries for the cohort (IPYNB) with R Notebook, the snapshot saves a notebook to your bucket that exports each table to CSV files and reads them back. Two things to know:

It needs your bucket’s Cloud Storage address in a setting called EXPORT_BUCKET, which Workbench 2.0 doesn’t set for you. Find the address on the Resources tab (your bucket’s details, starting gs://), then uncomment and edit the line near the top: Sys.setenv(EXPORT_BUCKET = "gs://…").
The code includes your workspace’s project ID for billing. That’s fine in your workspace, but don’t publish it.

title: Courses
text:
Each course is a series of classes. Every class is a Jupyter notebook you run in your own All of Us workspace, plus a page on this site with the overview, class plan, concepts, step-by-step Workbench instructions, and the results we found when we ran it.
All the series share one research question, type 2 diabetes, and one cohort definition, so what you learn in one carries over to the next.
Why All of Us? The program was built for precision medicine: care tailored to each person’s genes, environment, and way of life. Precision Medicine: where our classes fit explains what that means, how each series connects to the program’s goals, and what our group-level results can and can’t say about one person.

title: 7.2 Trees and Boosting
text:
Machine learning series, class 2 of 4 · R (+ a Python companion) · 95 minutes
Open the notebook on GitHub Python companion (7.2b) Machine learning series overview

title: 7.2 Trees and Boosting
text:
Overview
In 7.1, a logistic regression predicted new type 2 diabetes within 2 years with a test AUC of about 0.74, and LASSO did no better. Is that the limit of what enrollment data can tell us, or did the models miss something? In this class we try two of the most popular machine learning methods for tables of data, random forests and gradient boosting, on the same people and the same test set, and look inside them.

Why this class matters
“Machine learning” often means tree-based models: they win many prediction competitions on tabular data. Knowing when they help, and when a simple model is just as good, is one of the most useful judgements in applied prediction. So is being able to look inside a model, whatever kind it is.


By the end you’ll be able to

Explain how a decision tree, a random forest, and gradient boosting make predictions
Fit a random forest (ranger) and a boosted model (xgboost) with tidymodels
Tune boosting with cross-validation, and read the results
Compare models fairly: the same test set, with AUC, Brier score, and calibration
Look inside any model with permutation importance and partial dependence



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
Do flexible tree-based models predict new type 2 diabetes within 2 years better than logistic regression, from the same enrollment data?


🧪 The analysis
The 7.1 data and the same split; logistic regression, a random forest, and gradient boosting tuned by 3-fold cross-validation; AUC, Brier score, calibration; permutation importance; partial dependence for BMI and age


🎯 Why
Trees find curves and interactions by themselves. If they don’t beat logistic regression, the signal in these predictors is simple


✅ What we conclude
Whether flexibility helps here, which predictors each model relies on, and what shape of risk each learned


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Cause. Importance means “the model uses it”, not “it causes diabetes”


🔗 Connections
Everything in 7.1; logistic regression from 3.2





Time and cost







⏱️ Class time
95 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 15 minutes, plus up to 10 minutes the first time to install ranger and xgboost


💰 Cost
$0 in queries: it reads the file 7.1 saved, ml_t2d_2yr.csv


📋 Before class
run 7.1 to the end in the same workspace

title: 7.2 Trees and Boosting
text:
Key concepts

A decision tree
A decision tree is a flowchart of yes/no questions; each leaf predicts the share of its people who were diagnosed.
                      BMI under 30?

        Excellent/Very Good?     yes /      \ no

        risk 1%   risk 4%
(Made-up numbers, to show the idea.) Trees find curves and interactions by themselves, but a single deep tree overfits. The two methods in this class combine many trees:









Random forest
Gradient boosting




Idea
many deep trees, each on a random sample of people and predictors; predictions averaged
many small trees built one after another, each correcting the mistakes so far


Like

a student who studies their wrong answers, again and again


Tuning

R package
ranger
xgboost





Comparing models fairly








Measure
Asks
Better is

does the model rank future cases above others?
higher

the average of (predicted risk − what happened)²: ranking and the numbers at once
lower


Calibration
in each tenth of predicted risk, does the average prediction match the share diagnosed?
on the diagonal

Method
How
Shows

title: Machine Learning for Beginners
text: New to machine learning? This page explains everything the machine learning series assumes, in plain language, with examples from our type 2 diabetes question. Each class links back to the parts it uses.

title: Machine Learning for Beginners
text:
What is machine learning?
Machine learning is a set of methods that learn a rule from examples, so the rule can be used on new cases. Show a method thousands of people, what was known about them, and whether they were later diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. It learns a rule that turns “what’s known” into a predicted risk. Then we use the rule on people it has never seen.
You’ve already used one machine learning method: logistic regression (class 3.2). The difference is in why we use it.

title: Machine Learning for Beginners
text:
Explaining vs predicting









Explaining (classes 3.2, 5.3, 6.2)
Predicting (this series)




The question
Is income linked to type 2 diabetes, after accounting for age and sex?
For this person, what’s the chance of a diagnosis in the next 2 years?


What matters
one effect (an odds ratio or hazard ratio), and its confidence interval
how accurate the predicted risks are, for new people


Judged by
is the effect unbiased (confounders adjusted for)?
AUC and calibration on a test set


A predictor that causes nothing
a problem (confounding)
fine, if it’s known in time and it helps


The main worries
confounding, reverse causation
overfitting, leakage



A predictor can be useful without being a cause. People who rate their health as poor are more often diagnosed with diabetes soon after, perhaps because they already have it, undiagnosed. That answer helps a prediction, but changing someone’s answer wouldn’t change their risk.

title: Machine Learning for Beginners
section: Four parts of a prediction question
text:
Four parts of a prediction question
Every class in this series starts by filling in this table:








Part
Our choice in 7.1
Why it matters




Who is it for?
adults with no diabetes at enrollment
you can’t predict a diagnosis that has already happened


From what? (known when?)
age, sex, BMI, blood pressure, and survey answers, from around enrollment
a model used on a given day can only use what’s known that day


Predicting what?
a new type 2 diabetes diagnosis
the shared case definition, with its date


By when?
within 2 years
the prediction window: longer windows give more cases, but fewer people with long enough follow-up



The day the prediction is made is time zero. Everything used as a predictor must be known by then; the outcome must happen after it.

Why time zero matters in All of Us
Most people with type 2 diabetes in All of Us were diagnosed before they joined. In our ML data check, about 77% of cases were diagnosed before enrollment. Their surveys and measurements describe life with diabetes, so they can’t teach a model the warning signs. They’re left out, and the model learns from the people who were diagnosed afterwards:



Data
People at risk at time zero
New type 2 diabetes afterwards




Surveys and BMI at enrollment
about 264,000
about 15,500


Fitbit (from the first day of data)
about 34,000
about 2,000


Proteomics (from the blood draw)
about 5,800
about 380



That last row is why the protein class (7.3) has to be careful: thousands of proteins, and a few hundred cases.

title: Machine Learning for Beginners
section: Leakage: the most common way to fool yourself
text:
Leakage: the most common way to fool yourself
Leakage is when a predictor contains information you wouldn’t have at prediction time, often because it’s a result of the outcome. A leaky model looks brilliant in the analysis and fails in practice.



Predictor
Leakage?
Why




BMI measured at enrollment
✅ no
known at time zero


An HbA1c test result after enrollment
❌ yes
HbA1c is how diabetes is diagnosed


A metformin prescription
❌ yes
a treatment for diabetes


A survey answered after the diagnosis
❌ yes
the answer may reflect the diagnosis (class 5.2)


The number of doctor visits in the next year
❌ yes
it’s in the future, and people being diagnosed see doctors more


Being in the “case” group of our cohort
❌ yes
that is the outcome



Rule of thumb: an AUC above about 0.95 for a common disease, from routine data, is almost always leakage. Check every predictor’s date.

title: Machine Learning for Beginners
text:
Training and test data
A model always looks better on the people it learned from: it has partly memorised them. To know how it would do on new people, we hide some people from it.
everyone in the analysis
├── training set (75%): the model learns from these
└── test set (25%):     locked away; used ONCE, at the very end







Word
Means




Training set
the people a model learns from


Test set
people held back, to measure how the model does on people it never saw


Stratified split
both sets get the same share of cases (important when the outcome is rare)


Seed (set.seed())
makes a random split the same every time, and for everyone in the class

title: Machine Learning for Beginners
text:
Overfitting
Overfitting is learning the noise in the training set, not the pattern. An overfitted model scores very well on training data and worse on new data. It’s more likely when there are many predictors and few cases.










Too simple (underfit)
About right
Too flexible (overfit)




Training data
so-so
good
excellent


Test data
so-so
good
worse


Example
age alone
age, sex, BMI, …
a separate rule for every combination of answers



Methods such as LASSO (class 7.1) fight overfitting with a penalty that keeps the model simple.

title: Machine Learning for Beginners
text:
Cross-validation and tuning
Many methods have settings you choose before fitting, called tuning parameters: LASSO’s penalty, or the number of trees in a forest (7.2). We can’t use the test set to choose them: the test set would then be part of the training, and its result no longer honest.
Cross-validation chooses them using the training set only:
training set, cut into 5 folds:   [1][2][3][4][5]
round 1: learn from 2-5, score on 1
round 2: learn from 1, 3-5, score on 2
...                                   every person is scored once, by a model that didn't see them
Try each setting this way, keep the best, then fit once on the whole training set, and score once on the test set.

title: Machine Learning for Beginners
text:
Measuring a model

AUC: does it rank people well?
The AUC (area under the ROC curve) is the chance that a randomly chosen person who was diagnosed got a higher predicted risk than a randomly chosen person who wasn’t.



AUC
Means




0.5
no better than a coin toss


0.7
acceptable; typical of models built from routine data


0.8
good


0.9
excellent: rare for a common disease


1.0
perfect: suspect leakage



Why not accuracy? If 5% of people are diagnosed, a model that says “no” to everyone is 95% accurate, and useless. The AUC isn’t fooled by a rare outcome.


The ROC curve: what does a cut-off cost?
To act on a risk (offer a test, say), you choose a cut-off: everyone above it is flagged. Each cut-off trades one kind of mistake for another:








Word
Means
In our example




Sensitivity
the share of future cases that are flagged
of those diagnosed within 2 years, how many we’d have tested


Specificity
the share of everyone else that isn’t flagged
of those not diagnosed, how many we left alone


Positive predictive value
the share of flagged people who are diagnosed
of those we tested, how many went on to a diagnosis



The ROC curve draws sensitivity against 1 − specificity for every cut-off. The AUC is the area under it.


Calibration: are the numbers right?
The AUC only checks the order of the risks. A model can rank people perfectly and still say “10%” when the truth is “2%”. If a doctor tells a patient “your risk is 8%”, the 8% must be right.
Calibration checks this: group people by predicted risk (for example, into tenths), and compare each group’s average predicted risk with the share actually diagnosed. On a calibration plot, a well-calibrated model’s points lie on the diagonal.









Good AUC
Poor AUC




Good calibration
ranks well, numbers right: useful
numbers right on average, but can’t tell people apart


Poor calibration
ranks well, numbers wrong: fine for “who’s highest?”, not for “what’s my risk?”
not useful



Models often lose calibration when used in a different population (another hospital, another country), even when their AUC holds up.

title: Machine Learning for Beginners
text:
The methods in this series








Method
Idea
Class




Logistic regression
a weighted sum of predictors, turned into a risk
7.1 (and 3.2)


LASSO
logistic regression with a penalty that shrinks weak predictors to exactly zero: it chooses predictors
7.1, 7.3


Splines
let a number’s effect bend (risk may rise faster at high BMI)
7.1


Random forest
many decision trees, each on a random sample, voting together
7.2


Gradient boosting
trees built one after another, each fixing the last one’s mistakes
7.2



A decision tree is a flowchart of yes/no questions (BMI over 30? Age over 55?) ending in a risk. Trees find interactions by themselves, but a single tree overfits easily; forests and boosting combine many.
We don’t use deep learning (neural networks). It shines with images, text, and signals, and needs very large data. On tables of a few dozen predictors, it rarely beats the methods above.

title: Machine Learning for Beginners
text:
Prediction, fairness, and precision medicine
Prediction models are one route from group results to individual care: precision medicine, the reason All of Us exists. They also bring new risks:

A model can work worse for some groups, especially groups it saw few of. Check its AUC and calibration by group (7.4).
Predictors can carry unfairness. Income predicts diabetes. Should a clinical model use it? Leaving it out doesn’t remove the inequality; using it may label people by their circumstances.
The outcome is a diagnosis, not the disease. People who see doctors more are diagnosed sooner. A model can learn who gets diagnosed, not only who gets diabetes.
Reporting: the TRIPOD+AI guideline lists what a prediction model paper should report (7.4).

title: Machine Learning for Beginners
text:
Glossary







Word
Means




Feature
machine learning’s word for a predictor


Label
machine learning’s word for the outcome


Time zero
the moment a prediction is made: predictors before it, outcome after it


Prediction window (horizon)
how far ahead we predict, e.g. 2 years


Incident case
a new diagnosis after time zero (vs prevalent: already diagnosed)


Leakage
a predictor that contains information from after time zero, or from the outcome itself


Overfitting
learning the training set’s noise; good on training data, worse on new data


Tuning parameter
a setting chosen before fitting, e.g. the LASSO penalty


Cross-validation
choosing settings by fitting on part of the training set and scoring on the rest, in turn


Penalty (regularisation)
a cost on large coefficients that keeps a model simple


AUC
the chance a future case is ranked above a non-case; 0.5 = coin toss


Calibration
whether predicted risks match what happened


External validation
testing a model on a different population from the one it was built on

title: 4.2 A GWAS with PLINK
text:
Overview
In 4.1 we saw that people with type 2 diabetes carry the T allele of rs7903146 a little more often. A genome-wide association study (GWAS) does that for every variant, one at a time, adjusted for age, sex, and genetic ancestry. To keep it fast and cheap, we test every variant in one region (around the gene TCF7L2) instead of the whole genome. The steps are the same.

Why this class matters
GWAS is the main tool for finding genetic risk factors, and its results appear in thousands of papers. Knowing what goes into one (quality control, covariates, the significance threshold, linkage disequilibrium) is what lets you read those papers critically, and run your own.


By the end you’ll be able to

Explain what a GWAS tests, and why it adjusts for covariates such as ancestry
Apply standard quality-control filters to variants, and say why each matters
Prepare phenotype and covariate files, and run plink2 --glm
Read GWAS results: odds ratios, p-values, and the genome-wide threshold
Make and read a regional plot (coloured by linkage disequilibrium) and a Q-Q plot



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
Which variants in the TCF7L2 region are linked to type 2 diabetes?


🧪 The analysis
Logistic regression once per variant: case/control ~ copies of the allele + age + sex + 10 ancestry PCs, after variant QC


🎯 Why
The outcome is yes/no; one test per variant because we don’t know in advance which matters; adjusted so age, sex, or ancestry don’t masquerade as genetic effects


✅ What we conclude
Which variants pass the thresholds, their odds ratios, and whether the known variant replicates


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Which variant is causal (neighbours in LD move together), or how it acts; small samples miss real effects


🔗 Connections
Builds on 4.1; repeated in Hail in 4.3; its top variant starts 4.4





Time and cost







⏱️ Class time
120 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 3 minutes; every PLINK step takes seconds


💰 Cost
about $1 per student: no BigQuery query if 4.1’s sample is saved, plus the app (about $0.27 an hour)


📋 Before class
run 4.1, which saves the sample this class reuses

title: 4.2 A GWAS with PLINK
text:
Key concepts

One regression per variant
\[\text{log odds of type 2 diabetes} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{copies of the allele} + \beta_2 \times \text{age} + \dots\]
The odds ratio per copy is \(e^{\beta_1}\). The covariates (age, sex, 10 genetic PCs) are there because each differs between cases and controls and could create a misleading link. Ancestry matters most: allele frequencies and diabetes rates differ between ancestry groups.


Many tests, a strict threshold
Testing about a million independent variants at p < 0.05 would give about 50,000 false positives. So a GWAS uses p < 5 × 10⁻⁸ (genome-wide significance). For our region we also show a Bonferroni threshold: 0.05 divided by the number of variants tested.


Linkage disequilibrium (LD)
Nearby variants are inherited together, so when one is truly linked to diabetes, its neighbours show a signal too. A GWAS finds regions; finding the causal variant (fine-mapping) is a separate step. The regional plot colours each variant by its r² with rs7903146.


Quality control








Filter
Removes
Why




--maf 0.01
alleles carried by under 1%
too few carriers give unstable results


--geno 0.1
variants missing in over 10% of people
hard-to-measure variants; missingness can differ by group


--hwe 1e-10
genotype counts extremely far from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
usually genotyping errors (lenient, because our sample mixes ancestries)
