title: 4.2 A GWAS with PLINK
text:
Code walk-through

Quality control
qc_output <- system(str_glue(
1  "plink2 --pfile {shQuote(region_prefix)} ",
2  "--maf 0.01 --geno 0.1 --hwe 1e-10 ",
3  "--make-pgen --out {shQuote(qc_prefix)}"
), intern = TRUE)

4str_subset(read_lines(paste0(qc_prefix, ".log")), "removed|remaining")

1

Start from the region files extracted earlier (5,000 people, about 14,000 variants).

2

The three filters, in one command. PLINK applies them all and reports each one’s effect.

3

Save the variants that pass as new PLINK 2 files.

4

PLINK writes a .log file; str_subset() keeps only the lines saying how many variants each filter removed and how many remain.




The association test
glm_output <- system(str_glue(
  "plink2 --pfile {shQuote(qc_prefix)} ",
1  "--pheno {shQuote(pheno_file)} --pheno-name t2d ",
2  "--covar {shQuote(covar_file)} --covar-variance-standardize ",
3  "--glm hide-covar firth-fallback ",
  "--out {shQuote(gwas_prefix)}"
), intern = TRUE)

1

The phenotype file: one row per person, t2d coded 2 = case, 1 = control (PLINK’s convention).

2

The covariates (age, sex, PC1–PC10). Standardizing puts them on similar scales, which avoids a common multicollinearity error.

3

--glm runs logistic regression for every variant. hide-covar reports only the variant’s result; firth-fallback switches to Firth regression when the standard fit fails (e.g. a rare allele).

title: 4.2 A GWAS with PLINK
text:
What we found
Results from our test run in October 2026 (CDR v9), 2,500 cases and 2,500 controls.







Region extracted
5,000 people, 14,430 variants


Top variant
a short tandem repeat (STR) at 113,036,665 inside TCF7L2: OR 1.41, p = 2.4 × 10⁻⁸, just past genome-wide significance


rs7903146 (T allele)
adjusted OR 1.25, p = 3.3 × 10⁻⁶; 8th smallest p-value in the region


Unadjusted vs adjusted (rs7903146)
OR 1.17 → 1.25; p 5.6 × 10⁻⁴ → 3.3 × 10⁻⁶



💬 Discuss:

The top hit is a repeat, which is harder to sequence than single-letter variants. Why should a result like that be treated with caution? (Check that nearby SNPs show the same signal: here they did.)
Adjusting raised the odds ratio. How? Cases include more people of African and Admixed American ancestry, and the T allele’s frequency differs by ancestry: mixing groups pulled the unadjusted estimate toward 1. Adding a strong predictor (age) also sharpens the other estimates.
In the Q-Q plot, the unadjusted p-values were inflated across the board (confounding by ancestry); the adjusted ones followed the diagonal until the real signal at the end.
rs7903146 isn’t genome-wide significant with 5,000 people. The published finding came from tens of thousands: power.


The plots

title: 4.2 A GWAS with PLINK
text:
Instructor notes






TipInstructor tip: timing and pitfalls






If 4.1 wasn’t run, the samples cell rebuilds the sample: allow 2 extra minutes.
The regional plot needs the LD step (exporting everyone’s genotypes in the region); on a small app it can take a minute.
Expect “is the top hit the cause?”: no, a GWAS finds regions. Point to fine-mapping, and to the eQTL check in 4.5.
The plot is often called a LocusZoom plot, after the tool that popularised it.

With millions of tests, the threshold is p < 5 × 10⁻⁸; small samples have little power
Nearby variants move together (LD): a GWAS finds regions

title: 4.4 A Phenome-Wide Association Study (PheWAS)
text:
Overview
A GWAS asks which variants are linked to one disease? A PheWAS flips it: which diseases are linked to one variant? We take rs7903146 and test it against hundreds of diseases in the health records: first in All of Us’s free All by All browser, then ourselves, in R, on a random sample of 20,000 participants.

Why this class matters
A PheWAS shows everything a variant is linked to: its main disease, that disease’s treatments and complications, and sometimes surprises. It also teaches two of the most important ideas in observational research, through real examples: selection bias (why the sample must be random) and collider bias (why adjusting can create a link that isn’t there).


By the end you’ll be able to

Explain what a PheWAS tests, and how it differs from a GWAS
Explain phecodes: how diagnosis codes become diseases, with case and control rules
Read results in the All by All browser, including converting a beta to an odds ratio
Build phecode phenotypes from the EHR, and run a PheWAS with glm()
Explain why a PheWAS needs a random sample, and why many hits are consequences



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
Which diseases are linked to rs7903146?


🧪 The analysis
Logistic regression once per disease (phecode, with at least 100 cases), adjusted for age, sex, and 10 PCs, in a random sample of 20,000; Bonferroni correction


🎯 Why
One variant can affect several traits, and a disease’s consequences show up too. A random sample, because one chosen by diabetes status creates false links


✅ What we conclude
Which diseases are linked, and whether they look like consequences of diabetes


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Direct effects vs consequences, without care: adjusting for diabetes can create associations


🔗 Connections
The variant comes from 4.2; All by All checks our results in a much bigger sample; 4.5 asks whether it changes gene activity





Time and cost







⏱️ Class time
120 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 15 minutes. Slowest: the diagnosis-code query and download, and the PheWAS loop (about 5 minutes)


💰 Cost
about $1 to $2 per student: two BigQuery queries, plus the app


📋 Before class
nothing: this class works on its own

title: 4.4 A Phenome-Wide Association Study (PheWAS)
text:
Key concepts

Phecodes
Diagnoses are recorded as ICD codes: tens of thousands, very specific, in two systems (ICD-9-CM and ICD-10-CM). Phecodes group them into about 1,800 research diseases. For example, ICD-10 E11.9 and E11.65 and ICD-9 250.00 all map to phecode 250.2, Type 2 diabetes.







Rule
Means




Case
at least 2 days with a code for the phecode


Excluded
only 1 day, or a related phecode (e.g. type 1 when testing type 2)


Control
everyone else


Roll-up
a specific phecode also counts for its parent (250.2 → 250)





Why a random sample?
The case-control sample from 4.1–4.3 is half diabetes cases. In it, anything that goes with diabetes (blood pressure, kidney disease, obesity, diabetes medicines) also goes with the T allele, just because of how the sample was chosen: selection bias. So this class takes a random 20,000, with diabetes at its natural rate (about 1 in 5).

title: 4.4 A Phenome-Wide Association Study (PheWAS)
text:
Code walk-through

From ICD codes to phecodes
person_phecodes <- icd %>%
1  inner_join(phecode_map, by = c("vocabulary_id", "code"), relationship = "many-to-many") %>%
2  inner_join(phecode_rollup_map, by = c("phecode" = "code"), relationship = "many-to-many") %>%
  group_by(person_id, phecode = phecode_unrolled) %>%
3  summarise(n_days = sum(n_days), .groups = "drop")

1

Look up each person’s ICD codes in the phecode map. Codes with no phecode drop out; a few codes map to more than one phecode.

2

Add each phecode’s parents (e.g. 250.2 also counts for 250).

3

One row per person per phecode, with the number of days it was coded.




Cases, controls, and excluded
phecode_status <- function(pc) {
  cases <- person_phecodes %>%
1    filter(phecode == pc, n_days >= 2) %>%
    pull(person_id)

2  related  <- phecode_exclude %>% filter(code == pc) %>% pull(exclusion_criteria)
  excluded <- person_phecodes %>%
    filter(phecode %in% c(pc, related)) %>%
    pull(person_id)

3  case_when(phewas_samples$person_id %in% cases    ~ 1,
            phewas_samples$person_id %in% excluded ~ NA_real_,
            TRUE                                   ~ 0)
}

1

Cases: at least 2 days with a code for this phecode.

2

Related phecodes, from the PheWAS project’s exclusion table.

3

For everyone in the sample: 1 = case, NA = excluded (one code day, or a related phecode), 0 = control. case_when() uses the first rule that matches, so cases come first.

What we found
Results from our test run in October 2026 (CDR v9).
In All by All (CDR v8, about 400,000 participants): type 2 diabetes p = 2 × 10⁻¹⁵², beta 0.22 (OR ≈ 1.24); also blood glucose, HbA1c, diabetes medicines (metformin, insulins, sulfonylureas); and waist circumference with a negative beta (−0.015, p = 4 × 10⁻⁸). The TCF7L2 rare-variant burden tests: nothing significant.
Our PheWAS (20,000 random participants; 18.7% with type 2 diabetes):







Diagnosis codes
about 1.6 million person–code rows


Phecodes tested
992, in 4.8 minutes


Type 2 diabetes (250.2)
OR 1.20, p = 2.8 × 10⁻⁹


Also significant
insulin pump user (OR 1.28); type 2 diabetes with circulatory (1.39) and neurological (1.25) complications


Just below the line
diabetic retinopathy, polyneuropathy, gastroparesis


Morbid obesity (278.11)
OR 0.90 (p = 0.003); 0.85 (p = 8 × 10⁻⁶) after adjusting for diabetes




💬 Discuss:

The complications have larger ORs than diabetes itself. Why? (They come with longer or harder-to-control diabetes.)
Morbid obesity got more significant after adjusting for diabetes. Both the T allele and obesity cause diabetes, so diabetes is a collider; comparing people within diabetes groups creates a negative link between them. The unadjusted 0.90 is the cleaner estimate, and it agrees with All by All’s smaller waist.

T allele ──→ type 2 diabetes ←── obesity

title: 4.6 Proteomics: Blood Proteins in Type 2 Diabetes
text:
Overview
Proteins are what the body builds and uses: hormones, enzymes, signals. All of Us has measured about 5,400 proteins in blood plasma from about 10,000 participants, with the Olink platform. We ask which proteins are higher or lower in type 2 diabetes, check that the data’s normalization worked, and look at whether the proteins’ levels are set partly by genetics (pQTLs).

Why this class matters
Blood proteins come from organs all over the body, so they can show what’s happening in the kidney, liver, or fat tissue, which blood RNA (4.5) can’t. That makes them promising biomarkers. The class also teaches practical skills for big data: reading only the rows you need from a huge file, and checking for batch effects in data that was normalized before you got it.


By the end you’ll be able to

Explain how Olink measures proteins, and what an NPX value is
Read only the rows you need from a very large file, with awk
Apply QC flags, reshape long data into a matrix, and check for batch effects
Run differential abundance with limma, and read the results
Look up pQTLs in All of Us’s results



Analysis at a glance







❓ Questions
Which plasma proteins differ in type 2 diabetes, and are their levels partly genetic?


🧪 The analysis
A linear model per protein with limma on NPX, adjusted for age and sex, after QC and checks of normalization and plate effects; then a pQTL lookup


🎯 Why
NPX is already normalized and log₂, so linear models fit directly; but leftover plate effects can look like biology, so we check; ~5,400 proteins, so FDR


✅ What we conclude
Which proteins differ and which organs they point to; which have strong pQTLs


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Cause vs consequence vs treatment; for sure which organ a protein came from


🔗 Connections
RNA in 4.5; both in 4.7. pQTLs + GWAS = Mendelian randomization





Time and cost







⏱️ Class time
120 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 10 minutes. Slowest: loading the proteins (3–5 minutes)


💰 Cost
about $1 to $2 per student: one BigQuery query, reading a 2.6 GB file (pennies), plus the app


📋 Before class
nothing (limma installs quickly if you ran 4.5)

title: 4.6 Proteomics: Blood Proteins in Type 2 Diabetes
text:
Key concepts

How Olink measures proteins
Pairs of antibodies, each carrying a short DNA tag, bind the same protein. Only when both bind are their tags close enough to join into a DNA sequence, which is counted by sequencing. More protein, more counts. The All of Us platform, Olink Explore HT, measures about 5,400 proteins (assays) from one small sample.


NPX, and what’s already been done
NPX (Normalized Protein eXpression) is on a log₂ scale (1 = twice as much) and is relative: compare the same protein between people, not two proteins. It’s already normalized twice: to control samples on each plate (by Olink’s software), and across batches of plates (by All of Us). So we don’t normalize again, but we check that no plate stands out.


Limit of detection
Below its limit of detection (LOD), an assay can’t tell signal from noise. The All of Us file we use doesn’t seem to include an LOD column, so the class explains it rather than filtering on it: treat “significant” proteins with a very low average NPX with caution.

title: 4.6 Proteomics: Blood Proteins in Type 2 Diabetes
text:
Code walk-through

Reading only our people’s rows
wanted   <- c("ResearchID", "SampleID", "PlateID", "OlinkID", "UniProt", "Assay", "NPX", "SampleQC", "AssayQC")
1col_nums <- match(wanted, npx_columns)

awk_command <- str_glue(
2  "gzip -dc {shQuote(NPX_FILE)} | ",
3  "awk -F'\\t' -v OFS='\\t' -v id={col_nums[1]} ",
4  "'NR==FNR {{keep[$1]; next}} FNR==1 || ($id in keep) {{print {str_c('$', col_nums, collapse = ', ')}}}' ",
  "{shQuote(ids_file)} -"
)
5npx_long <- data.table::fread(cmd = awk_command, sep = "\t", header = TRUE)

1

The positions of the columns we need (awk refers to columns by number).

2

Uncompress the 2.6 GB file as it’s read, without saving an uncompressed copy.

3

Tell awk the columns are separated by tabs, and which column holds the participant ID.

4

First read our 600 IDs into a list called keep; then print the header, and every line whose ID is in keep, keeping only the columns we need. ({ } is how str_glue() writes a literal brace.)

5

fread() runs the command and reads the result into R: about 3 million rows instead of over 50 million.




Differential abundance
1design <- model.matrix(~ group + age + sex_at_birth, data = samples)
2fit     <- eBayes(lmFit(npx, design))
3results <- topTable(fit, coef = "groupcase", number = Inf)

1

The model for every protein: case vs control, adjusted for age and sex.

2

Fit it to every protein at once. No voom(): NPX is already on a log scale and isn’t a count.

3

Every protein’s result, sorted by p-value.

Results from our test run in October 2026 (CDR v9), 300 cases and 300 controls.







People with proteomics
1,446 cases, 6,154 controls

3.5 minutes; about 32.5 million rows read, 5,420 proteins


QC
over 99% of measurements passed; under 1% failed; a few WARN (kept, per Olink’s advice)

Outliers

Significant proteins
about 280–290, most of them higher in diabetes


Sensitivity: plate in the model
182 significant; logFC correlation with the main analysis 0.93


Sensitivity: outliers removed
533 significant; logFC correlation 0.995


Pathways (GO)
up in diabetes: inflammation and defense and metabolism (organic acid, small molecule metabolism)


Leptin, BMI challenge
logFC 0.68 without BMI (adjusted p ≈ 0.00007) → 0.18 with BMI (p ≈ 0.63): mostly body size


Top protein
NFASC (higher in diabetes)


pQTLs
18 of the top 20 proteins had very strong pQTLs


rs7903146
not in any fine-mapped pQTL



The proteins point to organs:








Organ
Proteins
A possible story




Kidney
HAVCR1 (KIM-1) and PDZK1 higher; UMOD lower
early diabetic kidney disease


Fat tissue
FABP4 higher; LPL lower
insulin resistance


Gut
LGALS4, MUC13, PRAP1 higher
possibly medicines such as metformin



💬 Discuss: the effects barely changed in the sensitivity analyses, but the number of significant proteins ranged from 182 to 533. Which would you report, and why? (Choose the rule before looking; report the others as sensitivity analyses. Adding 119 plate terms to a 600-person model costs power.)
💬 Discuss: which of these are causes of diabetes, consequences (kidney damage), or treatment effects? UMOD’s pQTL sits in the UMOD gene, a region also linked to kidney function in large GWAS: an example of how pQTLs help ask about cause (Mendelian randomization).

title: Omics Series
text:
Seven classes on the All of Us genomic and multi-omics data. Together they ask: what can DNA, RNA, and proteins tell us about type 2 diabetes?
The thread through the series is one genetic variant, rs7903146, in the gene TCF7L2: the strongest known genetic risk factor for type 2 diabetes. We find it, test it, follow its effects across hundreds of diseases, and then look for it in gene activity and blood proteins.

text: New to genetics and omics? This page explains everything the omics series assumes, in plain language. You don’t need to read it all at once: each class links back to the parts it uses.

title: Omics for Beginners
section: The big picture: DNA → RNA → protein
text:
The big picture: DNA → RNA → protein
Think of a cell as an IKEA store:










At IKEA
In the cell
Measured in All of Us by




DNA
the catalog: instructions for every product, kept in the store. Every store has the same catalog
all the instructions, in the cell’s nucleus. The same in nearly every cell, and fixed from birth
whole-genome sequencing, genotyping arrays (classes 4.1–4.4)


RNA (messenger RNA, mRNA)
a copy of the assembly instructions for one product, taken out to where the building happens. Popular products get many copies
a working copy of one gene, carried out of the nucleus. More copies = a more active gene
RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of blood (class 4.5)


Protein
the assembled furniture, built by following the instructions from a box of pieces
built from amino acids (the pieces) by the cell’s ribosomes (the people assembling), following the mRNA: hormones, enzymes, signals
Olink proteomics, blood plasma (class 4.6)



The analogy also shows why the layers don’t always agree (class 4.7): a store can print lots of instruction copies but run short of pieces; furniture can last for years after the instructions are thrown away; and some furniture in your home (plasma proteins) was built in a different store (another organ) than the one whose instructions you’re counting (blood cells).
DNA ──(copied)──→ RNA ──(translated)──→ protein
fixed             changes with          changes with
from birth        time, disease,        time, disease,
                  medicines             medicines
This is why the classes ask different questions of each layer:

DNA tells you about lifelong risk: a variant you’re born with can’t be caused by diabetes. That makes genetic results useful for asking about cause.
RNA and proteins show what’s happening now, including the consequences of a disease and its treatment. They’re harder to read as causes.

title: Omics for Beginners
text:
Genome vocabulary








Word
Means
Example in the series




Genome
all of a person’s DNA: about 3 billion “letters” (A, C, G, T) on 23 pairs of chromosomes



Gene
a stretch of DNA with the instructions for one product
TCF7L2, on chromosome 10


Position
where a letter is: chromosome:position, on a reference genome map. All of Us uses GRCh38
chr10:112998590


Variant
a place where people’s DNA differs
rs7903146


SNP (“snip”)
a variant where one letter differs
C or T at rs7903146


Indel
a few letters inserted or deleted



STR
a short tandem repeat: a short pattern repeated a different number of times in different people. Harder to sequence
the top hit in 4.2


Allele
one version of a variant. REF = the one in the reference genome; ALT = the other(s)
REF C, ALT T


Multi-allelic
a variant with more than one ALT allele
rs7903146 is C, T, or G in All of Us


Genotype
a person’s two alleles (one from each parent), often counted as 0, 1, or 2 copies of one allele
C/T = 1 copy of T


Allele frequency
how common an allele is in a group
T: about 28% of alleles in All of Us


rsID
a standard name for a known variant. All of Us files name variants by position instead
rs7903146 = chr10:112998590:C


Linkage disequilibrium (LD)
nearby variants are inherited together, so they move together. Measured by r² from 0 to 1
why a GWAS peak has many variants


Genetic ancestry
estimated from DNA; not the same as self-reported race or ethnicity
groups afr, amr, eas, eur, mid, sas


Principal components (PCs)
a few numbers per person that summarise their genetic ancestry; used to adjust for it
PC1 to PC10 in the models

The analyses








Analysis
Asks
Class




GWAS (genome-wide association study)
which variants are linked to one disease?
4.2, 4.3


PheWAS (phenome-wide association study)
which diseases are linked to one variant?
4.4


Differential expression
which genes are more or less active in one group?
4.5


Differential abundance
which proteins are higher or lower in one group?
4.6


eQTL / pQTL
which variants change a gene’s activity / a protein’s level?
4.5, 4.6



They’re all the same idea underneath: one regression per thing tested (per variant, disease, gene, or protein), then a correction for having done many tests.

title: Omics for Beginners
text:
Statistics you’ll meet







Term
Means




Logistic regression
a model for a yes/no outcome (diabetes: yes or no). Used in the GWAS and PheWAS


Linear regression
a model for a number (gene activity, protein level). Used for RNA and proteins


Odds ratio (OR)
from logistic regression: how the odds of the outcome change per copy of an allele. 1 = no effect; 1.25 = 25% higher odds


Beta
the effect on the log scale. For logistic regression, OR = e^beta (e.g. beta 0.22 → OR 1.25)


Log₂ scale
each step of 1 means twice as much. RNA (log-CPM) and protein (NPX) values use it. A logFC of 1 = twice as high; −1 = half


p-value
how surprising the result would be if there were no effect. Small = strong evidence


Multiple testing
testing thousands of things gives some small p-values by chance alone


Bonferroni
a strict fix: divide 0.05 by the number of tests


Genome-wide significance
p < 5 × 10⁻⁸: Bonferroni for about a million independent variants


FDR (false discovery rate, adjusted p-value)
a gentler fix used for genes and proteins: among results with FDR < 0.05, about 5% are expected to be false


Covariate
another variable in the model, to adjust for (age, sex, PCs)


Confounding
a third variable that affects both things you’re comparing, creating a misleading link. Ancestry is the classic one in genetics


Power
the chance of detecting a real effect. Small samples + small effects = low power


Selection bias
a misleading link created by how the sample was chosen (class 4.4)


Collider bias
a misleading link created by adjusting for a common effect of two things (class 4.4)

title: Omics for Beginners
section: Normalization: what’s done for you, and what you check
text:
Normalization: what’s done for you, and what you check
Normalization removes technical differences between samples (how deeply each was sequenced, which plate it was on), so the differences left are biological. Each data type needs something different:









Layer
Done before you get the data
What you do in class
What you check




Genotypes (4.1–4.4)
quality control of samples and variants
variant QC (frequency, missingness, Hardy-Weinberg); adjust for ancestry PCs
that the known variant replicates; the Q-Q plot


RNA counts (4.5)
reads aligned to the genome and counted per gene
normalize yourself: TMM factors (edgeR), log-CPM, voom weights
TMM factors near 1; boxplots line up after normalizing; the voom trend; PCA


Protein NPX (4.6)
plate-control and batch normalization; already on a log₂ scale
use as is (don’t normalize twice)
plates line up; how much plate explains of the main patterns; outliers; results with plate in the model









ImportantThe statistics packages don’t normalize for you



limma, used for both RNA and proteins, fits a model to whatever numbers you give it. It does not normalize. If you skip normalization, or normalize the wrong way, limma will still run and still give p-values: they’ll just be wrong. That’s why the classes show the normalization and check it, rather than hiding it in one line.

text:
How to read the code
The notebooks repeat a few patterns. Here’s one PLINK command from class 4.1, line by line:
1plink_cmd <- str_glue(
2  "plink2 --pfile {shQuote(file.path(pgen_dir, 'acaf_threshold.chr10'))} ",
3  "--keep {shQuote(keep_file)} ",
4  "--chr 10 --from-bp {REGION_START} --to-bp {REGION_END} ",
5  "--make-pgen --freq ",
6  "--out {shQuote(out_prefix)}"
)
7plink_output <- system(plink_cmd, intern = TRUE)

1

str_glue() builds one long piece of text (the command), filling in anything inside { } with the value of an R variable.

2

Read the PLINK 2 files for chromosome 10. shQuote() puts quotes around the file path, in case it contains spaces.

3

Keep only the people listed in keep_file: our sample.

4

Keep only the variants in this region of chromosome 10 (positions in base pairs).

5

Save the result as new, small PLINK 2 files, and calculate each variant’s allele frequency.

6

The start of the new files’ names.

7

system() runs the command as if you’d typed it in the Terminal. intern = TRUE keeps what PLINK prints, so the notebook can show it.

title: 5.1 Survey Basics
text:
Overview
Most All of Us participants answer surveys about their background, health, habits, family, and life circumstances. Survey answers tell us things health records rarely do (smoking, income, family history), but they have their own structure and their own traps. In this class we learn how the survey data is organised, how to find the questions we need, and how to turn raw answers into a clean table with one row per person.

Why this class matters
Survey answers are easy to misread. A missing answer, a skipped answer, and “prefer not to answer” mean different things, and a missing answer often means the question was never asked. Treating them all as “no” or as “missing” quietly changes who is in an analysis. And the people who answer later, optional surveys aren’t a random sample.


By the end you’ll be able to

Name the All of Us surveys, and explain why each was answered by a different number of people
Find questions by text and by concept ID, in the Workbench and in the public Survey Explorer
Tell the non-answers apart, and know when PMI: None or PMI: Other is a real answer
Explain skip logic: why a missing answer often means “never asked”
Handle select all that apply questions (several answers per person)
Build a tidy table with one row per person, and compare cases and controls



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
Which surveys did the people in our cohort answer, and how do we turn their answers into usable variables?


🧪 The analysis
Four BigQuery queries (the surveys, a question dictionary, who answered what, five example questions); counts and percents by group


🎯 Why
Coding non-answers and skip logic correctly decides who is in every later analysis


✅ What we conclude
Which surveys and questions we can use, how complete they are in cases and controls, and how to code them


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Anything about cause. And people who answer later surveys aren’t a random sample


🔗 Connections
Uses the sample from 1.1; builds on 2.1 (cleaning), 2.2 (reshaping), 3.1 (Table 1); 5.2 and 5.3 use these skills





Time and cost







⏱️ Class time
90 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 5 minutes. Slowest: the question dictionary


💰 Cost
about $2 per student: four queries on ds_survey, a large table, plus the app


📋 Before class
0.0 setup run once. cohort_sample.csv from 1.1 is used if it’s in your bucket; otherwise the notebook makes it

Key concepts

How the surveys work
Participants answer surveys online (or with staff), one module at a time. The Basics, Overall Health, and Lifestyle are answered when people join, so almost everyone has them. The others are offered later and are optional, so fewer people answer them.








Word
Means
Example

one item, with a concept ID and a concept code

Yes

race: White and Asian

follow-up questions shown only after certain answers
“How often do you smoke now?” only after Yes to 100 cigarettes



The answers are in the ds_survey table (questions and answers as text, plus their concept IDs). The standard OMOP observation table holds the same answers as concept IDs.


Non-answers








Code
Means
Usually treat as

missing

chose “prefer not to answer”
missing, or its own category


PMI: Dont Know, PMI: Not Sure
chose “don’t know” or “not sure”
missing, or its own category

PMI: Other

PMI is the program’s former name, the Precision Medicine Initiative.


Where to read the questions

Data Browser: how many participants gave each answer
In the Workbench: the question dictionary built in Part 4



Common ways to analyse survey answers









Answer type
Example

Model with




Yes / no

linear, or Poisson for counts



Missing answers: dropping them (a complete-case analysis) changes who is compared if some groups skip more. Alternatives: keep Prefer not to answer as its own category, or multiple imputation (the mice package).


No survey weights
National surveys like NHANES and BRFSS choose people at random and give each a survey weight (how many people in the US population they stand for), so their percents estimate the whole country. All of Us participants volunteer, and the program deliberately oversamples groups that research has often left out. There are no survey weights, so:








Can we say it?




“In our sample, 41% of cases rated their health fair or poor”
✅ it describes our sample


“41% of Americans with diabetes rate their health fair or poor”
❌ our sample isn’t a random sample of the country


How common diabetes is, from our sample
❌ our sample is half cases by design


“People with diabetes had higher odds of fair or poor health”
⚠️ with care: comparisons within a cohort transfer better than percents, but selection can still bias them



For population numbers: report sample estimates and say who the sample is; build approximate weights from Census totals (e.g. raking with survey::rake()); or compare with NHANES or BRFSS.

title: 5.1 Survey Basics
text:
Code walk-through

A question dictionary
questions <- run_query(str_glue("
  WITH q AS (
    SELECT survey, question_concept_id,
1           ANY_VALUE(question)       AS question,
           COUNT(DISTINCT person_id) AS n_people
    FROM `{CURRENT_DATASET}.ds_survey`
    GROUP BY survey, question_concept_id
  )
  SELECT q.*, c.concept_code
  FROM q
2  LEFT JOIN `{CURRENT_DATASET}.concept` AS c ON c.concept_id = q.question_concept_id
"))
3save_data(questions, "survey_questions.csv")

4find_questions <- function(pattern) {
  questions %>%
    filter(str_detect(question, regex(pattern, ignore_case = TRUE))) %>%
    arrange(desc(n_people))
}
find_questions("smok")

1

One row per question. ANY_VALUE() picks one text per ID: the same ID can be worded slightly differently in different survey versions.

2

The concept code (e.g. Smoking_100CigsLifetime) from the concept table: the name used in the codebooks.

3

Saved to your bucket, so you query once and search for free.

4

Search the dictionary by a word or pattern, ignoring upper and lower case.




Skip logic: one smoking variable from two questions
smoking <- smoking %>%
1  mutate(smoking_status = case_when(
2    str_detect(smoked_100, regex("^no$", ignore_case = TRUE))                    ~ "Never",
    str_detect(smoke_frequency, regex("every day|some days", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Current",
    str_detect(smoked_100, regex("^yes$", ignore_case = TRUE)) &
3      str_detect(smoke_frequency, regex("not at all", ignore_case = TRUE))        ~ "Former",
    TRUE                                                                          ~ NA_character_))

1

case_when() checks each rule in order, and uses the first that’s true.

2

No to 100 cigarettes: never asked the follow-up, so a never smoker, not “missing”.

3

Former needs Yes first: someone who skipped the first question and answered Not At All could be a former smoker or someone who never smoked.

title: 5.3 Social Factors
text:
Overview
How much people earn, how much schooling they had, whether they have health insurance, and whether they can afford enough food all shape their health. These are social determinants of health, and type 2 diabetes is one of the conditions most closely tied to them. In this class we code four social factors from the surveys, compare cases and controls, and answer the question 5.2 left open: is the link between alcohol and diabetes explained by confounding?

Why this class matters
Social factors are among the strongest risk factors for type 2 diabetes, and the most common confounders of other links. This class shows confounding happening, on real data: an odds ratio that changes when a confounder is added. It’s also where careful language matters most.


By the end you’ll be able to

Turn ordered answers (income, education) into groups, and keep Prefer not to answer as a category
Find and code questions from the Social Determinants of Health survey
Compare social factors between cases and controls, and model them with logistic regression
Show confounding: how an odds ratio changes when a confounder is added, on the same people
Tell a confounder from a step on the path (a mediator), and describe social factors as associations



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
Are income, education, health insurance, and food insecurity linked to type 2 diabetes? Does adjusting for them explain the alcohol result from 5.2?


🧪 The analysis
Percents by group; logistic regression adjusted for age and sex; the 5.2 alcohol model with and without income and education, on the same people


🎯 Why
Social factors are strong risk factors, and common confounders of other links


✅ What we conclude
How strongly each factor is linked to type 2 diabetes, and how much of the alcohol and smoking links they explain


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Cause. Diabetes can also lower income; and these factors reflect circumstances (where people live, discrimination, access to care), not individual choices


🔗 Connections
Uses files from 5.1 and 5.2; models from 3.2; “who gets diagnosed” from 3.4





Time and cost







⏱️ Class time
90 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 3 minutes


💰 Cost
about $1.50 per student: two queries on ds_survey, plus the app


📋 Before class
run 5.1 and 5.2: this class uses their files

BMI, for the income–diabetes link



To see confounding fairly, compare models on the same people: glm() drops anyone missing a variable, so a model with more variables can quietly use fewer people.


Careful words
Write “people with lower incomes had higher odds of type 2 diabetes”, not “low income causes diabetes”. Social factors reflect circumstances and structures, and diabetes can itself lower income.

title: 6.1 Wearables Basics
text:
Overview
Tens of thousands of All of Us participants share data from a Fitbit or from Apple Health (iPhone and Apple Watch). In this class we learn where the wearable data is, what it costs to use, and how to turn months of daily records into one clean value per person, ready for the analyses in 6.2 and 6.3.

Why this class matters
Wearable data is easy to misuse in three ways: a day the device wasn’t worn looks like an inactive day; a phone and a watch count steps differently; and one careless query on a minute-level table can cost tens of dollars. This class builds the habits that prevent all three: price every query, keep only valid days, and never pool different devices.


By the end you’ll be able to

Describe the Fitbit and Apple HealthKit data: tables, layouts, and who has them
Estimate and check the cost of a query, and query huge minute-level tables safely
Define a valid wear day, and check a wear measure against a better one
Summarise many days into one value per person
Explain why Fitbit, iPhone, and Apple Watch steps can’t simply be pooled
Describe who has wearable data, and what that means for generalisability



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
Who in our cohort has wearable data, how much, and how do we turn it into usable variables?


🧪 The analysis
Table sizes and costs; valid wear days; median daily steps per person, by device; steps by hour of the day; who has data


🎯 Why
Un-worn days, different devices, and huge tables each lead to wrong or expensive results if ignored


✅ What we conclude
How many cases and controls have usable data, and a per-person step summary for 6.2


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Anything about cause. And people with wearables aren’t typical: results describe them


🔗 Connections
Cohort from 1.1; units and cleaning from 2.1; long vs wide from 2.2; no survey weights from 5.1





Time and cost







⏱️ Class time
95 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 5 minutes


💰 Cost
about $1.40 in queries in our test run ($1.20 of it the Apple HealthKit query), plus the app


📋 Before class

Two sources of wearable data

Apple HealthKit

Valid wear days
A day with 300 steps could be an inactive day, or a device left on the charger. Studies keep only valid days:







Rule
Why

Then each person gets one value: their median daily steps over valid days.


Cost: big tables, clustering, and dry runs
The minute-level Fitbit tables are over 6 TB each (a full read is about $40). They’re clustered by person_id: each person’s rows are stored together, so a query filtered by person reads only those people. A dry run (free) prices a query before it runs, clustering included:

Reads

text:
Code walk-through

Two cost helpers
1run_if_cheap(sql, max_dollars = 1)
2last_query_cost()

1

A free dry run first; the query runs only if it costs less than max_dollars. With max_dollars = 0 it only prints the estimate.

2

What the most recent query actually billed.




Daily steps plus wear time, in one query
1WITH wear AS (
  SELECT person_id, date, SUM(minute_in_zone) AS wear_minutes
  FROM heart_rate_summary
  WHERE person_id IN (…)
  GROUP BY person_id, date
)
SELECT a.person_id, a.date, a.steps, …, w.wear_minutes
FROM activity_summary AS a
2LEFT JOIN wear AS w ON a.person_id = w.person_id AND a.date = w.date
WHERE a.person_id IN (…)

1

Fitbit counts minutes in each heart-rate zone; their sum is a cheap measure of wear time.

2

LEFT JOIN keeps every activity day, even days without heart-rate data.




HealthKit: long data, text values, one device at a time
SELECT a.person_id,
       DATE(SAFE_CAST(a.start_datetime AS TIMESTAMP)) AS date,
1       CASE WHEN d.product_type LIKE 'Watch%'  THEN 'Apple Watch'
            WHEN d.product_type LIKE 'iPhone%' THEN 'iPhone'
            ELSE 'other' END AS device,
2       SUM(SAFE_CAST(a.value AS FLOAT64)) AS steps
FROM activity_measurements AS a
LEFT JOIN device_and_source AS d ON a.device_source_id = d.device_source_id
3WHERE a.data_type = 'STEP_COUNT' AND a.person_id IN (…)
4GROUP BY 1, 2, 3

1

Which device recorded each measurement.

2

value is stored as text; SAFE_CAST turns it into a number (anything that isn’t becomes NULL).

3

In the long layout, data_type picks the measure.

4

One total per person, day, and device: adding the phone and watch together would count the same steps twice.

title: 6.1 Wearables Basics
text:
What we found
Results from our test run in November 2026 (CDR v9), 5,000 cases and 5,000 controls.

Fitbit, in our sample

926 people had Fitbit data (about 850,000 person-days, 2009 to 2024); 840 had 10 or more valid days, with a median of 390 valid days each.
64% of days were valid. Most of the rest had no heart-rate data, so we couldn’t tell whether the device was worn.
Median daily steps rose from 5,142 (all days) to 5,897 (valid days): the bias un-worn days create.



Is our wear measure any good?
For 100 people, we compared the cheap measure with the one published All of Us studies use:








Wear measure
Median minutes
Days with 10+ hours




heart-rate zone total (daily table)
1,440 (exactly 24 hours on 61% of days)
98.6%


minutes with a heart-rate reading (minute-level table)
1,392 (about 23 hours)
95.5%



These Fitbit users wear their devices almost around the clock. The zone total overstates wear, but at the 10-hour cutoff the two disagree on only about 3% of days: good enough for class; for a paper, use the minute-level count.


When people move

Controls took more steps through the working day; the groups were similar at night.


Phones, watches, and Fitbits


The iPhone records far fewer steps: it misses every step taken without it.
Within the same people (151 with both an iPhone and an Apple Watch), the iPhone recorded about 59% of their Watch steps.
So Fitbit is the main data for 6.2; Apple steps are a separate measure, never pooled with Fitbit.



Who has wearable data?




Cases
Controls




Fitbit, 10+ valid days
7.3%
9.5%


Apple HealthKit steps
1.8%
3.3%



People with Fitbit data were a little younger (mean age 58 vs 59), more often female (63% vs 59%), and less often cases (43% vs 51%). Selection: results describe wearable users.

title: 6.3 Sleep and Heart Rate
text:
Overview
In 6.2, more daily steps went with a much lower rate of new type 2 diabetes. Is the same true for sleep, and for resting heart rate? This class reuses the 6.2 design, measure first, then follow, written as a function so every measure gets exactly the same rules. Sleep comes from Fitbit; resting heart rate from Apple HealthKit. We finish with a first look at HealthKit blood glucose.

Why this class matters
Real research rarely asks one question once. Turning a design into a function makes it reusable and consistent. This class also shows three things wearable studies meet all the time: a link that might not be a straight line, a smaller data source with wider confidence intervals, and a data type whose users are selected by the outcome.


By the end you’ll be able to

Turn an analysis design into a reusable function
Build valid nights of sleep from Fitbit, and baseline resting heart rate from HealthKit’s long data
Recognise a non-linear (e.g. U-shaped) association, and choose a reference group for it
Compare results from data sources of very different sizes, and read confidence intervals
Describe a new data type (blood glucose) carefully before modelling it



Analysis at a glance







❓ Question
Among adults without diabetes, are sleep duration and resting heart rate linked to developing type 2 diabetes?


🧪 The analysis
The 6.2 design as a function: baseline sleep (Fitbit) or resting heart rate (HealthKit), then follow-up for new type 2 diabetes; incidence rates and Cox models. A description of HealthKit blood glucose


🎯 Why
Measured before any diagnosis, these avoid reverse causation, as in 6.2


✅ What we conclude
Whether the links appear in All of Us wearable users, and their shape


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Cause. Sleep and heart rate reflect overall health, stress, work, and fitness. Fitbit and Apple users are different, selected groups


🔗 Connections
The design from 6.2; valid days from 6.1; HealthKit’s long, text-valued data from 6.1; functions from 3.1; survival models from 3.4





Time and cost







⏱️ Class time
95 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 5 minutes


💰 Cost
about $1 in our test run: sleep $0.15, steps $0.01, resting heart rate $0.39, glucose $0.32, plus the cohort query and the app


📋 Before class
6.2 (the design), and 3.4 (survival analysis)

text:
Key concepts

The same design, a new exposure
first valid           end of baseline                          end of follow-up
measurement           (6 months later)                         (last EHR visit, death, or 2025)
    |──── baseline ────|──────────────── follow-up ─────────────────────|
      median sleep, or      does type 2 diabetes appear? when?

excluded: anyone with type 2 diabetes before the end of baseline
As in 6.2, the exposure is measured before any diagnosis, so the design avoids reverse causation by construction.


Not every link is a straight line
Steps (6.2) had a gradient. Sleep is often different: in many studies both short and long sleep go with worse health, a U shape. So:

One “per hour of sleep” number could average away a U.
The reference group is the middle (7 to 8 hours), so the others are compared with the expected lowest-risk group.



What the devices measure








Measure
Device
Watch out for




Sleep duration
Fitbit: movement and heart rate through the night; one main sleep per night
Fitbits usually record less sleep than people report; only nights the device was worn


Sleep stages
Fitbit (newer models)
rough estimates; older devices have no stages


Resting heart rate
Apple Watch: its own daily estimate
lower with fitness; higher with stress, illness, some medicines


Blood glucose
devices and apps that share through Apple Health (e.g. continuous glucose monitors, CGMs)
who uses one is not random

1build_followup <- function(baseline, cohort, end_of_data = as.Date("2025-01-01")) {

    inner_join(cohort, by = "person_id") %>%
    mutate(…) %>%
    filter(cohort != "excluded",
2           !(cohort == "case" & t2d_date <= baseline_end),
           age_at_baseline >= 18,
           followup_end > baseline_end) %>%
    mutate(event = …, years = …)
}

3sleep_followup <- build_followup(sleep_baseline, cohort)

rates_by <- function(data, group) {
  out <- data %>%
1    group_by({{ group }}) %>%
    summarise(people = n(), n = sum(event), person_years = sum(years)) %>%
    … %>%
2    hide_small_counts()
3  if (sum(is.na(out$new_cases)) == 1) stop("Only one group is hidden …")
  out
}

1

{ group } passes a column name into the function.

2

3

If exactly one group is hidden, its count could be worked out from the printed total and the other groups (the derived counts rule from 3.1), so the function stops before printing anything. In our test run this happened with four resting-heart-rate groups, so the notebook uses three.

title: 6.3 Sleep and Heart Rate
text:
What we found
Results from our test run in November 2026 (CDR v9).

Sleep (Fitbit)

54,158 Fitbit users had a sleep baseline: a median of 6.7 hours asleep a night. 79% had sleep stages, with a median of 20% REM and 15% deep sleep, in the usual healthy range.
24,507 were followed: 1,251 new cases of type 2 diabetes over 91,514 person-years (median 2.9 years).











Compared with 7 to 8 hours
Age and sex
+ BMI

under 6 hours

1.09 (0.89 to 1.33)
1.13 (0.92 to 1.38)


8 hours or more
0.93 (0.65 to 1.34)
0.98 (0.68 to 1.40)
0.90 (0.63 to 1.29)



Cox models on the 15,712 people with BMI and steps (591 new cases).

Short sleep (under 6 hours) went with about twice the rate of new type 2 diabetes. BMI explained part of it; daily steps almost none.
Long sleep wasn’t linked: no U shape here. Many studies of self-reported sleep find one; Fitbit measures sleep differently, and few people slept 8+ hours by its measure. We expected a U; the data decided.



Resting heart rate (Apple HealthKit)

11,258 HealthKit users had a resting-heart-rate baseline; 5,306 could be followed, with 133 new cases: far fewer than for sleep.
Every 10 beats per minute higher: HR 1.44 (1.19 to 1.75), adjusted for age and sex; 1.25 (1.00 to 1.55) with BMI.
A higher resting heart rate went with more new diabetes, but the interval is much wider than for sleep, and with BMI it barely excludes 1. Fewer people and fewer new cases: less certainty.

People with type 1 (or unclear) diabetes mostly use CGMs, record for months, and spend the least time in range.
Controls share only a few days, perhaps short trials of over-the-counter CGMs.
Who has glucose data, and how much, depends on diabetes status: selection by the outcome. This data suits questions about diabetes management, not about who develops diabetes.

💬 Discuss: resting heart rate is lower in people who are fit. Is its link with diabetes about the heart, about fitness, or about something else (stress, illness, medicines like beta-blockers)?

title: 6.3 Sleep and Heart Rate
text:
Instructor notes






TipInstructor tip






The function is the bridge from 6.2: show that it’s the 6.2 flow table, written once.
Ask for predictions before showing the sleep results: straight line or U? Many students will predict a U. The result (short sleep only) is a good “the data decides” moment.
Resting heart rate is the place to discuss power: the same kind of question, with far fewer people, gives a much less certain answer.
Derived counts: the four-group resting heart rate table would have revealed a small count through subtraction. Show students why rates_by() stops, rather than warns.
Glucose is the course’s clearest example of selection by the outcome.
Privacy: glucose traces are very personal. Only show group summaries outside the Workbench.

title: 6.3 Sleep and Heart Rate
text:
Key takeaways

A design written as a function applies the same rules to every exposure
Look at groups before using one number, and let the data decide the shape: here, short sleep, not a U
Smaller data sources give wider confidence intervals: “can’t tell” isn’t “no link”
Check for derived counts in every table with a printed total
Describe a new data type before modelling it: glucose users are selected by the outcome

title: Data Collections
text:
A curated dataset published for researchers, e.g., the All of Us Registered Tier
Comes with:

Versions (e.g., cdrv9)
Policies on how the data can be accessed and used
Access levels (Reader, Discover, …)

You don’t copy the data. Adding a collection to a workspace creates references to data that stays in the provider’s cloud project.
The workspace inherits the collection’s policies, permanently

Think of it as: data collection = the data source; workspace = where you analyze it






TipInstructor tip





Verily calls these “referenced resources”. Because the data isn’t copied, adding it is free; you pay for the queries and compute you run on it.

title: Data Collections
text:
A curated dataset published for researchers, e.g., the All of Us Registered Tier
Comes with:

Versions (e.g., cdrv9)
Policies on how the data can be accessed and used

You don’t copy the data. Adding a collection to a workspace creates references to data that stays in the provider’s cloud project.

Think of it as: data collection = the data source; workspace = where you analyze it

Verily calls these “referenced resources”. Because the data isn’t copied, adding it is free; you pay for the queries and compute you run on it.

title: Example Notebooks
text:
R and Python notebooks for learning to analyse All of Us data in the Researcher Workbench 2.0, organised in series. Each notebook does one thing, so each can be taught as its own class.
Written for beginners. Each notebook has learning objectives, a plain-language primer on the key concepts, an explanation of every step and function, “Read the output” guides, exercises with hidden answers, common errors, and key takeaways. Notebook 0.0 includes a 5-minute introduction to Jupyter and R.

title: Example Notebooks
text:
Folder layout
notebooks/
├── 0.0 setup.ipynb        start here
├── aou_setup.R            shared settings + helper functions (R)
├── aou_setup.py           the same settings for Python notebooks (read from the .R files)
├── my_settings.R          your bucket name (made by 0.0 setup; Git ignores it)
├── sql/                   the shared type 2 diabetes cohort query
├── core/                  1.1 – 3.4: build a cohort; clean, reshape, join; analyse
├── omics/                 4.1 – 4.7: genomes, GWAS, PheWAS, RNA-seq, proteomics
├── surveys/               5.1 – 5.3 (coming soon)
├── wearables/             6.1 – 6.3 (coming soon)
├── workflows/             an Optional Extras class: run one analysis on many files with dsub
└── archive/               earlier versions
Notebooks in a series folder load the shared files from the folder above (source("../aou_setup.R")), so keep this layout: cloning the repository does that for you.

title: Example Notebooks
text:
Core series (core/)
Nine R notebooks that take one study from start to finish: people with type 2 diabetes (cases) compared with people without diabetes (controls), including time to chronic kidney disease (CKD) after diagnosis. They use the same cohort query as every other series (sql/t2d_cohort.sql) and a sample of 5,000 cases and 5,000 controls. Every notebook opens with an “Analysis at a glance” box and a time and cost estimate.



Notebook
What it does
Time




aou_setup.R
Shared settings (the dataset) and helper functions. Your bucket name goes in my_settings.R, made by 0.0 setup and ignored by Git



0.0 setup
Checks your settings and the connection to the data



1.1 build_cohorts
The OMOP tables, concept IDs, and SQL; the cohort query; a sample; survey answers and measurements
90 min


1.2 survival_data
Time zero, event, and censoring; first CKD dates; follow-up
60 min


2.1 clean
Types, non-answers, messy text, duplicates, units, plausible ranges, missing data, a cleaning log
105 min


2.2 reshape
Long vs wide; one value per person; pivot_wider() and pivot_longer()
70 min


2.3 join_and_bind
bind_rows(); left, inner, full, and anti joins; checks after every join; the analysis table
75 min


3.1 table_one
A Table 1 with your own functions; missing data; the small-count check
75 min


3.2 logistic_regression
Odds ratios for type 2 diabetes; adjustment; reverse causation
85 min


3.3 linear_regression
Systolic blood pressure; model comparison; residuals
75 min


3.4 survival_analysis
Kaplan–Meier curves (ggplot2), log-rank test, Cox model, proportional hazards
90 min



Variables used: age, sex at birth, gender, race, ethnicity; two PTSD survey questions (asked only of people who reported PTSD); BMI, systolic blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, and HbA1c; type 2 diabetes and CKD dates; EHR and death dates.

How they fit together
sql/t2d_cohort.sql
     │
1.1 build_cohorts ──► cohort_sample.csv, survey_raw.csv, measurement_raw.csv
1.2 survival_data ──► ckd_dates.csv
     │

Only 1.1 and 1.2 query BigQuery (about $2 to $3 in total); every later notebook reads the saved files, so a class can start at any notebook once the data is saved.

title: Example Notebooks
text:
Getting started
You need an All of Us workspace with the Controlled Tier data collection and a bucket (Resources tab → + New resource → Cloud Storage bucket).

Get the notebooks into your workspace, either way:

Clone this repository: in your workspace, go to Apps → Git repositories → + Add repository and enter https://github.com/CWML/All-of-Us-Training-Resources.git. It’s cloned into apps you create afterward.
Download and upload: download the whole notebooks/ folder and upload it to your app with its subfolders, so aou_setup.R and sql/ stay one level above the series folders.

Launch an app, e.g. AoU Jupyter (it has R and Python kernels).
Open 0.0 setup and follow it. It saves your bucket’s folder name in my_settings.R, a file Git ignores, so git pull never clashes with it. The dataset (CURRENT_DATASET in aou_setup.R) is already set to Controlled Tier CDR v9 (wb-silky-artichoke-2408.C2025Q4R6). Don’t copy one from a Data Explorer query: the Data Explorer currently uses CDR v8 (C2024Q3R9)
Run a series in order: core 1.1 → 1.2 → 2.1 → 2.2 → 2.3 → 3.1 to 3.4; or omics 4.1 → 4.7.

R packages: tidyverse, lubridate, bigrquery, broom, survival. aou_setup.R installs any that are missing the first time it runs (this can take a few minutes).

title: Example Notebooks
text:
The study population
Every series uses the cohort in sql/t2d_cohort.sql:

Adults (18+ on 2025-01-01, the CDR v9 data cutoff, or at death) with at least one EHR visit
Cases: a type 2 diabetes diagnosis (concept 201826 or anything under it), and no type 1 diabetes diagnosis
Controls: no diabetes diagnosis of any type (concept 201820 or anything under it)
Race and ethnicity are described, not used to choose people

The core series takes a random sample of 5,000 cases and 5,000 controls (ages 18 to 100); the omics classes take their own samples among people with each data type.

title: Example Notebooks
text:
Point and click: Data Explorer
The Data Explorer, Workbench 2.0’s point-and-click tool, can build a similar cohort without SQL. Two cautions: it currently uses CDR v8 (C2024Q3R9), while these notebooks use CDR v9, and participant IDs changed between v8 and v9, so Data Explorer exports can’t be combined with the notebooks’ files. Its rules also differ a little (e.g. age today instead of on 2025-01-01), so its counts won’t match. Step-by-step instructions, with screenshots, are on the course website: Optional: build the cohort in the Data Explorer.

title: Coding with AI: Exercises and Prompt Cards
text:
Exercise 2: Explain this code
Why: an AI is an excellent tutor for code you didn’t write. But explanations can be confidently wrong, so check them against something you trust.
Paste this prompt and code into your AI tool:

Explain this BigQuery SQL line by line, for someone new to SQL. What does each part do, and why might it be needed?

ehr_people AS (
  SELECT
    v.person_id,
    MIN(v.visit_start_date) AS first_ehr_date,
    MAX(v.visit_start_date) AS last_ehr_date
  FROM `{CURRENT_DATASET}.visit_occurrence` AS v
  JOIN `{CURRENT_DATASET}.visit_occurrence_ext` AS ve
    ON v.visit_occurrence_id = ve.visit_occurrence_id
  WHERE STARTS_WITH(ve.src_id, 'EHR site')
     OR STARTS_WITH(ve.src_id, 'Participant Mediated EHR')
  GROUP BY v.person_id
),
Then check: the same lines in notebooks/sql/t2d_cohort.sql have comments written by people who tested them. Does the AI’s explanation agree? Did it know why the WHERE line is there?


Show answer


It makes a small table, ehr_people: one row per person with at least one health-record visit, and the dates of their first and last visit (MIN and MAX, per person because of GROUP BY).
visit_occurrence_ext is an All of Us extension table. Its src_id says where each visit came from.
The WHERE line keeps visits from EHR sites (records a hospital or clinic sent) and participant-mediated EHR (records participants shared themselves). It leaves out program visits (Staff Portal, Participant Portal: physical measurements and surveys), which aren’t health records.
An AI usually explains MIN, MAX, and GROUP BY well. It may not know what src_id holds in All of Us, and may guess. That’s the part to check against the comments, or the data dictionary.
crumbs: Coding with AI: Exercises and Prompt Cards

title: Coding with AI: Exercises and Prompt Cards
text:
Exercise 3: Fix this error
Why: most of the time you’ll use an AI for a specific error. The skill is giving it enough to help (the code and the error message) and nothing it mustn’t see (the data).
The code below joins BMI values onto the cohort. In the Workbench it fails. Here it uses a made-up data frame with the same columns, so you can run it on your own computer:
library(tidyverse)

# Made-up data: same column names as the course files, no real people
cohort_sample <- tibble(person_id = c("1001", "1002", "1003", "1004"),
                        cohort    = c("case", "control", "case", "control"))
bmi <- tibble(person_id = c(1001, 1003, 1004),
              bmi       = c(31.2, 27.5, 24.9))

cohort_bmi <- cohort_sample %>% left_join(bmi, by = "person_id")
The error:
Error in `left_join()`:
! Can't join `x$person_id` with `y$person_id` due to incompatible types.
ℹ `x$person_id` is a <character>.
ℹ `y$person_id` is a <double>.
Paste this prompt, with the code and the error:

This R code fails with the error below. Explain the cause in plain language, fix it, and add a check that the join didn’t add or lose rows.

Then: run the fixed code. Does cohort_bmi have the same number of rows as cohort_sample? Does person 1002 (no BMI) still appear, with NA?


Show answer

person_id is text in one table and a number in the other. A number and the same digits as text don’t match, so R refuses to join them. Make them the same type, then check the rows:
cohort_bmi <- cohort_sample %>%
  left_join(bmi %>% mutate(person_id = as.character(person_id)), by = "person_id")

stopifnot(nrow(cohort_bmi) == nrow(cohort_sample))   # a left join must not add or lose rows
Person 1002 stays, with bmi = NA: that’s what a left join does. In the course, every notebook turns person_id into text as soon as data arrives (mutate(person_id = as.character(person_id)), or col_types = cols(person_id = "c") when loading a file), so this can’t happen. See class 2.3 on checking every join.
Did the AI suggest as.numeric() instead? It works here, but very large IDs can lose digits as numbers. Text is safer for IDs.

title: Coding with AI: Exercises and Prompt Cards
text:
Exercise 4: Spot the mistakes
Why: AI code often runs and still breaks the rules, or gives the wrong answer. Reviewing it is your job.
A student asked an AI: “Write R code to compare HbA1c in people with type 2 diabetes, by race, in All of Us.” This is what it wrote. Don’t run it. Find as many problems as you can (there are at least seven):
sql <- "
SELECT *
FROM `{Sys.getenv('WORKSPACE_CDR')}.condition_occurrence` AS co
JOIN `{Sys.getenv('WORKSPACE_CDR')}.measurement` AS m
  ON co.person_id = m.person_id
WHERE co.condition_concept_id = 201820    -- type 2 diabetes
  AND m.measurement_concept_id = 3004410  -- HbA1c
"
t2d <- run_query(str_glue(sql))

head(t2d)

t2d %>%
  group_by(race) %>%
  summarise(n          = n(),
            mean_hba1c = mean(value_as_number),
            max_hba1c  = max(value_as_number))


Show answer










#
Problem
Why it matters
The fix




1
WORKSPACE_CDR
It isn’t set in Workbench 2.0: the query fails
CURRENT_DATASET, from aou_setup.R


2
201820 labelled “type 2 diabetes”
201820 is diabetes of all types; type 2 is 201826. The AI wrote an ID from memory
Look it up (Athena, the Data Browser, or a query on concept)


3
= 201826 alone would still miss people
Most diagnoses use more specific codes (e.g. type 2 diabetes with kidney complications)
Use concept_ancestor to include every code below it, as the cohort query does


4
SELECT * on measurement
One of the largest tables: you pay for every column read
Select only the columns you need; price it first with run_if_cheap()


5
head(t2d)
Prints individual rows: IDs, dates, values
Never print rows; show summaries


6
group_by(race)
There’s no race column in these tables: it’s in person (via concept). The AI invented a column
Join person, or use the cohort query, which already has race


7
Joining conditions × measurements
Each diagnosis row is paired with each HbA1c row: someone with 10 diagnosis codes and 5 tests becomes 50 rows. n counts rows, not people, and the mean is weighted toward people with many records
Find the people first (one row each), then one HbA1c per person (e.g. the latest), as in classes 2.2 and 2.3


8
n = n() with no hiding
Some groups may have 1 to 20 people
hide_small_counts(); combine small groups


9
max_hba1c
A maximum is one person’s value
Report means or medians, not maxima or minima


10
No check of units or plausible values
HbA1c can be stored in % or mmol/mol, and some values are errors
Count the units first, and keep plausible values (class 2.1)



The pattern: it looked right and might even have run. Every problem was caught by a rule you already know, not by trusting the answer.

title: Coding with AI: Exercises and Prompt Cards
text:
Exercise 5: The full round trip
Why: this is the whole class in one task: the AI improves code on your computer, GitHub carries it, and the Workbench runs it on real data that never leaves.
The task: the worked example’s count_by_group() hides counts of 1 to 20. But, as the class page warns, if a cohort has exactly one hidden count, it can be worked out by subtraction from the cohort’s total. Fix that.
On your computer, in your fork:

Start a branch: git checkout -b count-by-group.
Paste this prompt (with Claude Code, it can create the file itself; with a chat tool, paste the function from the worked example too):

Create notebooks/helpers.R with the function count_by_group(data, var) from the worked example on the Coding with AI page. Change it so that, if exactly one count in a cohort is hidden (1 to 20), the next-smallest count in that cohort is hidden too, with its percent, so no hidden count can be worked out by subtraction. Then write a small made-up data frame with columns person_id, cohort, and self_reported_category that triggers this, and a check that no cohort ends up with exactly one hidden count.

Read the change (git diff), and run the test on the made-up data. Does the check pass?
Commit (watch the pre-commit check run) and push: git push -u origin count-by-group.

In the Workbench, in your app’s terminal:

cd into your fork, then git fetch and git checkout count-by-group.
Open a new notebook in notebooks/core/ (leave it named Untitled…: Git ignores those), with the R kernel, and run:
source("../aou_setup.R")
source("../helpers.R")
cohort_sample <- load_cohort_sample()   # 1.1's sample, or rebuilt (one query, under $1)
count_by_group(cohort_sample, "self_reported_category")
Read the result in the Workbench. Are any counts hidden? In a cohort with hidden counts, are there at least two?

Back on GitHub: open a pull request in your fork, read Files changed, wait for the safety check, and merge.
✅ Check: the function passes the test on made-up data and runs on the real data; no cohort shows exactly one hidden count; the real result never left the Workbench.


Show one answer

count_by_group <- function(data, var) {
  data %>%
    filter(!is.na(.data[[var]])) %>%
    count(cohort, level = .data[[var]]) %>%
    group_by(cohort) %>%
    mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1),
           hide    = n <= 20,
           # one hidden count can be worked out from the cohort's total:
           # if exactly one is hidden, hide the next-smallest too
           hide    = hide | (sum(hide) == 1 & rank(n, ties.method = "first") == 2)) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    mutate(n       = if_else(hide, NA_integer_, n),
           percent = if_else(hide, NA_real_, percent)) %>%
    select(-hide)
}
The hidden count is always the smallest in its cohort (rank 1), so the next-smallest has rank 2. Your AI’s version may look different: what matters is that your test shows no cohort with exactly one hidden count.
Review questions to ask the AI: what if a cohort has only one level? What if the overall total isn’t shown anywhere? (Hiding is about what readers can work out, so think about every table you publish together.)

title: Coding with AI: Exercises and Prompt Cards
text:
Prompt cards
Copy, then change the parts in italics to your task. Every card works best when your instructions file (AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md) is in place, or pasted at the start of a chat.








Task
Prompt
What to check in the answer




Explain
Explain this code line by line, for someone new to R. Which parts are specific to All of Us?
Compare with the code’s comments, or the data dictionary. Ask about anything it skips


Fix an error
This code fails with the error below. Explain the cause, fix it, and add a check that would have caught it. (paste the code, and the error with any data values removed)
Run the fix; make sure it fixes the cause, not just the message


Test on made-up data
Write a small made-up data frame with these columns: …, including the tricky cases (missing values, small groups, duplicates). Then test the function on it.
Did the fake data include the cases that could break it?


Write a query
Write BigQuery SQL for the All of Us CDR v9 (OMOP) to …. Select only the columns needed. Use concept_ancestor for conditions. Don’t use any concept ID I haven’t given you: tell me what to look up.
Every concept ID, table, and column checked in reference/ or Athena; price it with run_if_cheap()


Cut a query’s cost
Which columns and tables does this query read? Can it read less and give the same result?
Compare the estimated cost before and after with run_if_cheap()


Make a summary safe
Change this so it shows only summaries: no rows, no maxima or minima, counts of 1 to 20 hidden, and no hidden count that can be worked out from the others.
Test with made-up data that has small groups


Add a check
Add checks after each step: row counts after every join and filter, and the categories after every recode.
Do the checks stop when something’s wrong, or just print?


Review
Review this code as a strict reviewer. List problems with correctness, cost, and privacy (All of Us rules: no rows, no counts of 1 to 20, no single-person values). Don’t rewrite it yet.
Fix the problems one at a time, and test each


Learn
Don’t write the code. Give me hints, one at a time, so I can write it myself.
Good for learning: you’ll remember what you wrote



When the AI isn’t sure, it should say so. If an answer names a concept ID, table, or column you didn’t give it, assume it’s a guess until you’ve checked it.

section: Try It: Practice with Synthetic Data
text:
Try It: Practice with Synthetic Data
Google hosts a free, synthetic (fake) OMOP dataset: CMS SynPUF. It has the same table layout as the All of Us CDR, with no real participants.
Add it as a BigQuery dataset reference:

Project ID: bigquery-public-data
Dataset ID: cms_synthetic_patient_data_omop

Then query it from an app:
library(bigrquery)
query <- "SELECT gender_concept_id, COUNT(*) AS n
          FROM `bigquery-public-data.cms_synthetic_patient_data_omop.person`
          GROUP BY gender_concept_id"
df <- bq_table_download(bq_project_query(Sys.getenv("GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT"), query))
👉 Use a separate practice workspace with no All of Us data. Controlled Tier perimeters may block outside data.






TipInstructor tip





Source: Verily, “Work with OMOP data in BigQuery” (their example uses Python). Example notebooks: github.com/verily-src/workbench-examples. Because it’s synthetic, students can share results and screenshots freely, unlike All of Us data. Queries are billed to your pod (BigQuery charges by data scanned; small queries like this cost very little). GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT and GOOGLE_PROJECT are both set in Workbench apps, with the same value.

title: Optional Extras
section: Add a File from a URL
text:
Add a File from a URL
Copy a public file from the web straight into your bucket. No download or upload needed.

















Resources tab → select your bucket → Add file via URL
URL: a public or signed link to the file
File name: what to call it in the bucket (the default is import- + date and time)
Click Add file to bucket and wait for it to finish


Files up to 100 MB

⚠️ In a Controlled Tier workspace this may fail (“Couldn’t add that file”): the perimeter blocks many outside downloads. Instead, upload the file in JupyterLab, or keep it in a GitHub repo and clone it.








TipInstructor tip





Source: Verily, “Add files to Cloud Storage via URL”, and the dialog in an All of Us Controlled Tier workspace (the option is available there). The transfer runs while you wait, so keep the page open. Tested October 2026 in the intro-to-AoU Controlled Tier workspace: a public GitHub raw URL (reachable from outside, HTTP 200) failed with “Couldn’t add that file. Try again later, or contact support for help.” Most likely the perimeter blocks the transfer. It should work in workspaces without a perimeter (e.g., a practice workspace with no All of Us data). GitHub over git/SSH does work inside the perimeter.

title: Optional Extras
text:
Connect GitHub
Why: back up your code, track changes, and share it with collaborators
Add your Workbench SSH key to GitHub (once):

Profile icon (top right) → Manage your profile → Groups & keys tab
Copy your public SSH key. Workbench creates one for you.
In GitHub: Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key. Paste it and give it a clear name, e.g., Workbench SSH key.
If your GitHub organization uses single sign-on (SSO), authorize the key for it







TipInstructor tip





Source: Verily, “Git integrations with cloud apps”. CLI alternatives: wb security ssh-key get (show the key) and wb security ssh-key generate (make a new one). The key is needed to push to any repo and to clone private ones; cloning a public repo over https works without it. GitHub is reachable from inside an All of Us (Controlled Tier) workspace: tested with ssh -T git@github.com, clone, and push. Source for the testing: the CWML guide “Sharing Your All of Us Workbench Code on GitHub”.



Full step-by-step instructions, including troubleshooting: GitHub Guide

title: Optional Extras
text:
Add a Repository
Apps tab → Git repositories → + Add repository

Public repo: use the https://github.com/… URL (no key needed)
Private repo: use the git@github.com:… URL (needs your SSH key)
It’s cloned automatically into apps you create afterward. For an app you already have, run this in its terminal:

wb git clone --resource=<repo resource name>
Then work as usual: git add → git commit → git push
⚠️ Commit code only. Clear notebook outputs first, e.g., jupyter nbconvert --clear-output --inplace *.ipynb. Never commit data files or results.






TipInstructor tip





This repository (CWML All-of-Us-Training-Resources) is a public example students could add. Outputs can contain participant-level data or small counts, which must not leave the Workbench.

title: Optional Extras
text:
GitHub: Things to Know

Test the connection: ssh -T git@github.com. “Hi username! You’ve successfully authenticated…” means it works.
Set your name and email once per app: git config --global user.name / user.email. For a public repo, use your GitHub noreply email.
Clone into your home folder (~), not ~/workspace/…. That’s a mounted bucket, and Git doesn’t work well there.
The clone lives on the app’s disk. Push before you delete the app.

⚠️ Before every push: clear outputs, leave out data files (.csv, .vcf…), check for passwords or tokens, and read git status. Pushed data by mistake? Deleting it in a new commit doesn’t remove it from Git history. Make the repo private and contact All of Us support.






TipInstructor tip





From the CWML guide “Sharing Your All of Us Workbench Code on GitHub”. It covers adding work to an existing repo (branch and pull request), creating a new repo, keeping in sync, and troubleshooting. Two copies of a notebook drift apart: work from the repo copy, not the copy in ~/workspace.

title: Optional Extras
section: AI Tools: Use Them Outside the Workbench
text:
AI Tools: Use Them Outside the Workbench
Interested in using an AI tool (e.g., Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini) for help with your code? Use it outside the Workbench, for coding help only.
Why not inside the Workbench?

All of Us does not allow participant-level data to leave the Workbench, and that includes sending it to an AI service
AI coding assistants like Claude Code can open files and run code on their own. It’s easy for them to read data files, query results, or notebook outputs that contain participant-level data.
Even one accidental read counts as a Data User Code of Conduct violation, even if nothing is stored

👉 How: get your code from GitHub (outputs cleared, no data), ask the AI on your own computer, then bring the fixed code back into your workspace
📘 Step by step: the class Coding with AI and GitHub






TipInstructor tip





Source: All of Us User Support Hub, “Frequently Asked Questions” (support.researchallofus.org/hc/en-us/articles/52861503885460): AI/ML tools used on participant data must run only within the Researcher Workbench, with no outgoing API; “transit of individual-level data to any external system is considered a DUCC violation, even if the data is not stored or used.” Summary statistics that follow the dissemination policy (no counts under 20) may be shared. Claude Code and Gemini CLI can be installed in Workbench apps, but both send what they read to outside services (Anthropic, Google), so this training recommends not using them there.

title: Optional Extras
section: What You Can Share with an AI
text:
What You Can Share with an AI
✅ Safe to share (no participant data):

Your code, with outputs cleared
Public example code: All of Us tutorial workspace notebooks and other notebooks published by All of Us, with outputs cleared (some are saved with outputs)
Table and column names: the CDR v9 Data Dictionary or the OMOP Common Data Model documentation
Concept IDs and names from Athena or the public All of Us Data Browser, e.g. 201820 = Diabetes mellitus
Error messages, after checking they don’t include data values (an ID, a date, a result)
A small fake dataset with the same columns, to test your code. Ask the AI to make one, or use the synthetic data from Try It: Practice with Synthetic Data.

❌ Never share: query results, data files, notebook outputs, screenshots of data, participant IDs, or counts of 1 to 20.
Example prompts:

“Using these OMOP tables from the data dictionary, write a BigQuery query that finds everyone with concept 201820 or any of its descendants.”
“Here’s the All of Us tutorial notebook for loading RNA-seq data. Rewrite it in R.”
“Here’s my R code and the error message. What’s wrong?”
“Make a fake data frame with columns person_id, age, and diabetes so I can test this code.”







TipInstructor tip





Source: All of Us User Support Hub, “Data Dictionaries” (https://support.researchallofus.org/hc/en-us/articles/360033200232-Data-Dictionaries), which links the data dictionary for each CDR version. Everything in the safe list contains no participant data. Error messages are the one to check: some quote a value from the data.
