title: Running Workflows: dsub, Cromwell, and Nextflow
text:
Overview
In 4.2 we ran a GWAS on one region of one chromosome, inside our app. A whole-genome analysis is 22 or more such jobs, each with large files. Run one after another in the app, that takes hours, and the app must stay open the whole time.
Workflow tools send each job to its own cloud machine, run them at the same time, save the results in your bucket, and shut the machines down. In this class we use dsub, the simplest of the three workflow tools in the Workbench, to run the 4.2 GWAS on all 22 chromosomes in parallel.

Why this class matters
Most genomic analyses, and many others (imaging, long text, wearable data at minute level), are the same step on many files. Workflow tools make that fast, cheaper (each step gets the machine it needs, only while it runs), and reproducible. In All of Us, they also need a few settings that aren’t in the general instructions: this class collects them in one place, tested.


By the end you’ll be able to

Say when to use a workflow tool instead of running code in your app
Describe the parts of a dsub job: image, inputs, outputs, script, and logging
Test a script locally first, then run it as one job, then as many (--tasks)
Monitor jobs with dstat, cancel them with ddel, and read their logs to fix errors
Compare dsub, Cromwell (WDL), and Nextflow, and know where to start with each



Analysis at a glance



❓ Question
How do you run one analysis on every chromosome? (The example: which variants in the All of Us ClinVar files are linked to type 2 diabetes?)


🧪 The analysis
The 4.2 GWAS (QC filters, then plink2 --glm, adjusted for age, sex, and 10 PCs), on each chromosome in its own dsub task


🎯 Why
22 tasks run in about the time of one; the app doesn’t have to do the work, or even stay on


✅ What we conclude
That the workflow gives the same results as the app, for all 22 chromosomes


⚠️ What it can’t tell us
Much about diabetes: the ClinVar files hold variants already studied for disease, and few are common. For a real GWAS, use the ACAF files


🔗 Connections
The sample, phenotype, and covariates from 4.1 and 4.2; the callsets from Where the omics data lives; the Workflows tab





Time and cost



⏱️ Class time
110 minutes


⏱️ Run time
about 30 minutes, mostly waiting for jobs (most tasks take 3 to 8 minutes; one can wait longer for its machine)


💰 Cost
about $1 per student: under $1 for 23 small job machines (n2-standard-2, about $0.10 an hour each, for a few minutes each), plus the app (about $0.27 an hour)


📋 Before class
read Workflows for Beginners; run 4.1 (and ideally 4.2): the notebook reuses their files, or rebuilds them with the cohort query


🖥️ App
an All of Us Jupyter app (it has dsub, gcloud, and PLINK)

title: Running Workflows: dsub, Cromwell, and Nextflow
text:
Key concepts

Two ways to run the same analysis









In your app (4.2)
With a workflow tool




Where it runs
on the app’s machine
on new cloud machines, one per task


How many at once
one after another
many at once (in parallel)


Machine size
the app’s size
chosen per task: big tasks get big machines


While it runs
the app must stay on; the notebook is busy
the app can do other things, or even be stopped


Best for
exploring, small data, plots
the same steps on many files: chromosomes, samples, batches



👉 Rule of thumb: develop and test in your app; once a step works and has to run many times or on big files, move it to a workflow. Most class projects don’t need workflows.


Is a workflow cheaper?
Often faster; cheaper only sometimes: the total computing is about the same, but you pay for each machine only while it works, at the size it needs. In our tests, the 22 tasks added up to about 2 hours of machine time (on SSD disks) but ran at the same time, and the job cost well under $1: the workflow’s gain is time. When it saves money and when it costs more: Workflows for Beginners.


The words







Word
Means




Job
one dsub command. It can have many tasks: here, one per chromosome


Image (container)
a packaged computer system with your software already installed (here, PLINK 2). Each task runs inside one


Input
a file the task needs. dsub copies it from a bucket onto the task’s machine first (localizing)


Output
a file the task makes. dsub copies it back to your bucket at the end (delocalizing)


Script
the commands each task runs


Logging
where dsub saves each task’s log. Your first stop when something fails


Google Batch
the Google Cloud service that creates, runs, and deletes the machines





How a dsub job runs
your app ── dsub ──► Google Batch ──► machine for chr1  ─┐
                                 ├──► machine for chr2  ─┤  each one: copy inputs in,
                                 ├──► ...                 ├─ run the script in the image,
                                 └──► machine for chr22 ─┘  copy outputs back, shut down
                                                           │
your bucket ◄──────────────── results and logs ───────────┘


What All of Us needs: the settings
All of Us workspaces sit inside a security perimeter, and job machines have no internet access. So every job needs:



Setting
Why




--network global/networks/network and --subnetwork regions/us-central1/subnetworks/subnetwork
the workspace’s private network


--use-private-address
no public internet address


--service-account your account (gcloud config get-value account)
the job runs as you, so it can read All of Us data and write to your bucket


--project and --user-project ${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}
your workspace’s project pays, including for reading the All of Us files


--image from the All of Us mirror of Docker Hub
job machines can’t reach Docker Hub itself, only Google’s registries


DSUB_CLOUD_SDK_IMAGE, pinned
dsub’s helper image (it copies the files). Its default is a moving tag; see below


--disk-type pd-ssd (recommended, not required)
dsub’s default standard disk is slow to copy big files onto: see What we learned









WarningPin your versions: the November 2026 break



dsub uses a small helper image, Google’s Cloud SDK, to copy files in and out. By default it uses whatever the latest version is. On 3 November 2026, version 592 of that image came out, and every dsub job started to fail with exit status 127 before running anything. The fix is to pin the version before it:
export DSUB_CLOUD_SDK_IMAGE=gcr.io/google.com/cloudsdktool/google-cloud-cli:591.0.0-slim
The same goes for your own images: use a version tag (plink2:alpha2.3_jan2020), not latest, so the software can’t change under you.


In a terminal, the full set of settings looks like this. It’s the command we used to test dsub in an All of Us workspace (November 2026, dsub 0.5.6), with one change: we’ve pinned the image’s version.
export DSUB_CLOUD_SDK_IMAGE=gcr.io/google.com/cloudsdktool/google-cloud-cli:591.0.0-slim
export ARTIFACT_REGISTRY_DOCKER_REPO=us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/all-of-us-rw-prod/aou-rw-gar-remote-repo-docker-prod
BUCKET=gs://your-bucket-name                                # from the Resources tab

dsub --provider google-batch \
  --project "${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}" --user-project "${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}" \
  --regions us-central1 \
  --network "global/networks/network" \
  --subnetwork "regions/us-central1/subnetworks/subnetwork" \
  --use-private-address \
  --service-account "$(gcloud config get-value account)" \
  --logging "${BUCKET}/dsub_test/logs" \
  --image "${ARTIFACT_REGISTRY_DOCKER_REPO}/ubuntu:24.04" \
  --output OUT="${BUCKET}/dsub_test/hello.txt" \
  --command 'echo "hello from dsub" > "${OUT}"' \
  --wait

gcloud storage cat "${BUCKET}/dsub_test/hello.txt"           # prints: hello from dsub
The notebook wraps these settings in an R function, aou_dsub(), so each job only lists what’s different.

Follow along in the Workbench

Open an All of Us Jupyter app, with this repository cloned (see the GitHub guide).
Open notebooks/workflows/workflows_dsub.ipynb, with the R kernel. gwas_one_chr.sh must be in the same folder.
Run the cells in order. Parts 4 and 5 start cloud jobs: read on while they run.

title: Running Workflows: dsub, Cromwell, and Nextflow
text:
Code walk-through

One script, two places
The GWAS lives in a shell script, gwas_one_chr.sh. It reads every file name from an environment variable, so the same script runs in the app (Part 3) and in each job (Parts 4 and 5): only the variables change.
set -euo pipefail
mkdir -p "${OUT_DIR}"

plink2 \
  --bfile "${BED%.bed}" \
  --keep "${KEEP}" \
  --maf 0.01 --geno 0.1 --hwe 1e-10 \
  --pheno "${PHENO}" --pheno-name t2d \
  --covar "${COVAR}" --covar-variance-standardize \
  --glm hide-covar firth-fallback \
  --out "${OUT_DIR}/chr${CHR}"







Line
Does




set -euo pipefail
stop at the first error. Without it, a failed step could still look like a successful job


--bfile "${BED%.bed}"
the PLINK files, given as the .bed file’s path; ${BED%.bed} drops the .bed


--keep … --glm
our sample, the QC filters, and the association test from 4.2


--out "${OUT_DIR}/chr${CHR}"
results named after the chromosome, e.g. chr21.t2d.glm.logistic.hybrid



Test it in the app first (Part 3), on chromosome 21, reading the mounted files. A mistake shows up in a minute, for free.


One job
job_chr21 <- aou_dsub(
  "--name", "gwas-chr21",
1  "--image", PLINK_IMAGE,
  "--machine-type", "n2-standard-2",
2  "--disk-size", DISK_GB, "--disk-type", "pd-ssd",
  "--script", "gwas_one_chr.sh",
  "--env", "CHR=21",
3  "--input", paste0("BED=", CLINVAR_GS, "/clinvar.chr21.bed"),
  "--input", paste0("BIM=", CLINVAR_GS, "/clinvar.chr21.bim"),
  "--input", paste0("FAM=", CLINVAR_GS, "/clinvar.chr21.fam"),
  "--input", paste0("KEEP=", KEEP_GS),
  "--input", paste0("PHENO=", PHENO_GS),
  "--input", paste0("COVAR=", COVAR_GS),
4  "--output-recursive", paste0("OUT_DIR=", WORK_GS, "/test_chr21"),
  wait = TRUE
)

1

PLINK 2 from the All of Us mirror, a pinned version.

2

Big enough for the inputs and outputs (set from the biggest ClinVar file), and fast: an SSD.

3

Every file the task needs must be an input, including the .bim and .fam files the script never names: the machine has nothing else.

4

A folder to copy back: everything the script writes in OUT_DIR.


The notebook then copies the job’s results back and compares them with the app’s: they should match.


Many jobs: the tasks file
To run many tasks, give dsub a tasks file: a tab-separated table with one row per task and one column per setting. The heading says what each column is.










--env CHR
--input BED
--input BIM
--input FAM
--output-recursive OUT_DIR




1
gs://…/clinvar.chr1.bed
gs://…/clinvar.chr1.bim
gs://…/clinvar.chr1.fam
gs://…/gwas_clinvar/chr1


2
gs://…/clinvar.chr2.bed
gs://…/clinvar.chr2.bim
gs://…/clinvar.chr2.fam
gs://…/gwas_clinvar/chr2


…






22
gs://…/clinvar.chr22.bed
…
…
gs://…/gwas_clinvar/chr22



Settings that are the same for every task (the image, the script, the three small GWAS files) stay in the command, with "--tasks", tasks_file added. dsub starts all 22 tasks at once. The notebook doesn’t wait: it checks on them with dstat.
dstat(job_all, "--summary")           # how many tasks are RUNNING, SUCCESS, FAILURE
dstat(job_all, "--wait", show = FALSE) # wait until every task has finished
dsub jobs don’t appear on the Workbench’s Workflows tab: that tab shows Cromwell and Nextflow workflows. Check dsub jobs with dstat.


Combine
Each task wrote its results to its own folder. The notebook copies them to the app with gcloud storage cp, stacks them with map(...) %>% bind_rows(), and draws a Manhattan plot. These are summary statistics (one row per variant), so they’re safe to look at. To publish them, follow the All of Us dissemination rules, as for any result.

title: Running Workflows: dsub, Cromwell, and Nextflow
text:
What we learned
We ran every step of this class in an All of Us workspace before teaching it (November 2026). Five lessons:







What happened
Lesson




With dsub’s default disk (a standard disk), chromosome 1 took 101 minutes: 59 to copy its 27.7 GB .bed file onto the machine (about 8 MB a second), and 37 for PLINK. With an SSD disk (--disk-type pd-ssd), the same task took 8 minutes: under 4 to copy (about 130 MB a second), about 2 for PLINK
Most of a task’s time can be copying files, not analysis. Standard disks are cheap but slow, and slowest when small. For big inputs, use --disk-type pd-ssd: for a few minutes it costs about a cent more, and it saves machine time


On chromosome 21 (a small file), PLINK itself took about 2 seconds; the whole task, a few minutes
starting a machine and copying files take minutes, whatever the job. That’s why tiny jobs don’t belong in a workflow


All 22 tasks on standard disks: about 580 minutes (9½ hours) of machine time, added up; the whole job took 101 minutes. On SSD disks: about 130 minutes (2 hours) added up; 21 of the 22 tasks took 3 to 8 minutes each
in parallel, a job takes as long as its slowest task. The SSD disks cut the machine time, and so the cost, by more than two thirds


On SSD disks, the whole job still took 32 minutes, because one task (chromosome 4) waited 30 minutes for its machine. Its log started 30 minutes late; once it started, it took 2½ minutes
sometimes a task waits for a free machine, and you can’t prevent it. dstat’s start-time doesn’t show the wait (it equals create-time): the first time stamp in the task’s log does


A long task’s log repeated You do not currently have an active account selected … Sleeping 10s
harmless: dsub’s log uploader, while the task runs. The job still succeeded and saved its log



👉 Find where the time goes: each log line has a time stamp. The gap between Localizing BED and the next line is the copy; the gap after PLINK v2 is the analysis.

text:
✋ Try It Out 1 · 5 minutes · while the 22 tasks run
Run only chromosomes 19 to 22, in a new job. (Hint: the tasks file has a header row, so chromosome 1 is task 1.)






NoteAnswer





Add the task numbers after the tasks file: "--tasks", tasks_file, "19-22". Rows 19 to 22 are chromosomes 19 to 22, because the table is sorted by chromosome. This is also how you rerun only the tasks that failed.

title: Running Workflows: dsub, Cromwell, and Nextflow
text:
✋ Try It Out 2 · 5 minutes · Part 7
A classmate’s job fails. The log says plink2: Error: Failed to open …/clinvar.chr7.bim. What’s wrong? And how would you make the job cheaper?






NoteAnswer





The .bim file wasn’t an input: the machine only has the files you give it with --input. PLINK needs the .bed, .bim, and .fam files together.
Cheaper: spot machines, "--preemptible", "--retries", "2". They cost much less, but Google can stop them at any time; --retries starts a stopped task again. They suit short tasks like these.
crumbs: Running Workflows: dsub, Cromwell, and Nextflow

title: Running Workflows: dsub, Cromwell, and Nextflow
text:
When a job fails
Read the log first. dsub saves three per task in the --logging folder: ….log (everything), …-stdout.log (what the script printed), and …-stderr.log (its errors).








Symptom (in dstat or the log)
Likely cause
Fix




FAILURE with exit status 127, before your script runs
dsub’s helper image broke or can’t be reached
pin DSUB_CLOUD_SDK_IMAGE to a version that works


An error about the image, or a job that never starts
the image isn’t from a Google registry
put the All of Us mirror in front of Docker Hub images


No such file or directory
a file the script uses wasn’t an input
add it with --input


No space left on device
the disk is too small
a bigger --disk-size


A task takes far longer than the others; in its log, a long gap after Localizing BED
copying a big file onto a slow standard disk (dsub’s default)
--disk-type pd-ssd


You do not currently have an active account selected … Sleeping 10s, over and over
dsub’s log uploader, while a long task runs
nothing: the task continues


One task finishes long after the others; its log starts late
it waited for a machine (none free, or the project’s limit)
nothing: it runs once a machine is free


A task is killed, or PLINK runs out of memory
the machine is too small
a bigger --machine-type (e.g. n2-highmem-4)


401 … Requester pays bucket access requires authentication, then a retry
a short delay while the machine signs in
nothing: dsub retries, and the job continues


Error: No variants remaining
the filters removed every variant on that chromosome
check the filters, or leave that chromosome out


Tasks wait in the queue for a long time
the project’s limit on machines or CPUs
wait, or run fewer tasks at a time



Cancel a job (all its tasks): ddel --provider google-batch --project "${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}" --location us-central1 --jobs JOB_ID

section: Scaling up: from ClinVar to ACAF
text:
Scaling up: from ClinVar to ACAF
For a real GWAS, use the ACAF files (every variant common in at least one ancestry group). The steps are the same; the files are much bigger. In the All of Us tutorial, one ACAF chromosome (21) took about 60 minutes to copy onto the machine and about 28 minutes for PLINK, on a machine with 32 CPUs (n2-highmem-32) and a 400 GB disk. With files this big, an SSD disk matters even more (we haven’t timed ACAF ourselves).









ClinVar (this class)
ACAF




Variants
those listed in ClinVar
all variants common in at least one ancestry group


File sizes (.bed)
4 to 28 GB per chromosome, 293 GB in all (v9)
many times bigger


Machine
n2-standard-2
n2-highmem-16 to -32


Disk
under 100 GB, SSD
400 GB or more, SSD


Time per task
a few minutes
1 to 2+ hours


Cost
under $1 in all
tens of dollars or more: test on one chromosome first



Ways to save: spot machines (--preemptible, with --retries); smaller tasks (split each chromosome into regions with PLINK’s --from-bp and --to-bp); and reading only what you need.
Clean up when you’re done: job results stay in your bucket, and bucket storage is billed every month (gcloud storage rm --recursive gs://…/data/workflows/test_chr21).

title: Running Workflows: dsub, Cromwell, and Nextflow
text:
Cromwell and Nextflow
dsub is the simplest tool: one script, a table of tasks. It’s great for one step on many files. When an analysis has many steps (e.g. QC → GWAS → plots), each using the outputs of the one before, a workflow language is easier: you describe the steps and how they connect, and the tool runs them in order, in parallel where it can, and can resume after a failure.




dsub
Cromwell
Nextflow




You write
a shell script and a dsub command
a WDL file (Workflow Description Language) and a JSON file of inputs
a Nextflow (.nf) file


Best for
one step on many files
multi-step pipelines; many published genomics workflows (e.g. GATK)
multi-step pipelines; the nf-core community pipelines


Run from
an app’s terminal or notebook
the Workflows tab, or java -jar $CROMWELL_JAR run … in an app
nextflow run … in an app (in All of Us, the Workflows tab doesn’t offer Nextflow: tested November 2026)


Ready-made workflows

Dockstore
nf-core, Dockstore


Learning curve
low
medium
medium



All three run their tasks on Google Batch, so the same All of Us rules apply: the private network, no public addresses, images from Google registries (or the All of Us mirror), and pinned versions. Each tool takes them in a short configuration file.

Which one should I use?
All three gave the same answer in our tests, in about the same time. What differs is how much you write, where you run it, and what’s already written for you.




What it does best
The catch (in All of Us)




dsub
The simplest: your shell script, plus a table with one row per file. The fastest way to run one step on many files. You can check each job with dstat and read its log
One step per job: for a pipeline, you run and check each step yourself. No resume. Jobs don’t show on the Workflows tab. You need an app to start them


Cromwell (WDL)
The Workflows tab: no configuration file, no app, inputs in a form, a page to watch the job, and batch jobs from a table. Call caching skips steps that already finished. Many published genomics pipelines are written in WDL (GATK, the Broad Institute, Dockstore)
WDL is wordy: inputs, outputs, and runtime for every task. In an app (run mode) you need your own cromwell.conf, with the pinned helper image, and the app must stay on


Nextflow
Short pipeline files, and many tasks at once with very little code (Channel.of(19..22)). -resume restarts where a pipeline stopped. It streams bucket files instead of copying them, which helps when a tool reads only part of a file. The large nf-core community of pipelines
Runs only from an app (the Workflows tab doesn’t offer it in All of Us), so the app must stay on. Every image must include ps. Google’s job logs are blocked, so you read errors from the task’s work folder. The Seqera web interface doesn’t work. Ready-made nf-core pipelines download code and images from the internet: inside the perimeter, they need extra setup (we haven’t tried one)



👉 A simple rule:

One step, many files (one command per chromosome or sample): dsub.
A published WDL pipeline, or you’d rather click than configure: Cromwell on the Workflows tab.
Your own multi-step pipeline, or your lab already uses Nextflow: Nextflow, from an app.
Not sure? Start with dsub. It teaches every idea, and the script you write moves into a WDL command or a Nextflow script almost unchanged.

Your collaborators matter too: a pipeline in the language your lab or field already uses is easier to share and get help with.


A task in each language
The same idea in each tool: PLINK on one chromosome, here allele frequencies of the common variants (--maf 0.01 --freq). They’re based on the All of Us tutorial notebooks (folder How to Use Workflow Tools in the tutorial workspace), and we ran both in November 2026: both gave exactly the same frequencies as PLINK in the app (see Tested: Cromwell and Nextflow).

WDL (Cromwell)Nextflow


version 1.0

workflow plink_freq {
  input {
    File bed
    File bim
    File fam
    String docker_image
  }
  call plink_check { input: bed = bed, bim = bim, fam = fam, docker_image = docker_image }
  output {
    File freq = plink_check.freq
  }
}

task plink_check {
  input {
    File bed
    File bim
    File fam
    String docker_image
  }
  command {
    plink2 --bed ~{bed} --bim ~{bim} --fam ~{fam} --maf 0.01 --freq --out chr
  }
  output {
    File freq = "chr.afreq"
  }
  runtime {
    docker: docker_image
    machineType: "n2-standard-2"
    disks: "local-disk 30 SSD"   # Cromwell copies the inputs here: SSD, as for dsub
  }
}
The inputs go in a JSON file (in an app) or a form (on the Workflows tab): the three gs:// paths, and the image from the All of Us mirror.


params.plinkDir = "gs://vwb-aou-datasets-controlled/v9/wgs/short_read/snpindel/clinvar/plink_bed"
params.mirror   = "us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/all-of-us-rw-prod/aou-rw-gar-remote-repo-docker-prod"

process plink_check {
  container "${params.mirror}/biocontainer/plink2:alpha2.3_jan2020"
  cpus 2
  memory "8 GB"

  input:
  tuple val(chr), path(bed), path(bim), path(fam)

  output:
  path "chr${chr}.afreq"

  script:
  """
  plink2 --bed ${bed} --bim ${bim} --fam ${fam} --maf 0.01 --freq --out chr${chr}
  """
}

workflow {
  Channel.of(19..22)
    .map { c -> tuple(c, file("${params.plinkDir}/clinvar.chr${c}.bed"),
                         file("${params.plinkDir}/clinvar.chr${c}.bim"),
                         file("${params.plinkDir}/clinvar.chr${c}.fam")) }
    | plink_check
}
Nextflow runs one task per chromosome on its own, in parallel. Unlike dsub and Cromwell, it doesn’t copy gs:// inputs onto the machine first: it mounts the bucket and reads the files as it goes.





The All of Us settings for each








Setting
Cromwell (cromwell.conf, backend GCPBATCH)
Nextflow (nextflow.config, executor google-batch)




Project
project = "${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}"
google.project


Where work files go
root = "gs://your-bucket/workflows/cromwell-executions"
workDir = "gs://your-bucket/workflows/nextflow-scratch"


Network
virtual-private-cloud { network-name …, subnetwork-name … }
google.batch.network, google.batch.subnetwork


No public address
default-runtime-attributes { noAddress: true }
google.batch.usePrivateAddress = true


Service account
batch { compute-service-account = … }
google.batch.serviceAccountEmail


Region
batch { location = "us-central1" }
google.location = "us-central1"


Paying for All of Us files
filesystems { gcs { project = … } }
google.enableRequesterPaysBuckets = true


Helper image (copies files), pinned
google.cloud-sdk-image-url = "gcr.io/google.com/cloudsdktool/google-cloud-cli:591.0.0-slim"
google.batch.copyImage = "gcr.io/google.com/cloudsdktool/google-cloud-cli:591.0.0-alpine"


Default image for tasks

process.container: an image from the mirror that has ps (we used the PLINK image)



The All of Us tutorial notebooks have complete configuration files; our test notebook has the versions that worked, with the changes marked. Check three things in any configuration: that every image comes from a Google registry or the All of Us mirror (not straight from Docker Hub), that helper images use a pinned version, and that Nextflow’s images include ps. The tutorials read the service account from PET_SA_EMAIL; it was empty in our app, so we used gcloud config get-value account, as for dsub.


Three ways to run a workflow










Cromwell in an app (run mode)
Cromwell on the Workflows tab (server mode)
Nextflow in an app




Start it with
java -jar $CROMWELL_JAR run plink_freq.wdl -i inputs.json
the Workflows tab: add the workflow, then + New job
nextflow run plink_freq.nf -c nextflow.config


Inputs
a JSON file
a form, built from the WDL (or an input table, for a batch)
in the .nf file, or --param value


Settings
your cromwell.conf
set by the Workbench: nothing to write
your nextflow.config


Does the app need to stay on?
yes, until it finishes
no: no app needed
yes, until it finishes


Results
<work folder>/cromwell-executions/<workflow>/<id>/call-<task>/
<output bucket>/<job name>/<workflow>/<id>/call-<task>/: check which output bucket you chose
the work folder, or a publishDir you choose


The workflow file comes from
the app’s disk
your bucket, or a GitHub repository (link your GitHub account first)
the app’s disk



👉 For most students, the Workflows tab is the easiest way to run WDL: no configuration file, no app, and a page to watch the job on. How to use it: the Workflows tab.

On the Workflows tab: a single job or a batch job?
When you start a New job, the tab asks “Run this workflow multiple times?”









Single job
Batch job




Runs the workflow
once
once per row of a table, all at the same time


Inputs
a form: you type each value
a CSV table in your bucket, one row per run, one column per input. You type which column goes with which input (in All of Us, the tab can’t preview the table)


Also needs

a reference column that labels each run (e.g. chr or a sample ID)


On Job status
one row
one row for the batch, with Number of jobs (e.g. 4)


Results
<job name>/<workflow>/<id>/call-<task>/
the same, with one <id> folder per row


Use it for
testing, or one file
the same step on many files: chromosomes, samples. The tab’s version of dsub’s --tasks


Our test
chromosome 21: about 4 minutes
chromosomes 19 to 22: about 11 minutes for all 4, and chromosome 21 matched the single job exactly



👉 Test with a single job first, then run the batch: a mistake in the WDL then costs one run, not one per row.



Tested: Cromwell and Nextflow
We ran each tool in an All of Us workspace in November 2026 (Jupyter app with OpenJDK 17, Cromwell 92, Nextflow 25.10.2; CDR v9), with the files from our test notebook. The check: allele frequencies on chromosome 21 (28,502 common variants), compared with PLINK in the app (0.5 minutes).

✅ worked

✅ worked

Each single run took 3 to 4 minutes, mostly starting machines: PLINK itself took 20 seconds to 2 minutes per chromosome. As for dsub, tiny jobs don’t belong in a workflow.

What we learned testing Cromwell and Nextflow







What happened
Lesson




Every Cromwell task in an app failed within 3 minutes: “The job was stopped before the command finished”. The task folder had only Cromwell’s scripts (no rc, stdout, or stderr)
the same break as dsub: Cromwell copies files with Google’s Cloud SDK image, and version 592 broke it. Pin version 591 in cromwell.conf (google.cloud-sdk-image-url). The All of Us tutorial’s configuration doesn’t have this line


The Workflows tab ran the same WDL with no fix
the tab runs its own Cromwell, set up by the Workbench, so it wasn’t affected


The Nextflow hello task failed: “Command ‘ps’ required by nextflow to collect task metrics cannot be found”
Nextflow runs ps inside your container to measure each task. The tutorial’s default image (ubuntu-slim) doesn’t have it, and nor does the official ubuntu image. Use an image that does (our PLINK image did), or install the procps package in your own


Nextflow said “Permission denied for all log views”
All of Us blocks Google’s job logs. Read the failed task’s own files instead: .command.err and .command.log, in its work folder (…/nextflow-scratch/xx/…)


Cromwell printed MANIFEST_UNKNOWN … falling back to OCI manifest
harmless: Cromwell couldn’t fingerprint the image (used only to reuse earlier results)


The image straight from Docker Hub failed
as for dsub: use the All of Us mirror for every image, in every tool


The Workflows tab’s bucket list opened on dataproc-staging-…, with “0 workflows found”
choose your workspace bucket in the list; the tab then finds .wdl files in all its folders


One job’s results went to the dataproc-staging-… bucket: the output step had picked it
check the output bucket on the last step of every new job


The page showed that bucket as dataproc-staging-aou-rw-…, but its gs:// address was dataproc-staging-wb-…
a bucket’s name on the page isn’t always its address: the Cloud ID (Resources tab, or the job’s outputs) is


For a batch job, the tab said the perimeter “prevents reading the input table”
type each input’s column name exactly as in the CSV header, and name a reference column (e.g. chr) that labels each run


A Git source asked us to “Link your GitHub account”
Workbench account settings → GitHub → install Verily’s GitHub app. Choose only the repositories you need, not all of them. Already chose all? On GitHub: Settings → Applications → Installed GitHub Apps → the Verily app → Configure → Only select repositories. Public repositories, such as this one, are still listed after you narrow it (tested)


The job’s Inputs → View showed -- for every value, though the job used them
a display problem: keep your own record of the inputs (e.g. the CSV, or a JSON file)


The tab didn’t list .nf files: not plink_freq.nf, not main.nf next to a nextflow.config, from the bucket or from GitHub
in All of Us, run Nextflow from an app


Halfway through, the notebook’s R session restarted, and every result in memory was gone
files on disk and in the bucket survive. Rerun the setup cells, not Run All (it would rerun every test). In run mode, a workflow also stops if the app stops: watch the auto-stop setting









TipInstructor tip





Tested November 2026 (All of Us Jupyter app, CDR v9): dsub 0.5.6 (the chromosome 21 job, all 22 tasks, chromosome 1 on standard and SSD disks), Cromwell 92 in run mode and on the Workflows tab, and Nextflow 25.10.2 in an app. Also tested on the Workflows tab: a batch job from an input table (chromosomes 19 to 22), and a WDL from GitHub (branch main). The tab didn’t offer Nextflow. Not tested: the ACAF files, nf-core pipelines, and the tab’s JSON mapper file for batch inputs. With call caching on, an identical rerun should finish in seconds (not yet tried): worth showing in class. The pinned 591 helper images will be deleted by Google about 12 months after release: check around November 2027 and move to a newer version that works. The tutorials note that the Nextflow web interface (Seqera) doesn’t work in All of Us workspaces, because they have no internet access, and that Nextflow 26.04 has a stricter syntax than the app’s 25.10. Job machines and bucket storage are billed to the workspace’s pod and don’t appear in the app cost estimate. For a 2-hour class, demo the Workflows tab live (about 10 minutes, including the 4-minute run) rather than run mode.

title: Running Workflows: dsub, Cromwell, and Nextflow
text:
Instructor tip: timing and pitfalls

Start the 22-task job before the break, or before Part 8: it runs while you teach. Machines take a few minutes to start.
Students in the same workspace share the project’s limits on machines and CPUs. In a large class, have pairs share one run.
The commonest failures are settings, not code: a missing network flag, an image straight from Docker Hub, or a helper image that changed. The settings in aou_dsub() were tested in November 2026; if jobs fail with exit status 127 before the script runs, check the dsub issues on GitHub for a newer working helper version.
The comparison in Part 4 (app vs job) is the key check. A small difference in p-values comes from the PLINK version (the image’s 2020 version vs the app’s newer one): a good moment to talk about pinning and reporting versions.
dsub’s printed messages include the workspace project ID, the bucket address, and your service account: clear outputs before committing, and share the notebook through GitHub, never by downloading it.
Students may look for their jobs on the Workflows tab: dsub jobs aren’t there (it shows Cromwell and Nextflow). Use dstat.

title: Running Workflows: dsub, Cromwell, and Nextflow
text:
Key takeaways

Use a workflow tool when the same step has to run on many or big files: each task gets its own machine, and they run in parallel
A dsub job is an image, a script, inputs (copied onto the machine), outputs (copied back), and a log
Test small first: the script in the app, then one job, then all of them
Every file a task needs must be an input: the machine has nothing else
In All of Us: the private network, no public address, images from the mirror, and pinned versions
dstat to monitor, ddel to cancel, and the log to find out why a task failed, or where its time went
Copying big files can take longer than the analysis: use an SSD disk (--disk-type pd-ssd)
For multi-step pipelines, use a workflow language: WDL with Cromwell, or Nextflow. The Workflows tab runs WDL with no configuration file and no app
Pin helper images in every tool (dsub, Cromwell, Nextflow): one new version broke both dsub and Cromwell in November 2026

title: About All of Us
text:
Vision and Goals

Enable precision medicine using data on lifestyle, environment, and genetics
Shift from one-size-fits-all to personalized healthcare
Boost health research and medical breakthroughs
Make healthcare tailored and equitable
Support diverse studies reflecting all populations

What precision medicine means, and how each course series connects to it: Precision Medicine: where our classes fit.

title: About All of Us
text:
What Makes It Unique

Participant-centered: participants can view and access their own data
Open science: de-identified data available to registered researchers
Research opportunities: health disparities, environmental impacts, disease prevention and treatment
Phenotypic and genotypic data in one place
Scalability and innovation: complex analyses, AI and machine learning

TipInstructor tip





Source: All of Us Researcher Workbench Office Hours, “Release of the Curated Data Repository (CDR) v9 Dataset” (2026-07-24), and the CDR v9 data dictionary. Counts change with every release. EHR data now comes from health care sites, from records participants share themselves, and from a health-information-exchange pilot. To verify on the Support Hub before relying on them: whether physical measurements also include self-reported height and weight, and the exact sample types used for DNA. Medical imaging (X-rays, MRI, CT) is not part of v9: the data dictionary has no imaging tables, and the v9 release talk doesn’t list it among current or upcoming data types. EHR procedure records only show that an imaging exam happened.

title: About All of Us
text:
The Curated Data Repository (CDR)

Data are organized in a curated data repository (CDR), released in numbered versions (current: CDR v9; refreshed every 1–2 years)

Participant identifiers removed; the Controlled Tier keeps more detail (e.g. real dates of health events)
Cleaned, validated, and standardized to the OMOP Common Data Model

Researcher Workbench 2.0 runs on Verily Workbench, on Google Cloud

Tables (EHR, surveys, measurements, Fitbit) are in Google BigQuery: query them with SQL from R or Python, or with the Data Explorer
Genomic and multi-omics data are files in Cloud Storage buckets (e.g. PLINK, VCF, Hail formats)

Costs go to your Google Cloud billing account: BigQuery charges by the data a query scans, apps by the hour while running, and the genomic data bucket is Requester Pays (reading it is billed to you)







TipInstructor tip





CDRv9 is shown on the Workbench 2.0 home page (Controlled Tier tutorial workspace). Verily builds and runs Workbench 2.0; the data and computing are on Google Cloud. Version 9 of the Controlled Tier is the dataset C2025Q4R6.

title: Billing
text:
Initial credits

$300 in initial credits per registered researcher

Applied automatically to compute costs
Expire 365 days after you first get Workbench access
Tied to your personal pod, user-pod-firstname-lastname-####. A workspace’s Workspace details panel (right side, under Pod) shows which pod pays for it.

When credits run out or expire:

You can’t launch or open analysis environments
Stored resources (buckets, disks) may be deleted








Important



Set up a Google Cloud billing account and billing pod before your credits run out or expire. At Yale, ask at least 2 to 3 weeks ahead: see Getting a Google Cloud billing account at Yale.

title: Billing
text:
Billing pods

A pod connects your workspaces to a Google Cloud billing account

Workspace costs are charged to the pod
Think of the pod as your billing account inside the Workbench

One pod can pay for many workspaces
You can invite other users to your pod (e.g., lab members). Their workspaces in your pod are then billed to your account
All of Us researchers have the Pod Manager role, so you can create your own pod







WarningWatch out




A pod links to only one billing account
A workspace’s pod can’t be changed later. To switch pods, you have to duplicate the workspace.









TipInstructor tip





Initial credits are linked to the personal user pod. Check a workspace’s Workspace details panel (Overview tab, right side) to see which pod it uses; a Yale billing pod would show its own name there.

section: Getting a Google Cloud billing account at Yale
text:
Getting a Google Cloud billing account at Yale






ImportantAsk early



Setting up the account takes about 2 weeks: Burwood, Yale’s Google reseller, requests it from Google’s distributor. Ask at least 2 to 3 weeks before your initial credits run out or expire.


Email cloud.support@yale.edu with the subject “setting up an All of Us billing account” and include:

Your All of Us Workbench email (e.g., yourname@researchallofus.org)
Your COA number: the account is charged to it
Whether this is an NIH-funded project, and if so, the NIH grant number. NIH-funded accounts are set up through NIH STRIDES, which needs it

Yale Cloud Support will send the next steps for linking the Google Cloud billing account and creating your pod.

What you get

Your own Google Cloud billing account, charged to the COA you gave
You keep access to it, so you can link it to new pods, or relink pods, yourself, without asking Yale Cloud Support again







WarningChoose who you invite to your pod



Anyone you invite to your pod can run workspaces that are billed to your COA. Invite only people on the same grant.








TipInstructor tip





Email is the way to ask for now. Yale Cloud Support is building a ServiceNow request form for this; link it here when it’s live. Yale Cloud Support may give additional or different guidance.

title: Research Use Statement
text: When you add an All of Us data collection to a workspace (see Setting Up a Workspace), you answer these questions about your research. Our example answers are for an instructional workspace.

title: Research Use Statement
text:
Research Use Statement: Question 1










What is the primary purpose of your project?

Research
Education ← our example (instructional workspace)
For-profit
Other

8 pages of questions in total
Answer for your own project. Answers marked Publicly displayed appear in the Research Hub Directory.








TipInstructor tip





This example workspace is for teaching, so we answer as an education project. Students doing research should choose Research purpose and describe their actual project.

title: Research Use Statement
text:
Research Use Statement: Question 2





Summarize your research purpose in plain language:

2.1 Your scientific question(s), and why they matter
2.2 Your approach: datasets, methods, and tools
2.3 Your anticipated findings

Each answer: 100–1,000 characters
⚠️ Answers under 100 characters give an error. Add enough detail to explain your project.








TipInstructor tip





Example answer for this instructional workspace (used for 2.1–2.3): “This workspace is intended solely for instructional purposes and not for research. I will use this workspace to teach others how to navigate the All of Us Workbench, create workspaces, build cohorts and datasets, and analyze the data provided within the workbench.” Students should describe their real project: hypothesis, methods, and expected findings, with as little jargon as possible.

title: Research Use Statement
text:
Research Use Statement: Question 3










How will you share your findings?

Choose all that apply: journals, conferences, community forums, social media, blogs, press…
Name the venue if you know it (journal, conference, blog, etc.)
Other requires a short explanation

Our example: Other. The workspace is for teaching, so there are no findings to share.








TipInstructor tip





All of Us encourages sharing results with both scientific and community audiences, to recognize participants’ contributions. Example answer: “The purpose of this workspace is to provide instruction, not research. I do not plan on disseminating anything from the work done here.”

title: Research Use Statement
text:
Research Use Statement: Question 4










How does your project fit the All of Us Scientific Framework?
Select all outcomes you expect:

Wellness, resilience, healthy living
Health equity for underrepresented (UBR) populations
Risk assessment and prevention
Earlier, more accurate diagnosis
Better treatment and precision interventions

Our example: None of these apply (teaching workspace)

title: Research Use Statement
text:
Research Use Statement: Question 5










Population of interest: will your study focus on historically underrepresented populations?

Yes: select the groups, e.g., race/ethnicity, age, sex at birth, gender identity, sexual orientation, geography, disability, access to care, education, income
No: a diverse sample in general, or well-represented populations

Our example: No (teaching workspace)








TipInstructor tip





All of Us asks this to track how well it serves underrepresented communities and to guard against stigmatizing findings. Encourage students to think about whether their design, methods, or analyses could harm individuals, groups, or communities. Fields marked * are altered, suppressed, or generalized in the Registered Tier for privacy; see the Data Dictionary.

title: Research Use Statement
text:
Research Use Statement: Question 6










AI/AN Policy Assessment
Will your study produce findings specific to American Indian and Alaska Native (AI/AN) populations?

AI/AN-only study population
AI/AN case or control group
Results broken down so AI/AN-specific findings may appear
No AI/AN-specific analyses

Then explain your answer (required)
Our example: no AI/AN-specific analyses. If that changes, you must update your answers.








TipInstructor tip





All of Us has a policy on respectful research with AI/AN populations; this question checks whether it applies to your project. Students whose work could produce AI/AN-specific findings should read the policy before starting.

title: Research Use Statement
text:
Research Use Statement: Question 7













Request a review of your research purpose?

Research using demographic variables can unintentionally produce findings that stigmatize participants or communities
You can ask the Resource Access Board (RAB) to review your purpose

Reply within 5 business days; keep working meanwhile

This answer is private (not on the Research Hub)

Our example: No concerns. The RAB is available any time via the User Support Hub.








TipInstructor tip





See the All of Us Stigmatizing Research Policy for more detail. If students are unsure, encourage them to request the review; it’s a precaution, not a penalty.

title: Research Use Statement
text:
Research Use Statement: Page 8













Review and confirm
These answers are publicly displayed to inform All of Us participants:

Q1 Primary purpose of your project
Q2 Summary of research purpose
Q5 Population of interest
Q6 Approach to handling AI/AN data

Check that they’re detailed and in plain language, then click Confirm
You can go Back to change answers now, or edit them later after the workspace is created








TipInstructor tip





Q3 (dissemination), Q4 (scientific framework), and Q7 (RAB review) are not displayed publicly.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text: This page uses our example workspace, intro-to-AoU, created for instruction only.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Creating a Workspace
Left sidebar → Workspaces → + New workspace












TipInstructor tip





Three steps: Enter details → Set policies → Add description.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Step 1: Enter Details





You fill in:

Workspace name: only visible to people with access; you can change it later
Summary: a short description (up to 140 characters)

Filled in automatically:

Workspace ID: made from the name; used by the CLI. Changing it later breaks links to the workspace.
Pod: your default billing pod

Click Next
⚠️ The pod can’t be changed after the workspace is created








TipInstructor tip





The auto-selected pod is your personal user pod (user-pod-firstname-lastname-####). If you’ve set up a Yale billing pod, choose it here from the drop-down.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Step 2: Set Policies





Sharing (group policy):

No, don’t apply policy: the default; fine for most projects
Limit discoverability: only members of the selected groups can see the workspace

Region:

Where your apps and resources are kept. Pick the one closest to you (Yale: us-east4).
Can be changed later; only new resources use it

Click Next
⚠️ Group policies can’t be removed once applied








TipInstructor tip





Group policies also carry over to duplicates of the workspace. Access still has to be granted separately; a group policy only limits who can be given access. Region also affects cost: Verily notes prices can vary by about 25% between regions. Yale is on the East Coast, so us-east4 (Virginia) is the closest region.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Step 3: Add Description





Description:

What the workspace is for: its purpose, data, and tools
Helps you and your collaborators
You can edit it any time

Click Create workspace
⚠️ The description is publicly accessible. Anyone can see it, so don’t put sensitive details in it.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Your New Workspace
Go to the Resources tab → + Data from catalog















TipInstructor tip





Workspace tabs: Overview, Resources (data and cloud storage), Apps (JupyterLab, RStudio, SAS…), Workflows. Edit and Share are at the top right. A new workspace starts with 0 resources and 0 active policies; the policies come in when you add a data collection.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Adding a Data Collection
A new workspace has no data until you add a data collection.
Resources tab → + Data from catalog (or Add to workspace on the Exchange), then:

Select collection: All of Us Registered Tier or Controlled Tier
Select resource: e.g., the CDR version
Review policies: answer the Researcher Use Statement questions
Review selection → Add to your workspace

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Step 1: Select Collection











Pick the collection you need. Here: All of Us Controlled Tier
You add references: pointers to the existing data

No copying or data migration
The source data isn’t affected

Status column:

Perimeter required: adding it puts a security perimeter on your workspace
✅ No extra policy needed (e.g., GTEx)


Click Next








TipInstructor tip





Only collections you have access to appear here (the same list as your Data collections page). The GCP filter is on by default.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Step 2: Select Resources











The collection version (cdrv9) holds 9 resources
Choose some or all. Here: Select all resources
Two kinds of resources:

BigQuery datasets: data tables you query with SQL
Cloud Storage buckets/objects: files, e.g., genomic data


Click Next

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Step 3: Review Policies










The Controlled Tier has 6 policies, including:

App policy: only approved apps can run; other apps in the workspace are deleted
Region policy: apps and resources must stay in approved US regions
Research Use Statement: click Fill out the questions. You can’t continue until it’s complete.

⚠️ Your answers are public in the Research Hub Directory
⚠️ Policies can’t be removed once set








TipInstructor tip





The answers aren’t used to make data access decisions; they’re for transparency to participants. All of Us expects a separate workspace for each project, so the answers should be specific to this project. Scroll down in the dialog to see all 6 policies.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Answer the Research Use Statement
Adding an All of Us data collection asks you to answer the Research Use Statement questions. They’re covered step by step on their own page: Research Use Statement.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Step 3: Confirm Policies













Scroll to the bottom of Review policies:

Perimeter policy: the workspace is enrolled in a secure perimeter (can take up to 30 min); services outside it may fail
Group policy: collaborators must be in the All of Us Controlled Tier group
Data usage sharing: usage metrics go to All of Us

Check I’m sure… → Next
⚠️ These policies are permanent for this workspace








TipInstructor tip





Bucket browsing in the perimeter: previews up to 5 MB, and only .ipynb, .r, .rmd, and .sas files can be viewed. The group is P_b_aou-prod-ct, so collaborators need Controlled Tier access too.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Step 4: Review Selection











Check the list of resources: 9 from the All of Us Controlled Tier
Missing something? Go Back
Click Add to your workspace

The resources then appear in your workspace’s Resources tab. Allow up to 30 min for the perimeter enrollment to finish.

title: Setting Up a Workspace
text:
Data Collection Rules

Add it to every workspace that needs All of Us data
Policies are permanently applied to the workspace
One tier per workspace: Registered or Controlled, not both
The workspace also takes on the collection’s:

Perimeter policy
Network policy: no internet access for batch VMs and Dataproc workers

Each user still needs the matching tier access on their own account

title: Workflows
text:
Two sub-tabs:

Setup: the workflows added to this workspace. Start new jobs here.

To start: click + Add workflow

title: Workflows
text:
What Is a Workflow?
A pipeline that runs analysis steps for you, in order or in parallel, without an app running. Each step runs in its own container on a temporary cloud machine.
Use it when you need to: run the same analysis on many files or samples (e.g., genomics), or make it easy to reproduce and share








Tool
Language
Where you run it




Cromwell
WDL
Workflows tab (or an app)


Nextflow
Nextflow (.nf)
An app (in All of Us, the tab offers WDL only)


dsub
Shell commands, one step
An app’s terminal



👉 Most class projects don’t need workflows: an app is enough. Ready-made workflows: Dockstore






TipInstructor tip





Source: Verily, “Workflows overview” and “Workflow engines”. All three tools use the Google Batch API to run tasks, and read and write files in buckets (gs:// paths). Tasks run with the workspace’s service account, which can access every bucket in the workspace. Costs (task machines and storage) are billed to the workspace’s pod and are not shown in the app cost estimator.

title: Workflows
text:
Adding a Workflow
















Step 1: Provide source. Where’s the workflow file?

Workspace bucket: pick your workspace bucket. Workbench lists the workflow files it finds there, by folder (search by path).
Git repository: a repo with the workflow (see the GitHub guide). Link your GitHub account first

Select the workflow → Next
Step 2: Review details → add it
Upload the workflow file (.wdl or .nf) to your bucket first. Until there’s one to select, Next stays grey.








TipInstructor tip





The list may open on the dataproc-staging-aou-rw-… bucket (the staging bucket created for a Spark (Dataproc) app) and say “0 workflows found”: choose your workspace bucket (rw-…) in the same list. It then finds .wdl files in all its folders, grouped by folder; search by the start of the path, e.g. data/workflows/. In our All of Us workspace (November 2026) the tab listed only .wdl files: no .nf files, from a bucket or from GitHub, even main.nf next to a nextflow.config. Run Nextflow from an app. Git sources: the tab first asks you to link your GitHub account (Workbench account settings, GitHub, then install Verily’s GitHub app); choose only the repositories you need, not all. You then pick a branch or a tag; a tag keeps a class on a fixed version. The workflow’s details save the repository, file, and branch.

title: Workflows
text:
Running a Workflow
Setup tab → select the workflow → + New job

Job details: a name, and Run a single job (or a batch)
Inputs: a form, one box per input in the workflow. gs:// paths for files; plain text (no quotation marks) for strings
Outputs: check the bucket (it can default to dataproc-staging-…), and a folder named after the job
Submit job, then follow it on Job status: Starting → Running → Completed

Batch jobs: run one WDL workflow many times in parallel, e.g., once per sample

Choose Run a batch job with inputs defined by an input table
Pick a CSV in your bucket (one row per run), type which column goes with each input, and name a reference column that labels each run
Test with a single job first







TipInstructor tip





Source: Verily, “Use the Cromwell engine to run WDL workflows” and “Create batch jobs”. Cromwell call caching is on by default, so re-running reuses results from steps that already finished; deleting intermediate files is also on by default; keep both. Results go to <bucket>/<job name>/<workflow>/<job ID>/call-<task>/. Single job vs batch job: a single job runs the workflow once, with inputs typed into a form; a batch job runs it once per row of a CSV table in the bucket, all at the same time. In All of Us the tab can’t preview the table (perimeter), so you type the column name for each input, exactly as in the CSV header, plus a reference column that labels each run (e.g. chr). Job status shows a batch as one row with its number of jobs; results get one job ID folder per row. Tested November 2026: a single job on chromosome 21 took about 4 minutes; a batch of chromosomes 19 to 22 took about 11 minutes, and its chromosome 21 result matched exactly. Limits: 1,000 outstanding jobs per user and 5,000 submitted in 24 hours; for a batch, the limit applies to each job, and a batch that exceeds it is rejected entirely. Genomic Variant Store (GVS) is an example of a large WDL workflow from the Broad Institute; Verily has a guide for it.

title: Workflows
text:
A Workflow Job, Tested





The input form







Job status: finished




PLINK on chromosome 21 (a WDL from Optional Extras: Running Workflows): about 4 minutes from Submit to Completed, with the same results as PLINK in an app. No configuration file, and no app needed.






TipInstructor tip





Tested November 2026 in an All of Us workspace: a single WDL job from the workspace bucket, with the PLINK image from the All of Us mirror. The Workflows tab’s Cromwell wasn’t affected by the Cloud SDK 592 break that stops Cromwell in an app (see Running Workflows). Also tested: a batch job (chromosomes 19 to 22 from a CSV table, about 11 minutes) and the same WDL from GitHub (3 minutes 55); both matched. One job’s outputs went to the dataproc-staging bucket because the output step had picked it, and that bucket’s gs:// address (Cloud ID: dataproc-staging-wb-…) differed from its name on the page (dataproc-staging-aou-rw-…). The job’s Inputs view showed – for every value, though the job used them. The job details page shows who started it (an email): paint it out in screenshots.

title: Workflows
text:
dsub: Jobs from an App
For one-step jobs, e.g., run a command on many files. dsub is ready to use in All of Us Jupyter apps. In All of Us, every job needs the network settings, no public address, and an image from the All of Us mirror:
export DSUB_CLOUD_SDK_IMAGE=gcr.io/google.com/cloudsdktool/google-cloud-cli:591.0.0-slim
MIRROR=us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/all-of-us-rw-prod/aou-rw-gar-remote-repo-docker-prod

dsub --provider google-batch \
  --project "${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}" --user-project "${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}" \
  --regions us-central1 --use-private-address \
  --network global/networks/network \
  --subnetwork regions/us-central1/subnetworks/subnetwork \
  --service-account "$(gcloud config get-value account)" \
  --logging gs://<your-bucket>/logs/ \
  --input  BAM=gs://<your-bucket>/sample.bam \
  --output BAI=gs://<your-bucket>/sample.bam.bai \
  --image  "${MIRROR}/biocontainers/samtools:<version>" \
  --command 'samtools index ${BAM} ${BAI}' \
  --wait
👉 A full class, tested in All of Us: Running Workflows. More examples: tutorial notebook 05_How_to_use_workflow_tools (dsub, Cromwell, Nextflow)






TipInstructor tip





Source: Verily, “Run dsub jobs”, and the All of Us tutorial notebooks. Tested November 2026 in an All of Us Jupyter app (dsub 0.5.6, CDR v9). Without –use-private-address and the network settings, jobs can’t start inside the perimeter; with it, images must come from Google registries, so Docker Hub images go through the All of Us mirror. DSUB_CLOUD_SDK_IMAGE pins dsub’s helper image: Cloud SDK version 592 (3 November 2026) made every job fail with exit status 127. PET_SA_EMAIL was empty in our app; gcloud config get-value account gives the account to use. Each dsub job starts its own cloud machine, billed to your pod.
